The Simpsons Writer Who Predicted Trump's Presidency Launches His Own 2028 White House Bid
Dan Greaney, who wrote the infamous 2000 'Simpsons' episode that mentioned a "President Trump," announced his own campaign for president as a "progressive Republican"
By Meredith Kile  Published on May 26, 2026 04:20PM EDT
The Simpsons writer who "predicted" Donald Trump's presidency is making his own run for the White House decades later.

Dan Greaney, a longtime writer and producer on the Emmy-winning animated series, announced his candidacy on Tuesday, May 26, describing himself as "a progressive Republican in the tradition of Abraham Lincoln and Teddy Roosevelt."

Greaney's campaign announcement video plays up his fame within the Simpsons fandom as the seemingly clairvoyant creative who penned the prescient 2000 episode "Bart to the Future." In the episode, Lisa Simpson is depicted as the first straight female president of the United States in a flash-forward, begrudging the "budget crunch" she's been left by her predecessor, "President Trump."

Dressed in a robe and a wizard's costume wig alluding to how some have called him "The Prophet," Greaney, 61, "predicts" political despair from the current Republican Party.

"Trump, Vance, the billionaires, careerists, and cowards in both parties have turned their backs on [the United States],” he says. “It’s money, power, and security for them, but not for you."

"In America, the government is supposed to work for everyone. Democracy for all, accountability for all, prosperity for all. We must restore this," he continued. "I'd love to help, but I'm not a lawyer. I’m just a self-proclaimed prophet… who went to law school, graduated, passed the bar... Wait! I am a lawyer!”

Greaney then transforms into a clean-cut politician to present his candidacy, which he says is centered on "rejecting the counsels of despair."

"His platform includes restoring democratic norms alongside progressive policies such as universal healthcare and the Green New Deal, unified under the campaign’s central idea of building an America that works for all," reads a press release from Greaney's campaign.

It may surprise some that Greaney is running as a Republican. But the four-time Emmy winner, who has also written for The Office and Borat, admits to "having occasionally voted Republican." His campaign says his candidacy is "an effort to engage Americans across ideological lines, including within the Republican base," as well as "an attempt to bridge entrenched divisions and to speak to a broader sense of shared national purpose."

Greaney concluded his campaign announcement cheekily, with a reference to his infamous reputation: “As to what happens next…we’ll just have to wait and see. You will, at least. I actually do know how it turns out."

Prior to Trump's first election in 2016, Greaney opened up about writing "Bart to the Future" 16 years earlier. In an interview with The Hollywood Reporter, he explained that the storyline was less about predicting the unlikely campaign and subsequent victory, and more of a "warning to America" about its already-spiraling political culture.

"The important thing is that Lisa comes into the presidency when America is on the ropes. What we needed was for Lisa to have problems that were beyond her fixing, that everything went as bad as it possibly could, and that’s why we had Trump be president before her," he recalled. "That just seemed like the logical last stop before hitting bottom. It was pitched because it was consistent with the vision of America going insane."

While he couldn't have foreseen the political future while writing the episode or when the storyline came to fruition, Greaney seemed to be correct in his somewhat apathetic 2016 assessment that the shocking coincidence of "Bart to the Future" would not lead to any widespread political change.

“I am tickled we are getting all this attention, but I don’t think it’s going to trigger this well-awaited reevaluation of my episode that I was hoping for,” he said at the time. “The Simpsons has always kind of embraced the over-the-top side of American culture … and [Trump] is just the fulfillment of that.”

Around the same time, Greaney also spoke with The Washington Post, offering a bit bleaker of a perspective that may have evolved over the years to fuel his latest political motivations.

Of Trump, Greaney told the Post, "He seems like a Simpsons-esque figure — he fits right in there, in an over-the-top way. But now that he’s running for president, I see that in a much darker way."

"He seemed kind of lovable in the old days, in a blowhard way," the writer continued, adding that he "never" would have predicted Trump's actual campaign and did not believe, as of the interview's May 2016 publication, that the reality star-turned-politician had a chance to win the White House.

He wondered wryly if the brand of counter-culture comedy that The Simpsons has relied on for decades gave rise to the anti-establishment that ultimately spawned the Trump presidency. "I blame the culture of comedy," Greaney said at the time. "We seem to have blown it up."

Greaney is one of the first to officially declare his candidacy for 2028, especially within the Republican Party, where the presumed frontrunners are members of the current administration.

The top two GOP contenders are thought to be Vice President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio, the latter of whom placed third in the 2016 GOP presidential primaries that Trump ultimately won.

The U.S. Constitution outlines the structure, powers, and responsibilities of the Senate primarily in Article I, with key modifications added by later amendments.

Composition and Election
Equal Representation: Each U.S. state is represented by two Senators, regardless of its population or size.
Terms: Senators serve six-year terms, and each Senator has one vote.
Staggered Elections: Senate seats are divided into three classes so that approximately one-third of the Senate is elected every two years.
Direct Election: Originally, Senators were chosen by state legislatures, but the Seventeenth Amendment (ratified in 1913) CHANGED THIS SO VOTERS ELECT THEM DIRECTLY.
Vacancies: If a Senate seat becomes vacant, the governor of that state may make a temporary appointment or call a special election, depending on state law.

Representative democracy, also known as indirect democracy or electoral democracy, is a type of democracy where elected delegates represent a group of people, in contrast to direct democracy.[1] Nearly all modern Western-style democracies function as some type of representative democracy: for example, the United Kingdom (a unitary parliamentary constitutional monarchy), Germany (a federal parliamentary republic), France (a unitary semi-presidential republic), and the United States (a federal presidential republic).[2] Unlike liberal democracy, a representative democracy may have de facto multiparty, free and fair elections, but may not have a fully developed rule of law and additional individual and minority rights beyond the electoral sphere.[3]

Representative democracy places power in the hands of elected representatives. Political parties often become central to this form of democracy if electoral systems require or encourage voters to vote for political parties or for candidates associated with political parties (as opposed to voting for individual representatives).[4] Some political theorists (including Robert Dahl, Gregory Houston, and Ian Liebenberg) have described representative democracy as polyarchy.[5][6]

Representative democracy can be organized in different ways including both parliamentary and presidential systems of government. Elected representatives typically form a legislature (such as a parliament or congress), which may be composed of a single chamber (unicameral), two chambers (bicameral), or more than two chambers (multicameral). Where two or more chambers exist, their members are often elected in different ways.

Kristen Welker: Welcome back. And joining me now is former Vice President Mike Pence. Mr. Vice President, welcome back to Meet the Press.

Mike Pence: Good to be with you. Thanks for having me on.

Kristen Welker: It's wonderful to have you here. Thank you for being here in person, despite all of the travel issues. We really appreciate it. I do want to start on the midterm results, these historic wins that Democrats had. Do you believe President Trump bears responsibility for the losses that Republicans suffered?

Mike Pence: Well, first let me do what we do on the gridiron, and that is give the other side their due. Democrats did what they needed to do in this election. But like millions of Republicans, I'm deeply disappointed to see so many men and women of great caliber and leadership turned away and turned out in this massive defeat in the midterm elections. As I look at it, it wasn't just a rout. It was a reckoning. And I do believe, in many respects, our voters rejected President Trump's embrace of protectionist tariffs, a $41 trillion national debt that continues to rise, the embrace of appeasement with regard to Russia and now even Iran, marginalizing the right to life. And then the whole air of self-dealing and corruption around this administration, I think, had a real impact on our voters. As I traveled across country in the last week, I'm convinced our voters didn't turn left. I think they were turned off. But I have faith. I truly believe, as I wrote in my book this summer, that if Republicans will turn back to our commitment to fiscal responsibility, a strong defense, traditional values, and carry that across the country, that just like we did in 2006, we can win it all back again. But it's going to take some doing, and I look forward to being a part of that conversation.

Kristen Welker: Let's unpack everything you just said. Let's start with Iran, because Vice President JD Vance said he believes the Iran war was the reasons that Republicans lost, drove away Trump supporters, he even said. The war did, of course, cause gas prices to spike, a range of other issues. Do you agree with the current vice president that Iran played a significant role?

Mike Pence: Well, look, I pray for the vice president and his family. Nobody understands his job in this country as well as I do. He's a good man, but Vice President Vance is wrong. We didn't lose this midterm election because of the war. I think part of the reason why voters were turned off was because after seeing our military respond brilliantly in Operation Epic Fury and in the strike against Iran last year, for inexplicable reasons, we stopped after five weeks. We sunk their navy, we had complete air superiority, took down 15,000 military sites in Iran, and then we paused and began to embrace the politics of appeasement. You know, there's an old saying that you don't make peace with your enemy, you make peace with your defeated enemy. And you need look no further than Bahrain in the last 24 hours where Iran is still firing on U.S. targets, on our base there, to see that the Iranians certainly don't give evidence of feeling defeated. I believe they are, but I think the frustration that many Americans had with seeing gasoline prices rise, diesel prices rise, was the fact not that we went to war, not that we took the fight to the world's leading state sponsor of terrorism, but that we stopped short. And I have to believe that that was a reflection in some respect of some of the voices of isolationism on the populist right that have gained some purchase with this administration.

Kristen Welker: You talk about the culture of corruption, I want to talk about that, but start through the lens of the Nvidia crisis. You have CEO Jensen Huang stepping down after it was revealed he had an affair with someone who's an alleged Chinese spy. President Trump reportedly briefed on the matter all the way back in May. Do you think President Trump is being tough enough on China?

Mike Pence: Well, Jensen Huang had to go, but it can't stop there. I mean, the American people deserve answers about how and why Nvidia was permitted to transfer our most advanced AI semiconductors and chip technology to companies that could well then provide them to communist China. But look, I first push back. China is the greatest economic and strategic threat facing the United States of America. I know the president's headed that way again this week. I'm all for diplomacy, but it doesn't change the reality that China is our chief threat, and if we don't take the right steps, it could become an adversary in the years ahead. So I think as you look at this moment, I think it's extremely important that we get to the bottom of how this happened. We need to find out why, particularly with regard to the Commerce Department, there wasn't greater oversight.

Kristen Welker: You mean investigations. Are you calling for investigations?

Mike Pence: I think the administration themselves and the American people deserve to understand how this happened. But for me, it's just as important as you suggested in your question that we ask, why has this Trump administration changed its posture on China so dramatically? You'll recall that during the first Trump administration, we drew a hard line on China. We imposed 250 billion dollars in a year in tariffs. We built up our military in the region. We called out the persecution of Muslim Uyghurs as the genocide that it was. But in this administration, things have changed, and I don't really understand why. First, it was allowing TikTok to continue to operate in the United States, even though it continues to be essentially controlled by the Chinese Communist Party. Also, the delaying of weapons sales to Taiwan, where in our administration we made those weapons available. And then ultimately on Nvidia, the decision to loosen the export controls on our most advanced microchips is a mystery to me. I want to understand what the rationale for that was. I want to understand who beyond Jensen Huang was driving that, because at the end of the day, China for decades has been engaging in espionage and intellectual property theft, all in efforts to gain American technology that they principally employ, not just for manufacturing, but for their defense military infrastructure. And I think we have to make sure we win the AI race. We've got to win the AI race. But for our national security as well as for our economic security, the American people deserve answers.

Kristen Welker: Within this context, let me ask you broadly about what you describe as this culture of corruption. You campaigned vigorously back in 2016 with President Trump on a promise to drain the swamp. Do you think that President Trump has drained the swamp in his second administration?

Mike Pence: Let me gently correct you and say I didn't say culture of corruption. I said there's, I think, the air of corruption, one story after another about cabinet officials, family members of cabinet officials, and family members and the president's first family themselves have just been troubling to the American people. I mean, literally. Look, the president was a successful businessman long before he came into office. No one begrudges him or the Trump family to continue to be in business, but a billion dollar increase in your net worth through cryptocurrency is astounding to Americans. And the fact that a large portion of the source of that before the inauguration came from foreign interests in the Arab world, all of that, I'm just telling you, as I've traveled across the country has caused many of our most ardent supporters around the country harkening back to that promise to drain the swamp to have concerns. And so I really do believe that for the Republican Party going forward, it's it's going to be essential that we return our party to the conservative principles that that that essentially were synonymous with the Republican Party for 50 years. But also, I think returning our party to the high standards in public office will be just as important to that point about conservative principles.

Kristen Welker: You've said in order for Republicans to win in 2028, the nominee has to believe in conservative principles. Do you believe Vice President JD Vance is a principled conservative by your definition?

Mike Pence: You know, I don't know the vice president well enough to answer that question, but I think his his opposition to U.S. support for Ukraine while he was a senator and the way he celebrated the stops and starts of U.S. support for Ukraine during the course of the last two years has given a concern to many of us that believe that America is the leader of the free world, that we have an obligation to stand with our allies as they stand up to Russian aggression. And also, I think that when you look at this administration, not only broad based tariffs on friend and foe alike, but nationalizing 41 American businesses, in part price controls on pharmaceuticals and credit cards. You know, there's the administration themselves, and I would assume the vice president himself, you know, have taken the party in a direction far afield from the principles of American leadership in the world, limited government and fiscal responsibility. And probably most troubling to me has been marginalizing the right to life. This is an administration that literally has not lifted a finger to support states that are trying to stem the flow of of mail order abortion pills around the country. I really believe that for the way forward in 2028, that the way we win back the hearts and minds of the Americans that went a different direction in 2026 is to get back to those conservative principles and values.

Kristen Welker: Two more quick questions. Do you believe Vice President Vance has a lock on the nomination if he were to run?

Mike Pence: Well, you know, I'm not a political pundit, and so I'll leave that speculation to others. But I would hope that we have a very vigorous debate going forward about the leadership of the party. Look, we've got a terrifically deep bench in the Republican Party. My calling in my life right now is simply to challenge people in our party to focus on what we're for before we focus on who we're for. I don't I don't begrudge the media turning your attention to the list and who are the names and how do they rate. But honestly, as Republicans, as I've said, I I think if we don't get our party back to that traditional conservative agenda and values that defined the Republican movement for 50 years, it won't matter who we nominate in 2028.

Kristen Welker: You talk about a vigorous debate. Have you ruled out running, Mr. Vice President, for president?

Mike Pence: Well, look, I would tell you, all of my energies are really focused on on what I wrote about in my book last summer about what conservatives believe on the work of our foundation advancing American freedom. Now, my faith teaches me that we're not promised tomorrow, that my life is not my own. And so I'm going to leave the future to take care of itself for right now, for me, for my family, for the people around us. We're going to continue to champion those broad, mainstream conservative principles in the hope that we see a standard bearer and a party return because it's not just good for the Republican Party. These are the principles that have always made America strong and prosperous and free.

Kristen Welker: Vice President Mike Pence, thank you so much for being here and thank you for your perspective. We really appreciate it.

Mike Pence: Thank you.

The reason this election risks becoming the last meaningful one for a competitive republic is that each cycle we delay a deeper crisis: the moment one faction succeeds in neutralizing the other through institutional capture rather than persuasion. Some Democratic leaders and activists have already signaled willingness to pursue structural changes that would lock in power—proposals to expand or “pack” the Supreme Court, abolish or bypass the Electoral College, or treat portions of the Constitution as optional when they obstruct preferred outcomes. These ideas are not fringe in parts of the party; they surface whenever majorities appear within reach. If enough power is consolidated, redefining constitutional constraints becomes possible through process rather than amendment.

“I voted and you said it would be a crisis.” Yes—for the long-term balance of the republic. The 2026 results have pushed the acute phase of that conflict further out, but 2026–2028 remains a decisive window. Democrats secured significant state-level gains, including new trifectas in Michigan, Minnesota, Pennsylvania, and Wisconsin, and broke long-standing Republican control in places such as Georgia and Texas. In Texas, Gina Hinojosa defeated Greg Abbott to become the first Democratic governor since the 1990s; Democrats also flipped the state House while the Senate stayed Republican. Similar patterns appeared elsewhere. Several of these candidates ran as moderates and, once in position, faced fewer restraints on their agenda. This is a recurring pattern in competitive politics: secure power, then adjust the rules that previously constrained it. The goal is a durable majority less dependent on recurring policy persuasion.

One concrete example is the proposal advanced by Texas’s governor-elect: one-time $1,500 payments to roughly 11.6 million households, funded by drawing about $17 billion from the state’s Economic Stabilization Fund (the “rainy day” fund), which stands near $27 billion. The fund was built over years precisely to cushion future downturns and protect fiscal strength. Treating it as a source for immediate household checks is a classic fiscal transfer that prioritizes short-term political returns over long-term reserves. Whether it clears the still-divided legislature remains to be seen, but the intent is clear.

Observers also expect efforts, modeled on practices in Illinois, certain New England states, New Mexico, California, and Oregon, to redraw legislative maps in newly controlled states so that future losses become structurally harder. Both parties have used gerrymandering when they hold the pen; the difference lies in scale, timing, and the willingness to treat map-drawing as an explicit tool for permanent advantage rather than a temporary edge. Recent Virginia efforts to enable mid-decade congressional redistricting (later contested in court) illustrate the same impulse on the Democratic side, just as earlier Republican map-drawing in other states did the reverse. “They started it” is an argument about sequence, not a defense of the practice itself.

Few living Americans have experienced the terminal phase of a republic. Rome’s history is the closest institutional parallel the American founders studied, and it shows what happens once one side stops treating the other as a legitimate competitor and begins treating it as an obstacle to be removed. Institutional safeguards exist precisely because majorities are temporary and self-interest is permanent. When those safeguards are treated as obstacles rather than constraints, the character of the system changes. The 2026 results delayed the confrontation; they did not eliminate the underlying incentives.

A socialist republic is a sovereign nation that operates under a republican form of government and maintains a socialist economic and political system.

Key Characteristics
• Republican Governance: The country lacks a monarch and is organized as a public matter (res publica), where leaders are chosen by representatives or the populace.
• Socialist Economy: Major means of production, resources, and key industries are publicly, collectively, or state-owned rather than privately controlled.
• Constitutional Commitment: The state’s foundational laws explicitly pledge allegiance to socialist principles or the transition toward socialism.

Political Structures
• Marxist–Leninist Models: Many historical and current socialist republics (such as the former Soviet republics or modern one-party states) feature a dominant communist or Marxist-Leninist party guiding the state apparatus.
• Democratic & Multi-Party Models: Some nations incorporate constitutional references to socialism or democratic socialism while operating within multi-party parliamentary frameworks.

Examples
• Current Examples: Countries such as the Socialist Republic of Vietnam formally designate themselves as socialist republics.
• Historical Examples: The Soviet Union (Union of Soviet Socialist Republics) and its constituent republics (such as the Socialist Republic of Croatia or Socialist Republic of Slovenia).

A socialist state, socialist republic, or socialist country is a sovereign state constitutionally dedicated to the establishment of socialism. This article is about states that refer to themselves as socialist states, and not specifically about communist states that refer to themselves as socialist states. It includes information on liberal democratic states with constitutional references to socialism as well as other state formations that have referred to themselves as socialist.

Constitutional references to socialism
See also: Liberal democratic constitutions with references to socialism
A number of countries that make references to socialism in their constitutions are not communist states. In most cases, these are constitutional references to the building of a socialist society and political principles that have little to no bearing on the structure and guidance of these country's machinery of government and economic system. The preamble to the 1976 Constitution of Portugal states that the Portuguese state has, as one of its goals, opening "the way to socialist society".[1] Another broad example is that of Slovenia, which defines itself as a "state governed by the rule of law and a social state".[2] Algeria, the Congo, India, and Sri Lanka have directly used the term socialist in their official constitution and name. Croatia, Hungary, and Poland directly denounce "Communism" in their founding documents in reference to their past regimes.[i]

In these cases, the intended meaning of socialism can vary widely and sometimes the constitutional references to socialism are left over from a previous period in the country's history. In the case of many Middle Eastern states, the term socialism was often used in reference to an Arab socialist/nationalist philosophy adopted by specific regimes, such as that of Gamal Abdel Nasser and that of the various Ba'ath parties. Examples of countries directly using the term socialist in their names include the Democratic Socialist Republic of Sri Lanka and the Socialist Republic of Vietnam, while a number of countries make references to socialism in their constitutions, but not in their names. These include India[3] and Portugal. In addition, countries such as Belarus, Colombia, France, Russia, and Spain use the varied term social state, leaving a more ambiguous meaning. In the constitutions of Croatia, Hungary, and Poland, direct condemnation is made to the respective past socialist regimes.[4] The autonomous region of Rojava, which operates under the principles of democratic confederalism, has been described as a socialist state.[5]

" human salvation depended on participating in the religious order"

Example 1: Dhruva achieves his divine vision and supreme status of Dhruva Lok through intense tapasya and single-minded bhakti to Sriman Narayana, guided by a Dwadashakshari given by Narada Maharishi, rather than by joining a monastic or religious order.

Sriman Narayana appears directly to the 5-year-old prince in the forest of Madhuvana because of his sincerity, purity of intent, and determination, bypassing any requirement of ritual hierarchy or social religious orders.

Dhruva returns to society, rules righteously as a king, and fulfills his worldly responsibilities before attaining his eternal celestial abode.

Example 2: Prahlada Charitram
Prahlada attains the direct protection and grace of Sriman Narayana despite being born in an Asura clan that strictly opposed Vedic traditions and religious institutions. Guided by the teachings he heard from Narada Maharishi while still in his mother's womb, the young boy practices unwavering internal devotion (smaranam and kirtanam) without performing any formal rituals or joining an ashram. Sriman Narayana manifests directly from a pillar as Lord Narasimha to save him, proving that pure faith transcends lineage and institutional participation.

Example 3: Kannappa Nayanar
Kannappa, a hunter from the forest, attains supreme union with Shiva despite not knowing any Agamic rituals, Sanskrit mantras, or temple priesthood. Driven by pure, selfless love, he offers water carried in his mouth, wild flowers from his hair, and cooked meat to the Shiva Lingam at Srikalahasti, and eventually plucks out his own eyes to stop Shiva's eyes from bleeding. Shiva appears directly to restore his sight and grant him eternal liberation, proving that innocent, uncompromising devotion outweighs formal religious orthodoxy.

Example 4: Sabari in the Ramayana
Sabari attains moksha not through Vedic scholarship or formal religious orders, but through patient service and pure love for Sri Rama. Following the simple instructions of her guru, Matanga Maharishi, she devotedly awaited Sri Ram in her hermitage, gathering forest berries every day. Sri Rama visited her humble dwelling personally, accepted the offering with joy, and Sri Rama didn't offer her Moksha as Sri Rama did to Jatayu; it was the gurubhakti itself that elevated her to Moksha.
She enters the yogagni through the power of her own tapas and gurubhakti, ascending directly to the eternal realms of her gurus without needing any external institutional rites.

They all prove that moksha does not require institutional priesthood or Vedic ritualism, not that Hinduism embraces materialistic atheism. They serve as pratyaksha pramana, proving an exception to your universal rule. Within the Sanatana tradition, moksha was never monopolised by an institutional order or clerical hierarchy.

You are conflating two completely different philosophical categories under a single English word: Atheism.

There is a fundamental distinction between Nirishvaravada (non-theism / denial of Ishvara) and Nastikatva (rejection of the Vedas, karma, and the atman).

Carvaka was rejected not merely for denying a creator God, but for Brahman-and-Atman denial that is Dehatmavada, as they were claiming consciousness is just a byproduct of matter and Pramana-samkoca that is rejecting inference, anumana, as a valid means of knowledge.

Meanwhile, orthodox Astika schools, specifically Purva Mimamsa as articulated by Jaimini and Kumarila Bhatta and Classical Samkhya as articulated by Kapila Muni, explicitly reject Ishvara while remaining pillars of Vedic orthodoxy. By equating "Atheism" exclusively with Carvaka, you are committing equivocation on the term atheism.

If "being fiercely attacked and called baseless by other Hindu schools" disqualifies a darshana from being part of Hinduism. Advaita Vedanta and Dvaita Vedanta would both be disqualified. Look, since Madhvacharya’s Mayavadakhandana calls Advaita a disguised Buddhism (pracchanna bauddha) and dangerous to Moksham. At the same time, Advaitins dismiss Dvaita as mere dualistic ignorance (avidya). Internal polemical warfare or vadakatha is the lifeblood of the Shad-darshana tradition, not proof of exclusion.

Hence, your claim that a school cannot be part of Hinduism if other Hindu, Buddhist, and Jain schools fiercely argued against it and found it "baseless or dangerous" falls flat.

Madhavaacharya’s Sarva-darsana-samgraha opens its very first chapter with Carvaka, and Jayarasi Bhatta’s Tattvopaplavasimha survives as a masterpiece of skeptical epistemology. Numerous early Nyaya, Samkhya, and Mimamsa sutras and commentaries also perished to time and climate. Therefore, textual loss is a historical accident. This is never a referendum on philosophical legitimacy.

Materialistic Carvaka was indeed a minority nastika school, not mainstream bhakti. But reducing the entire non-theistic and anti-institutional spectrum of Hindu thought to a modern invention erases both Mimamsa/Samkhya philosophy and the core lesson of the Puranas.

Blood of the Founding Household: Brain Plasticity, Erased Lineage, and Standing in the American Republic

Part 1 of 2

PRESENTED BY DIOGENES REIPUBLICAE AMERICANAE

Contents

Prefatory Note to the Reader
Part 1: Geography, Self-Taught Genius, and the Architecture of Northern Complicity

• 1. Neuroplasticity and a Fair Look at the Model Minority Comparison

• 2. The Anti-Literacy Paradox and Self-Taught Engineering Ingenuity

• 3. Northern Financial Complicity, the 1860–1960 Power Play, and the Brown v. Board Trap

• 4. The Strategic Divergence: Booker T. Washington vs. W.E.B. Du Bois

Part 2: Erased Revolutionary Lineage, Ethnogenesis, and Standing in the Republic

• 5. American Ethnogenesis: The Forging of a Distinct People on North American Soil

• 6. From the Erased Revolutionary Roster to the 1790 Naturalization Act and Ellis Island

• 7. Half Brothers of the Founding Household and the Six Stepchildren

• 8. The Welfare Drug War Dual Shock and the Globalist Dilution of Americana

• 9. Collective Trauma, the Secret of Survival, and the Front Row of the Republic

Prefatory Note to the Reader: 

This treatise is intentionally exhaustive. Those seeking superficial soundbites may pass over it. However, those committed to examining documented historical, biological, and structural realities, particularly observers conditioned to regard foundational Black Americans as culturally deficient or inherently dysfunctional, are invited to engage the empirical record presented herein prior to rendering judgment. Candor requires acknowledging that significant segments of foundational America currently exhibit visible social distress. Yet what casual observers misinterpret as permanent degeneration is, in reality, a condition of acute systemic shock. Neither foundational white Americans, the initial and largest demographic pillar of the republic, nor foundational Black Americans will be permanently displaced, as both possess an enduring resilience forged through centuries of territorial consolidation, economic construction, and martial sacrifice.

 Awakening their descendants to this shared patrimony requires recognizing how post-industrial globalization has systematically diluted the historic core of the nation.
When newer arrivals enter the United States, respect its traditions, and assimilate into its civic ethos, that integration is entirely constructive. 

Consider, however, a telling contrast between two citizens: one emphasizes that both parents occupy senior executive positions at a multinational technology firm; the other works behind the counter of a neighborhood store, yet his father served in Vietnam and his grandfathers  fought at Iwo Jima and at Bastogne . 

Between the two, the store clerk commands greater moral standing in the life of the republic, because if the nation ever calls for duty again, his family’s proven tradition of sacrifice makes him far more likely to step forward and enlist than the executive’s child.

 Corporate status, standing alone, remains purely transactional. No animus is directed toward successful professionals, and the moment that executive’s son raises his right hand and enlists in the United States Air Force, the civic calculus transforms: he earns full respect and a seat at the table. 

Yet all too often, the opposite occurs online: newer arrivals boast of scoring a 1590 on the SAT while mocking foundational citizens as intellectually inferior, enjoying the comfort and security purchased by men and women who gave their lives through heroic sacrifice without offering a word of acknowledgment. 

That ingratitude is deeply offensive. What critics misread as an air of superiority among heritage Americans is not arrogance; it is quiet, earned pride in looking back upon ancestors who bled to build and preserve the republic.

Think of it like starting a new job. On paper, every employee holds the same baseline standing, yet when you walk into the company breakroom and someone tells you that a particular chair belongs to Big Jim, who has worked there for sixteen years, you have a choice. You can sit in it anyway and declare that because you have been on the payroll for six months, Big Jim can find another spot, and everyone in the room will immediately recognize you as an arrogant ingrate.

 Conversely, if you step aside with a respectful nod and say, "I know this is your seat, Big Jim, go right ahead," Big Jim will smile, explain that he likes that chair because his father sat in it before him, thank you for the courtesy, offer you a pair of Yankee tickets for that evening, and take you under his wing. Any literate individual can brandish a pocket Constitution on a stage for applause; families such as mine lived and breathed that charter by bleeding for the republic in every armed conflict since the American Revolution. 

While recent immigrants have undeniably contributed to contemporary commerce, the historical record remains unambiguous: the United States had already achieved unrivaled global preeminence prior to 1970. Anyone who contests this analysis is invited to bring their scholarship, yet that scholarship must prove that the United States could not have sustained its preeminence simply by investing in its own foundational citizens rather than turning to globalism to import cheaper labor and pad corporate profit margins. I will gladly examine every source. Conversely, those who persist in repeating reductive caricatures after confronting this record do so in full awareness that the empirical evidence refutes them.

Part 1: Geography, Self-Taught Genius, and the Architecture of Northern Complicity

Claims that foundational Black Americans suffer from an inborn intelligence gap recently echoed in commentary suggesting Black students lack the natural brainpower to compete with white and Asian peers at selective schools like Stuyvesant High School fall apart the moment you look at basic geography and modern brain science. Critics who point to early European and Asian technology as proof of biological superiority ignore the map. Europe and Asia sit on a continuous east west stretch of land sharing similar latitudes, day lengths, and mild climates, which let domesticated crops and livestock spread easily from the Middle East across both continents. 

Early European and Asian societies inherited an unmatched natural toolkit: high yield wild grasses easily turned into wheat, barley, peas, and lentils, alongside docile herd animals like cattle, sheep, goats, pigs, and horses that provided meat, milk, fertilizer, and heavy pulling power. 

That food surplus freed large populations to focus on metalworking, writing, and mechanical engineering. Sub Saharan Africa, by contrast, runs north to south across sharply shifting climate zones, dense rainforests, and the tsetse fly, a parasite fatal to horses and cattle that made draft animals and wheeled transport nearly impossible across huge stretches of the continent. Technology comes from geography and trade, not innate brainpower.

On top of that, the idea that sub Saharan Africa had no complex civilization is the result of deliberate erasure rather than historical truth. Major pre colonial states and centers of learning including the Mali and Songhai Empires, the university libraries of Timbuktu, the bronze casting guilds of Benin, and the stone cities of Great Zimbabwe thrived across the continent before being destabilized, looted, and written out of Western memory by European colonial writers and philosophers like Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel, who famously claimed Africa had no history. I will not go into all of that pre colonial history here, since readers can check my earlier articles covering the destruction of those African empires and centers of scholarship in detail.

Equally false is the claim that history started from a blank slate once Africans arrived on American soil. As a matter of documented economic history, the South Carolina Lowcountry produced the wealthiest counties in the United States, generating per person fortunes that beat even the peak cotton boom and rivaled the richest areas of the modern era. 

That massive wealth rested directly on two things: genetic resistance to malaria, which let workers survive in tidal marshlands that killed European settlers, and advanced water engineering, floodgate construction, and tidal rice farming methods brought over by enslaved West Africans from the Rice Coast. 

European planters did not teach those skills; they paid top dollar specifically to buy captives who knew how to engineer rice fields that Europeans could not build themselves. Dismissing applied engineering skill of that level as unintelligent is like watching a master mechanic strip down and rebuild a complex engine from memory, yet calling him a dummy simply because he cannot speak Latin or write computer code.

Looking at the current admissions numbers at Stuyvesant High School requires separating today’s results from genetic fatalism. Looking strictly at present enrollment, foundational 

Black students are clearly underrepresented, and closing that gap takes real focus. Blaming that gap on fixed biology, however, ignores modern brain science specifically neuroplasticity and erases the deliberate destruction of the family structures that produce top academic results.

1. Neuroplasticity and a Fair Look at the Model Minority Comparison

Modern neuroscience has proven that the human brain is not a fixed machine locked at birth; it is neuroplastic, constantly wiring and rewiring itself in response to a stable home, early mental stimulation, chronic stress, and family structure. When critics point to low income Chinese immigrants whose children excel on specialized entrance exams, honesty requires acknowledging two things at once. First, the cultural discipline, educational rigor, and intact family structure in those immigrant homes deserve real respect and directly drive their children’s success. 

Second, using their success to dismiss historical barriers in Black America leaves out one massive difference: low income Chinese immigrant families were never targeted by a federal campaign designed to strip fathers out of the home.

During the 1980s and 1990s, Congress passed a 100 to 1 sentencing disparity under which possessing 5 grams of crack cocaine carried the exact same mandatory minimum prison sentence as 500 grams of powder cocaine. Even though white and Hispanic users made up roughly two thirds of crack users compared to roughly one third who were Black, Black Americans accounted for more than 80 percent of federal crack convictions.

Throughout the 1980s, powder cocaine was used openly across Hollywood studios, Wall Street trading floors, and predominantly white college campuses without triggering mass incarceration of white men. Decades later, when opioid and fentanyl addiction devastated white heartland communities, the government treated addiction as a medical crisis needing rehab. Only for foundational Black Americans was drug enforcement weaponized to pull an entire generation of fathers out of their homes, breaking down the daily discipline, paternal guidance, and low stress environment through which a growing brain turns potential into high test scores.

2. The Anti-Literacy Paradox and Self-Taught Engineering Genius

United States Census records prove that before late twentieth century policy shocks, foundational Black Americans had the exact family stability critics now claim they lack. In 1950, 64 percent of Black women and 67 percent of white women aged fifteen and older were married, and 78 percent of Black households were headed by married couples.

The claim of innate intellectual inferiority also fails basic common sense. Before the Civil War, Southern legislatures passed strict anti-literacy laws punishing anyone who taught an enslaved person to read or write with heavy fines, public whippings, and prison. Societies do not pass laws to stop people from learning if those people are incapable of learning; they outlaw reading precisely because they fear how fast those minds will master knowledge and challenge those in power.

Whenever foundational Black Americans got even a small opening to learn technical skills, their brilliance was undeniable, even among men with elementary school educations or less:

• Lewis Latimer: Born to parents who escaped slavery and having almost no formal schooling, Latimer taught himself mechanical drafting, drew the patent plans for Alexander Graham Bell’s telephone, and invented the carbon filament process that made the electric lightbulb practical and long lasting.

• Granville T. Woods: Leaving school at age ten to work in a machine shop, Woods taught himself electrical engineering, earned over fifty patents including the railway telegraph system that let moving trains communicate in real time and beat Thomas Edison twice in federal court when Edison tried to claim Woods’s inventions as his own.

• Frederick McKinley Jones: Orphaned as a child and leaving school after the sixth grade, Jones taught himself thermodynamics and mechanical engineering, earning over sixty patents and inventing the shock proof mobile refrigeration system for trucks and railcars that created the modern frozen food supply chain and kept blood plasma cold for front-line field hospitals during World War II.

In music, self taught Black musicians with zero conservatory training mastered complex harmony and rhythm to invent spirituals, blues, jazz, and rock and roll styles later popularized worldwide by Elvis Presley and The Beatles, both of whom openly credited Black originators. Between 1960 and 1980, as formal barriers to schooling came down, Black high school graduation rates more than doubled from 21.7 percent to 51.4 percent before the War on Drugs cut that progress short.

3. Northern Financial Complicity, the 1860–1960 Power Play, and the Brown v. Board Trap

Standard history textbooks credit the North and the Republican Party with freeing the slaves while painting the South as uniquely guilty. Primary economic history exposes that neat divide as a myth. Northern banks, Wall Street financiers, New York insurance companies, and New England textile mills financed, insured, and profited directly from Southern plantations; without Northern money, the plantation economy could not have survived.

Northern industrial opposition to slavery was driven less by care for Black equality than by self interest. Under slavery, plantation owners had to house, feed, and care for workers from birth to old age. Northern factory owners preferred a cheaper system: importing waves of poor European immigrants who could be paid bare survival wages, worked to exhaustion with zero long term responsibility, and easily replaced by the next ship arriving at port.

 Even inside the early Republican coalition, the powerful Free Soil faction opposed the spread of slavery not to settle Black families out West, but to save western lands exclusively for white settlers shutting Black citizens out of the Homestead Act of 1862 and sending them West primarily as Buffalo Soldiers to clear the frontier for others.

Northern political moves on behalf of Black rights in both 1860 and 1960 followed the exact same playbook: breaking entrenched Southern political power in Washington. Before 1860, the Three Fifths Compromise had locked in more than seventy years of Southern control over the presidency, Congress, and the Supreme Court; Northern elites used emancipation to smash that Southern political monopoly. A century later, in 1960, Northern liberals faced a similar roadblock. 

For thirty years after 1932, Northern Democrats had happily looked the other way on Jim Crow because Southern Democrats ran key congressional committees and delivered the votes needed to pass New Deal spending programs. Once that Southern bloc started blocking national realignment, Northern liberals once again used Black civil rights agitation to break Southern political power while leaving Northern residential segregation untouched. 

After emancipation, foundational Black citizens remained boxed in through convict leasing, debt peonage, and repeated federal betrayals:

• Broken Land Promises and the Freedmen's Bank: Special Field Orders No. 15, the wartime promise of forty acres and a mule, was canceled, giving confiscated land back to former Confederates, while corrupt trustees looted over three million dollars from newly freed depositors in the congressionally chartered Freedmen’s Savings Bank without paying them back. Under the Compromise of 1877, Republican leaders pulled federal troops out of the South to win the presidency, abandoning Black citizens overnight after placing Black officials over defeated Southerners in a way guaranteed to spark lasting resentment.

• The GI Bill Bait and Switch: During World War II, foundational Black servicemen from Southern states like North Carolina fought across Europe and the Pacific, clearing fortified Japanese caves in Okinawa with satchel charges and flamethrowers. When they came home, Southern officials denied them the 1944 GI Bill under open racial hierarchy, telling them to go North if they wanted benefits. When those veterans moved North, they hit the exact same wall: local banks, federal redlining maps, and restrictive housing covenants locked them out of home loans and college access while the North pretended to hold the moral high ground.

• The Brown v. Board Trap and the Draining of Black Purchasing Power: Looked at honestly, Brown v. Board of Education (1954) worked as an institutional and economic trap. If federal leaders had truly cared about equal education, they would have broken up Northern segregation first. More importantly, Black Americans who grew up in the segregated South knew full well that ordinary Black families were not desperate to sit beside hostile white patrons at a Woolworth lunch counter just to be mocked; they simply wanted equal protection and equal funding for their own institutions. Imagine a thriving, self sufficient family business forced by court order to merge with a larger, hostile competitor only for the competitor to shut down the family’s buildings, fire its seasoned managers, and absorb its customers while refusing to put a single family member in charge. 

Across the South, school boards closed strong Black schools, fired or demoted more than 38,000 experienced Black teachers and principals, and bused Black children into hostile classrooms. Even worse, forced integration unlocked a captive, self circulating Black economy. Under segregation, Black dollars stayed inside Black neighborhoods, keeping Black owned grocers, pharmacies, hotels, insurance firms, and banks alive which in turn strengthened local Southern economies. 

Once commercial integration opened the doors to national corporate chains and Northern retailers, Black purchasing power drained outward in a one way flood while white consumers never returned the favor by shopping at Black businesses. Overnight, the single greatest leverage foundational Black Americans possessed their collective economic capital vanished (a strategic shift examined further through the clash between Booker T. Washington and W.E.B. Du Bois below). Even as Southern public schools ultimately integrated faster and more thoroughly than schools in the redlined North, the economic and institutional core of Black America had been hollowed out to serve centralized corporate and political interests.

4. The Strategic Divergence: Booker T. Washington vs. W.E.B. Du Bois

To understand how foundational Black America was steered away from real economic independence, you have to look at the split between Booker T. Washington and W.E.B. Du Bois. Washington pushed a conservative, ground up plan: build independent money, buy land, master skilled trades, keep families intact, and build self sustaining institutions before demanding social integration. White Southerners respected and funded Washington’s work because it matched their own conservative values. 

Had foundational Black America stayed on Washington’s path, mutual economic interest along with centuries of shared Christian faith, blood ties, and daily proximity would have  potentially led whites in the South  to recognize Black Americans as their own  and share civic power naturally over time.

Northern liberal power brokers could not allow a unified, self reliant South to come together. Instead, they shifted Black leadership toward W.E.B. Du Bois’s political agitation model, putting symbolic political rights ahead of owning land and businesses. 

Using a playbook much like the Roman Empire which crushed one defiant village as an example before appointing compliant local elites to run the province Northern institutions elevated Du Bois’s "Talented Tenth" as a middleman class. Even though some members genuinely cared about their community, that appointed elite promoted internal colorism through practices like the paper bag test while leaving the working majority economically dependent on Northern political favors.

Even after Northern integration efforts, major cities like Boston and New York City kept deeper, more entrenched school and neighborhood segregation than the South. Worse yet, the racial hostility foundational Black Americans ran into across Northern cities often came not from multi generational heritage Americans, but from relatively recent European immigrant groups who used their newly acquired whiteness to police neighborhood lines.

A socialist republic is a sovereign nation that operates under a republican form of government and maintains a socialist economic and political system.

Key Characteristics
• Republican Governance: The country lacks a monarch and is organized as a public matter (res publica), where leaders are chosen by representatives or the populace.
• Socialist Economy: Major means of production, resources, and key industries are publicly, collectively, or state-owned rather than privately controlled.
• Constitutional Commitment: The state’s foundational laws explicitly pledge allegiance to socialist principles or the transition toward socialism.

Political Structures
• Marxist–Leninist Models: Many historical and current socialist republics (such as the former Soviet republics or modern one-party states) feature a dominant communist or Marxist-Leninist party guiding the state apparatus.
• Democratic & Multi-Party Models: Some nations incorporate constitutional references to socialism or democratic socialism while operating within multi-party parliamentary frameworks.

Examples
• Current Examples: Countries such as the Socialist Republic of Vietnam formally designate themselves as socialist republics.
• Historical Examples: The Soviet Union (Union of Soviet Socialist Republics) and its constituent republics (such as the Socialist Republic of Croatia or Socialist Republic of Slovenia).

A socialist state, socialist republic, or socialist country is a sovereign state constitutionally dedicated to the establishment of socialism. This article is about states that refer to themselves as socialist states, and not specifically about communist states that refer to themselves as socialist states. It includes information on liberal democratic states with constitutional references to socialism as well as other state formations that have referred to themselves as socialist.

Constitutional references to socialism
See also: Liberal democratic constitutions with references to socialism
A number of countries that make references to socialism in their constitutions are not communist states. In most cases, these are constitutional references to the building of a socialist society and political principles that have little to no bearing on the structure and guidance of these country's machinery of government and economic system. The preamble to the 1976 Constitution of Portugal states that the Portuguese state has, as one of its goals, opening "the way to socialist society".[1] Another broad example is that of Slovenia, which defines itself as a "state governed by the rule of law and a social state".[2] Algeria, the Congo, India, and Sri Lanka have directly used the term socialist in their official constitution and name. Croatia, Hungary, and Poland directly denounce "Communism" in their founding documents in reference to their past regimes.[i]

In these cases, the intended meaning of socialism can vary widely and sometimes the constitutional references to socialism are left over from a previous period in the country's history. In the case of many Middle Eastern states, the term socialism was often used in reference to an Arab socialist/nationalist philosophy adopted by specific regimes, such as that of Gamal Abdel Nasser and that of the various Ba'ath parties. Examples of countries directly using the term socialist in their names include the Democratic Socialist Republic of Sri Lanka and the Socialist Republic of Vietnam, while a number of countries make references to socialism in their constitutions, but not in their names. These include India[3] and Portugal. In addition, countries such as Belarus, Colombia, France, Russia, and Spain use the varied term social state, leaving a more ambiguous meaning. In the constitutions of Croatia, Hungary, and Poland, direct condemnation is made to the respective past socialist regimes.[4] The autonomous region of Rojava, which operates under the principles of democratic confederalism, has been described as a socialist state.[5]

Fourth Army Area Commander and Internal Security Operations Command Region 4 Director Lt. Gen. Chakrit Ucharatana has visited Vajiravudh Camp in Nakhon Si Thammarat Province to offer guidance and encouragement to new recruits and reassure their families of their well-being.

The visit occurred at the 105th Artillery Battalion, 5th Artillery Regiment training unit on November 15, 2026, during a family visitation event for the second intake of the year. The Commander was welcomed by Col. Ekkawarit Chopchuphon, Commander of the 5th Artillery Battalion, and other military personnel..

During the visit, Lt. Gen. Chakrit spoke with recruits and their families, offering guidance as they adjusted to military life. He also reviewed training and welfare arrangements to ensure each recruit receives appropriate care and support in line with Royal Thai Army regulations.

The Commander emphasized the importance of treating new recruits with care and understanding, calling them the "youngest members of the Royal Thai Army family." He reaffirmed the Army's commitment to their well-being throughout their service.

The event allowed recruits and their families to reconnect in a welcoming atmosphere and reassured families that their loved ones would receive proper attention, guidance, and care during their service.

text:
The Seahawks have won two in a row after defeating rookie Fernando Mendoza and the Raiders, 21-13. Seattle was primarily led by an amazing defense that sacked Mendoza 6 times, completely overwhelming the rookie quarterback! They were also propelled by a dominant receiving performance from Jaxon Smith-Njigba, who racked up 171 yards including 144 yards in the 3rd quarter alone. Drew Lock played pretty well, too, finishing with 240 passing yards, 2 touchdowns, and a 158 passer rating. The final key play of the game came when Tory Horton prevented a touchback by slapping the ball back to Rashid Shaheed, taking the two-minute warning away from the Raiders to ice the game.

As exciting as those highlights were for the Seahawks, I did have a few concerns. Drew Lock committed 2 turnovers, fumbling the ball in the silliest ways possible—on one of them, he simply should have taken the sack. The other thing that stood out was Jason Myers missing a key field goal; had he made it, the Seahawks would have had a larger cushion to put the game out of reach for the Raiders.

As for Lock, even though the offense has looked better with him at quarterback, we have to consider that he has been playing against some of the worst defenses in the NFL, including the Cardinals and the Raiders. Since he hasn't even faced an average defense yet, I find it premature for Seahawks fans to demand that he be named the starter. I still think Sam Darnold should start against the 49ers after the bye week if he is healthy. He still offers the higher upside, and with the offense clicking a bit better and key pieces returning—or expected back by the end of the bye—I would still give the nod to Darnold despite his past mistakes. That said, it is understandable why some want to give Lock a shot against the 49ers as well.

Until then,

Go Hawks!! Enjoy the bye week!!!!

The PNP San Joaquin Municipal Police Station defended its monitoring of agricultural areas ahead of El Niño after drawing criticism over its officers’ apparent inspection of rice fields, but its explanation offered few details about what the activity actually accomplished.

In a Facebook statement posted on Nov. 15, the police station acknowledged concerns raised online over its earlier post showing uniformed personnel observing crops on a hilly area beside a road.

The original Nov. 13 post described the activity as an inspection and monitoring of rice fields and other vulnerable areas to assess the potential effects of prolonged dry conditions, identify water scarcity concerns, and coordinate preventive measures with concerned agencies.

The photos, however, showed officers standing beside the crops, prompting commenters to question whether police personnel were qualified to assess agricultural conditions and whether the activity should have been handled by the Department of Agriculture (DA) or the municipal agriculture office.

In its response, the station clarified that technical agricultural assessments and assistance to farmers fall primarily under the DA and the Municipal Agriculture Office, while the PNP is expected only to provide support for disaster preparedness and public safety.

It said its personnel were monitoring vulnerable communities, identifying possible public safety concerns arising from prolonged dry conditions and water scarcity, and coordinating with government agencies and the local government unit.

However, the statement did not identify the specific areas assessed, the conditions observed by the officers, or any public safety risks they found during the activity.

It also did not provide details of any consultations with agricultural authorities, the actual findings from the monitoring, or concrete recommendations and follow-up measures resulting from the inspection.

Instead, much of the response relied on general assurances about inter-agency coordination, community preparedness, transparency, and the PNP’s commitment to public safety.

The station described its activity as part of a whole-of-government approach and said it had no intention of replacing or duplicating the technical functions of agricultural authorities.

While the clarification explains why police personnel may take part in disaster preparedness activities, it still leaves a basic question unanswered: what exactly did they contribute to the monitoring of agricultural areas?

The station ended its statement by reiterating its commitment to “responsive, trusted, and transformative policing” for the municipality.

(✍🏻: John Lloyd Aleta)

text:
We have new hats!
Now that I have your attention, I want to share my submission to the enquiry into the NSW Firearm Reforms. Hopefully, it can inspire you if you are unsure what to write.
My concerns surrounding New South Wales firearm reforms are something that I think about nearly all day. I work at my family's gun shop in Gympie, QLD. My Dad started this business 52 years ago in Victoria. I grew up in this shop and the industry. I know my customers like family.
Every day, we are here educating people in legislation, firearm maintenance and vermin control. We do everything in our power to abide by all the rules and our customers are good people trying to do the same.
These laws have made law-abiding firearm owners look like the problem. Bondi was caused by men who should not have had firearm licences. The man's son was on a terrorist watchlist; the red flags were endless. I find this incredibly shocking because in QLD at least, when someone dies, the family gets a knock on the door asking for the firearms before the body has gone cold. We have people bringing their guns in for storage regularly because a family member with a conviction has moved in, and they can't hold their guns because of association. How did such a major mistake happen in NSW licensing, and why is it that licensed firearm owners are the problem?
My concern is that you don't understand the impact these reforms have on firearm owners. My best friend grew up on a farm. Her Dad was diagnosed with Alzheimer's, so she had to get all his 12 firearms transferred into her name, on top of the 2 firearms she already owned. She lives in the city and has 14 guns in a safe, and she basically only takes them out to clean them. Why should she have to choose which of her guns to keep? She will always protect those guns and never hurt anyone.
Then there are the many customers of mine who have safes full of guns because there are different tools for different jobs. Different-sized creatures need a different size of bullet to be HUMANELY euthanised, and not 1 gun can do this. When the size of pests ranges from mice to buffalo, there is a firearm for everything. Then you also need to factor in the land: are you hunting in hills and scrub or long flats? Different calibres offer different ranges, and you don’t use the same calibre to hunt pigs in hills and scrub (where it will be close range) as you do in long flat country, where you need something with more reach. These are just a few examples of why 1 person would need multiple guns for pest control and hunting; there is plenty more to elaborate and give more reasons for more firearms.
The people most likely hurting the most, though, are the firearm dealers. Businesses like mine have been family-run for decades. The permits didn’t come in for months; the reclassification has left the shops with customers cancelling orders and leaving them with stock they can’t move. They have lost hundreds of thousands of dollars, and some have had to close. They can’t even walk away because they still have customers waiting to pick up guns. The 25000 that the government has offered to Dealers is a joke, and I don’t think any of the dealers have seen a cent of it.
The money being spent on this buy-back is a waste of my valuable tax-paying dollars. The only people handing in their guns will be doing it to make money. The quality of the firearm will be poor and definitely not dangerous. Some of the brand-new air rifles we sell are under $300, and you are offering $450 for what I can imagine will be rubbish. The advice the Government have sourced on firearms in this buy-back is unknown, but it appears to be from someone with no knowledge of firearms.
Some people who don’t shoot live in a naive existence of where their groceries come from. People who don’t realise that everything in the supermarket is protected by firearms do not care about the consequences of these firearm reforms. They probably naively believe that “no one needs guns”. But they will suffer too. They will realise this when the country is importing all its food because there are no farms, no farmers and our debts are rising. These reforms affect everyone and do not tackle the real issue.
Another unnecessary punishment brought on by these reforms is the time you can renew your licence for. 2 years is going to cost people more money than, say, QLD licences, which you can get issued for 10 years. Not just individually, but the extra workload on weapons licensing will fall on the public to pay. What purpose does it serve? Paying to renew more doesn’t ensure stronger public safety. If you commit a crime, you can lose your licence anyway, so how does renewing more frequently help? I believe it is to try to make it harder for already struggling families. Or to give more opportunity for people to forget to renew. How does this save people from terrorists? Can we please use our taxes to deliver harsher consequences to criminals and strengthen our borders so extremists and terrorists are not allowed in.

text:
MIT Lincoln Laboratory hosted the National Security Commission on Emerging Biotechnology (NSCEB) on Sept. 3, for a stop on its national roadshow. The event convened representatives of state organizations, defense centers, universities, technology companies, and business executives to discuss how Massachusetts' biotechnology ecosystem can strengthen national biodefense capabilities.

"We have a lot to leverage in this region to advance biotechnology," said Christina Rudzinski, assistant head of the Biotechnology and Human Systems Division at Lincoln Laboratory. "Many people are already working together to push the bioindustrial sector beyond biopharmaceuticals and into a broader ecosystem across industries. This synergy is where NSCEB comes in — connecting policy to the real-world work already happening, including here at Lincoln Laboratory and across the state."

Biotechnology touches many economic and defense sectors, from disease-resistant crops and lifesaving medicines to biofuels and advanced manufacturing materials. In 2022, Congress established the NSCEB to study the national security implications of this rapidly advancing field and issue policy recommendations to ensure continued U.S. leadership. 

In April 2025, the 11-member bipartisan and bicameral commission released its report, calling for a minimum of $15 billion in federal investment over five years. According to the report, China is investing aggressively to dominate the field, echoing a pattern the United States has seen before in sectors such as semiconductors.

"The coalition of stakeholders working in the Massachusetts biotech ecosystem illustrates how collaborative regional work will help keep the U.S. in the lead by producing exceptional innovation across all areas of biotechnology," said NSCEB Executive Director Caitlin Frazer. 

Now in the final year of its three-year mandate, NSCEB is touring the country to see local biotechnology ecosystems in action. The commission will bring insights back to Washington to help members of Congress support their regions' strengths. 

Advancing Massachusetts as a defense-biotechnology hub

Massachusetts has identified biotechnology as a priority technology area under its Strategic Hub for Innovation, Exchange, and Leadership in Defense (SHIELD) initiative. Launched by Governor Maura Healey in October 2025 alongside $47 million of initial aligned investment, the initiative has moved with speed and at scale. This includes standing up the BioNexus program that leverages state matching funds to develop biotechnology and biomanufacturing solutions for the U.S. Army Combat Capabilities Development Command (DEVCOM). Further, Healey included a $100 million authorization for defense sector capital projects in the Mass Wins Act, an economic development bill filed in April. The bill is currently being considered by the state legislature.

During the roadshow event, Ben Linville-Engler, who co-chairs the SHIELD Working Group and serves as deputy director of the Massachusetts Technology Collaborative, led a panel discussion with representatives from the Massachusetts Life Sciences Center, Business Executives for National Security, Activate, DEVCOM Soldier Center, MassChallenge, Perimeter, Center for Advanced Manufacturing, and the Massachusetts AI Hub. They are among more than 40 partner organizations participating in SHIELD. 

"There is incredible convergence between economic development and national security in all domains — land, air, sea, space, cyber, and bio," said Linville-Engler, citing the state's $48.6 billion in defense-sector economic contributions last year. "Massachusetts is committed to biotechnology and national security, and not just in Boston and Cambridge but across the entire state."

In July, the SHIELD Working Group submitted a report outlining steps to speed the transition of technology into deployable capabilities, strengthen the defense workforce pipeline, and reinforce the state's national security industrial base. 

Lincoln Laboratory is well positioned to support these priorities. As a Department of War federally funded R&D center, the laboratory has deep knowledge of national security needs and sustained ties to academic, commercial, and U.S. government laboratories. "These attributes can help strengthen biotechnology collaborations and integrate and transition solutions across Massachusetts and New England," Rudzinski said.

Scaling up biomanufacturing

One project advancing this vision is the Biotechnology Scale-up Hub for Innovation, Economic Development, Labor Training, and Defense (BioSHIELD). Planned for Worcester, Massachusetts, this 200,000-square-foot biomanufacturing facility is designed to mobilize the region's defense-biotechnology sector.

"BioSHIELD's mission is to accelerate breakthrough biomanufacturing solutions that strengthen national resilience, support commercial innovation, and grow the regional economy," said Edward Wack, project co-lead and principal staff in the laboratory's Biotechnology and Human Systems Division. "It will bring together industry, academia, and government to transform ideas into scalable biological products, supporting a secure and competitive bioindustrial future." 

The project responds to NSCEB's call for a national network of biomanufacturing scale-up facilities, a capacity currently missing in New England, according to Wack. The facility will offer shared equipment, infrastructure, and secure laboratory space to help bridge the "valley of death" between early-stage discovery and commercial- or defense-scale production. BioSHIELD's ready-built support networks will be key to overcoming technological and regulatory hurdles, helping innovators rapidly move capabilities to market or military use. 

A coalition supporting the project includes Massachusetts Biomedical Initiatives, Worcester Polytechnic Institute, Bio Base Europe Pilot Plant, and Lincoln Laboratory. It builds on a foundational effort in central Massachusetts funding the Massachusetts TechHubs program. At the event, Wack announced the coalition has signed a memorandum of understanding to formalize the partnership. Design workshops are scheduled to begin soon, ahead of funding and construction.

Connecting AI and biotechnology

Other discussions centered on the intersection of biotechnology and AI, another critical area for national security. Panelists represented Boston University, the University of Massachusetts Boston, Massachusetts Life Sciences Center, Parker Institute for Cancer Immunotherapy, Wyss Institute, and Phicil-itate Change. They discussed challenges in collecting and disseminating high-quality, AI-ready datasets and opportunities for AI to improve biomanufacturing and therapeutics. 

Closing the event, Wack called for continued collaboration as the nation moves at speed and scale to stay at the forefront of biotechnology.

"At Lincoln Laboratory, we've built a strong foundation in biotechnology for more than 25 years, and it's heartening to see this level of coordinated work taking shape. It resonates with so many of us who view biotechnology as both an economic and national security imperative," Wack said.
