text:
Muawiya and his followers are going to hell according to the Prophet of Allah. 

The prophet drew a great divider between heaven and hell using Ammar Ibn Yassir (RA). In the famous Sahih hadith in Bukhari and Muslim, the prophet said that Ammar (RA) will be killed by a rebellious group. Ammar, who is a Shia of Ali (AS), will call Muawiya and his group to obey Allah and invite them to Paradise by joining Imam Ali (AS) and his Shia. 

Muawiya's group had no interest in becoming Ali's Shia. Muawiya wanted to become ruler and make his children and their children kings over the people. Muawiya rejected Ammar's offer and invited Ammar to their side to fight Imam Ali (AS) and his Shia, essentially inviting Ammar to join them in hell. 

"...The Prophet (ﷺ) passed by `Ammar and removed the dust off his head and said, "May Allah be merciful to `Ammar. He will be killed by a rebellious aggressive group. `Ammar will invite them to (obey) Allah and they will invite him to the (Hell) fire."

Sahih al-Bukhari, Book of Jihad, Hadith 2812

Classical Sunni scholars and historians have criticized Mu’awiya’s actions, particularly his rebellion against Imam Ali (AS), his role in the killing of Ammar ibn Yasir (RA), and his establishment of hereditary rule through Yazid.

1. Imam al-Nawawi (d. 676 AH) – Commentary on the Hadith of Ammar
 • In his commentary on Sahih Muslim, Imam al-Nawawi affirms that Mu’awiya’s army was the rebellious group mentioned in the hadith:

 “This hadith is one of the clear miracles of the Prophet (ﷺ), as Ammar was killed by Mu’awiya’s group. The scholars said: This hadith is among the greatest proofs against Mu’awiya and his followers.”
(Sharh Sahih Muslim, vol. 18, p. 38)

2. Imam Ibn Hajar al-Asqalani (d. 852 AH) – Commentary on Sahih al-Bukhari
 • In Fath al-Bari, he confirms that Mu’awiya’s side was rebellious and unjust:

 “The saying of the Prophet (ﷺ) that a rebellious group will kill Ammar is a clear evidence that Ali was in the right and that Mu’awiya was wrong.”
(Fath al-Bari, vol. 13, p. 35-36)

3. Imam Fakhr al-Din al-Razi (d. 606 AH) – Tafsir of Qur’an 49:9
 • Qur’an 49:9 commands fighting against the rebellious group until they submit to justice.
 • Imam Razi applies this verse to Mu’awiya’s rebellion:

 “There is consensus that Ali (AS) was the Imam, and Mu’awiya and his party were the rebellious ones.”
(Tafsir al-Kabir, vol. 26, p. 141-142)

4. Al-Zamakhshari (d. 538 AH) – Tafsir of Qur’an 28:15 (On Mu’awiya’s Tyranny)
 • While explaining Qur’an 28:15 (about a tyrant harming believers), al-Zamakhshari links it to Mu’awiya’s killing of righteous people:

 “Mu’awiya and his party are included in this, for they killed Ammar, a righteous believer.”
(Tafsir al-Kashshaf, vol. 3, p. 233)

5. Ibn Abi’l-Hadid (d. 656 AH) – Commentary on Nahjul Balagha
 • Ibn Abi’l-Hadid, a Sunni Mu’tazili scholar, acknowledges that Mu’awiya was not on the path of truth:

 “There is no doubt that Mu’awiya sought the world, not the hereafter. His rebellion against Ali was not for religion but for power.”
(Sharh Nahjul Balagha, vol. 1, p. 338)

6. Imam al-Dhahabi (d. 748 AH) – Criticism of Mu’awiya’s Rule
 • Although al-Dhahabi generally tries to maintain a neutral stance, he admits that Mu’awiya introduced monarchy and favored oppression:

 “Mu’awiya, during his rule, committed acts contrary to justice. He appointed Yazid, a known wrongdoer, as his successor, which was a grave mistake.”
(Tarikh al-Islam, vol. 2, p. 330-331)

7. Imam Ahmad ibn Hanbal (d. 241 AH) – Rejecting Mu’awiya’s Virtue
 • When Imam Ahmad was asked about hadiths praising Mu’awiya, he replied:

 “What virtue does he have? He fought against Ali, and he is not equal to Ali in any way.”
(Al-Tamheed by Ibn Abd al-Barr, vol. 20, p. 252)

8. Al-Suyuti (d. 911 AH) – Mu’awiya’s Innovations
 • Al-Suyuti in Tarikh al-Khulafa notes:

 “Mu’awiya was the first to introduce monarchy into Islam.”
(Tarikh al-Khulafa, p. 104-105)

Summary:

 • Sunni scholars do not explicitly call Mu’awiya a kāfir, but they confirm he was rebellious (bāghi), sought power over religion, and opposed Imam Ali (AS).

 • The killing of Ammar (RA) was a clear prophetic proof against Mu’awiya.

 • Mu’awiya’s introduction of monarchy and appointment of Yazid were heavily criticized.

 • Imam Ahmad ibn Hanbal denied any virtue for Mu’awiya in comparison to Imam Ali (AS).

The Royal Navy faces questions over whether its three fleet solid support ships will be built with British steel, as Liberty Steel Dalzell in Motherwell, which holds an order for 34,000 tonnes of plate for the £1.6bn Navantia programme in Belfast, has struggled to pay bills and workers. Dalzell is the only UK mill able to make the plate; the government said it was closely monitoring the situation, and the first ship is planned for delivery in 2031.

Walkouts had been due on 16, 17 and 19 November.

UK Defence Journal

A modified Malloy T-150 drone firing BAE Systems' APKWS rockets intercepted several one-way attack drones in succession, without landing or reloading, during a US experiment at Eglin Air Force Base. text:
🚨 PREAKNESS PUSHED ASIDE AGAIN AS MARYLAND FACES A $600 MILLION GAMBLE ON HORSE RACING

The Kentucky Derby and Belmont Stakes are moving forward with a lucrative new Thoroughbred Championship Series, leaving Baltimore’s Preakness Stakes out of the six-race competition.

Now Churchill Downs and the New York Racing Association are establishing separate nominations, further dismantling the 40-year system that allowed horses to enter all three Triple Crown races through one nomination.

Bill Finley of Thoroughbred Daily News argues the changes threaten the Preakness’s national relevance and could effectively destroy the traditional Triple Crown.

Maryland has already made an enormous financial commitment:

▪️ $85 MILLION to acquire the Preakness intellectual property rights.

▪️ $500–$565 MILLION in estimated redevelopment and acquisition costs involving Pimlico and Laurel Park.

▪️ $600 MILLION+ in combined commitments to rebuild Maryland racing.

Gov. Wes Moore’s administration has moved the 2027 Preakness to Sunday, May 23, providing 22 days after the Kentucky Derby instead of 14.

But Finley argues that won’t be enough to attract top Derby contenders.

His proposed solution? Move the race four weeks after the Derby and increase the Preakness purse from $2 million to $10 million, with state subsidies covering the expense.

That would mean asking Maryland taxpayers to contribute even more money to a sport already receiving extraordinary public investment.

Meanwhile, Churchill Downs and NYRA are positioning their own races within a new championship structure.

The question for Annapolis isn’t simply whether Maryland can preserve the Preakness name.

It’s whether hundreds of millions in public investment can sustain the race’s prestige and economic value when the sport’s other major operators are moving in a different direction.

Should Maryland taxpayers finance a $10 million purse to compete, or should Churchill Downs and NYRA be pressed to negotiate a championship structure that includes all three historic races?

⠀
A roughly $4.2 BILLION cryptocurrency.

More than 95% of its maximum supply already circulating.

A network designed for inexpensive payments.
⠀

But here's the contradiction.
⠀
Low fees make Bitcoin Cash attractive to use.
⠀
They also leave miners heavily dependent on block subsidies rather than transaction revenue.
⠀
Is bitcoin-cash:native an overlooked investment in scarce digital cash?
⠀
Or does inexpensive settlement struggle to create enough lasting monetary demand?
⠀
Let's examine the numbers.

01 | WHAT IS BITCOIN CASH?
⠀
Bitcoin Cash is a separate cryptocurrency that emerged from Bitcoin's 2017 chain split.
⠀
Its focus is peer-to-peer electronic cash.

⠀
Its potential uses include:

• Payments
• Remittances
• Merchant transactions
• Self-custody savings
• Native token applications

The investment thesis combines monetary scarcity with practical transfer utility.

But having a fixed supply and a functioning payment network does not automatically create investment demand.

People must choose to acquire and retain BCH.

All-Time High: ~$3,785.82
Decline From ATH: ~94.5%.
⠀
The displayed FDV uses the provider's current supply figure.
⠀
Using the full 21 million maximum instead produces approximately $4.38 billion.
⠀
NETWORK FUNDAMENTALS:
⠀
Tracked DeFi TVL: ~$4.59M
Daily Chain Fees: ~$85
Daily Transactions: ~15,722
Daily Active Addresses: ~25,903.
⠀
Addresses are not unique people.
⠀
Transactions are not automatically merchant payments.
⠀
03 | THE DIGITAL CASH OPPORTUNITY
⠀
Bitcoin Cash's opportunity is straightforward:
⠀
Let people transfer value without depending on a central payment operator.
⠀
But a useful payment system needs more than low blockchain fees.
⠀
Users need convenient wallets.
⠀
Merchants need usable conversion options.
⠀
Recipients need liquidity.
⠀
And customers need a reason to choose BCH over alternatives.
⠀
Stablecoins offer more predictable purchasing power.
⠀
Conventional payment services offer familiar consumer experiences.
⠀
BCH must compete on the complete payment experience.
⠀
A cheap transaction is useful.
⠀
A reliable, repeatable financial workflow is more valuable.
⠀
04 | THE SCALING APPROACH
⠀
Bitcoin Cash emphasizes base-layer transaction capacity.
⠀
Its Adaptive Blocksize Limit Algorithm adjusts the block-size limit according to network conditions and historical usage.
⠀
The mechanism entered the protocol through the May 2024 upgrade.
⠀
This supports the goal of accommodating growth without depending solely on scarce blockspace.
⠀
However, capacity and demand are different.
⠀
A network can have substantial available capacity while processing relatively little paid activity.
⠀
More capacity also places requirements on infrastructure as usage grows.
⠀
The investment question is whether practical adoption expands enough to justify continued development and security expenditure.
⠀
05 | THE BCH VALUE-CAPTURE MODEL
⠀
BCH is the asset transferred across its network.
⠀
Users also pay transaction fees in BCH.
⠀
However, miners receive those fees.
⠀
Simply holding BCH does not provide a proportional claim on transaction income.
⠀
The primary investment argument is therefore monetary:
⠀
More people may want BCH for payments, savings, or liquidity.
⠀
But fast turnover can support substantial payment volume with relatively small retained balances.
⠀
A merchant can receive BCH and immediately sell it.
⠀
A customer can acquire BCH shortly before spending it.
⠀
Payment adoption becomes a stronger investment signal when users also choose to maintain balances.
⠀
06 | THE ISSUANCE QUESTION
⠀
Bitcoin Cash's subsidy halves every 210,000 blocks.
⠀
Under its current schedule, the block subsidy is 3.125 BCH.
⠀
At an approximately ten-minute target interval:
⠀
Daily Issuance: ~450 BCH
Annual Issuance: ~164,250 BCH
Annual Supply Growth: ~0.82% against current circulating supply.
⠀
Actual issuance depends on realized block production.
⠀
At $208.38, target annual issuance has a market value of approximately $34.2 million.
⠀
That is not a prediction of miner selling.
⠀
It illustrates the additional supply the market may need to absorb.
⠀
A low inflation rate is helpful.
⠀
It does not guarantee sufficient demand.
⠀
07 | THE SECURITY-BUDGET CHALLENGE
⠀
At the snapshot price, target daily block subsidies are worth approximately $93,800.
⠀
Reported daily transaction fees are approximately $85.
⠀
These illustrative figures imply that fees represent less than 0.1% of combined subsidy-and-fee compensation.
⠀
The comparison uses target block production and a single day's fee observation.
⠀
It is not a complete miner-profitability analysis.
⠀
Nevertheless, it highlights the long-term issue.
⠀
Future halvings reduce subsidy per block.
⠀
Security economics must adjust through price, activity, mining costs, or other market changes.
⠀
Low fees benefit users.
⠀
They also require substantial transaction growth to become a meaningful replacement for declining subsidies.
⠀
08 | THE HASHRATE QUESTION
⠀
Using SHA-256 does not give BCH access to Bitcoin's security budget automatically.
⠀
Mining participation depends on the incentives miners receive from securing each network.
⠀
Investors should examine:
⠀
• Sustained hashrate
• Mining-pool concentration
• Changes in mining profitability
• Reorganization risk
• Confirmation policies
⠀
The relevant issue is not whether a specific attack is imminent.
⠀
It is how expensive the network makes sustained interference.
⠀
Fast transaction detection should also be distinguished from confirmed settlement.
⠀
Merchants and exchanges can require different confirmation thresholds depending on transaction size and risk.
⠀
09 | THE DEVELOPMENT AND UPGRADE QUESTION
⠀
Bitcoin Cash's May 2026 upgrade added scripting capabilities including bounded loops, functions, and Pay-to-Script.
⠀
These changes expand what developers can build.
⠀
Separately, BCHN maintainers announced on November 14 that they would implement the Faster Blocks proposal for intended mainnet activation on May 15, 2027.
⠀
Their announcement acknowledges controversy and significant ecosystem upgrade requirements.
⠀
That is a future implementation commitment.
⠀
It should not be described as a faster block interval already operating today.
⠀
Upgrades create possibilities.
⠀
Applications, adoption, and successful deployment determine their practical value.
⠀
10 | THE VALUATION QUESTION
⠀
Using approximately 20.117 million circulating BCH:
⠀
$500 implies ~$10.06B market capitalization.
⠀
$1,000 implies ~$20.12B.
⠀
$2,000 implies ~$40.23B.
⠀
$3,000 implies ~$60.35B.
⠀
Using the full 21 million maximum:
⠀
$1,000 implies $21B.
⠀
$2,000 implies $42B.
⠀
$3,000 implies $63B.
⠀
These are valuation illustrations, not price targets.
⠀
A fee multiple alone cannot adequately value a monetary asset.
⠀
Equally, scarcity alone cannot establish its value.
⠀
Many assets are scarce.
⠀
The premium depends on how strongly people want to hold this particular one.
⠀
A large decline from the historical peak does not answer that question.
⠀
11 | THE BULL AND BEAR CASE
⠀
THE BULL CASE:
⠀
Payments attract repeat users.
⠀
Wallet and merchant infrastructure improves.
⠀
Native applications create additional utility.
⠀
More users retain BCH balances.
⠀
And demand grows faster than new issuance.
⠀
THE BEAR CASE:
⠀
Stablecoins and competing payment systems capture usage.
⠀
Recipients immediately convert BCH.
⠀
Application adoption remains limited.
⠀
Fee income stays small.
⠀
And declining subsidies intensify the security-budget challenge.
⠀
BCH can remain technically functional while delivering weak investment returns.
⠀
Network survival and asset appreciation are separate outcomes.
⠀
12 | THE FINAL VERDICT
⠀
Bitcoin Cash has a clear proposition:
⠀
Scarce, permissionless digital cash with inexpensive base-layer transfers.
⠀
Its supply is already close to the maximum.
⠀
Its development also extends beyond simple payments.
⠀
But the investment case still needs durable monetary demand.
⠀
Low fees do not establish adoption.
⠀
Merchant acceptance does not establish repeat spending.
⠀
And payment volume does not establish long-term holding demand.
⠀
Watch recurring usage.
⠀
Watch retained balances.
⠀
Watch mining economics.
⠀
Watch whether new capabilities produce useful applications.
⠀
A 94.5% decline does not establish undervaluation.
⠀
BCH's thesis strengthens when people consistently choose it as money they want to use and retain.
⠀
Bookmark this analysis before the next Proof-of-Work rotation.
⠀

⠀
bitcoin-cash:native, $LTC, or dogecoin:native?

text:
🔴| THE PATTERN IS NOT A THEORY. IT IS A CHRONOLOGY WITH DATES, LAWS, AND ORDER NUMBERS. HERE IS THE RECEIPT FOR EVERY COUNTRY THAT REFUSED ALIGNMENT, AND THE THREE QUESTIONS THAT EXPOSE WHAT THE DOCUMENTS DO NOT SAY.

The Chronology

IRAQ 2003. The model case. 19 March 2003 invasion. CPA Order No. 1 de-Ba'athification. CPA Order No. 2, 23 May 2003, dissolved the Iraqi army roughly 400,000 armed men sent home unpaid. The order was signed by L. Paul Bremer, the American proconsul. That is not a policy. That is a legal instrument written by an occupying authority and stamped on a sovereign state.

Seventeen years later, 5 January 2020, the Iraqi Parliament voted to demand the withdrawal of all foreign forces. The vote was taken after the American assassination of Qasem Soleimani and Abu Mahdi al-Muhandis at Baghdad airport on 3 January 2020. The United States did not leave. It maintains roughly 2,500 troops at Ain al-Asad (33.79°N 42.44°E) and Erbil (36.19°N 44.01°E) with no Status of Forces Agreement ratified by the Iraqi Parliament.

That is the receipt. A parliament voted the forces out. The forces stayed. The government that hosts them is the government Washington built.

LIBYA 2011. UNSC Resolution 1973, 17 March 2011. A no-fly zone. NATO used the mandate to run a regime-change air campaign. Muammar Gaddafi was killed on 20 October 2011. The state collapsed. The open-air slave markets in Tripoli were documented by CNN in November 2017. Hillary Clinton, then Secretary of State, was recorded laughing about Gaddafi's death: "We came, we saw, he died."

YUGOSLAVIA 1999. NATO bombing without Security Council authorisation, 24 March to 10 June 1999. The country was then dismantled through courtrooms and referendums into seven entities. Slobodan Milošević died in the custody of the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia on 11 March 2006, before verdict.

VENEZUELA 2026. Nicolás Maduro was arrested and removed to New York in January 2026. The United States installed a client structure under Delcy Rodríguez. Marco Rubio stated the policy: "Venezuela will not be able to sell oil unless the United States decides to allow it." The US Treasury custodial accounts hold the oil revenue. Delcy Rodríguez announced the sale of non-strategic state companies and the return of expropriated assets to "former owners affected by expropriation processes." Citgo, valued around $10 billion, was sold by a Delaware court for $5.9 billion. Roughly $7 billion in PDVSA assets were frozen in 2019. 31 tonnes of gold sit at the Bank of England.

CUBA 1962 to present. The embargo. UN General Assembly resolution on the embargo passed 130 to 17 in October 2026 the 34th consecutive year. Washington votes with 16 other states against the rest of the world.

IRAN 2026. The February war. The assassination of Imam Ali Khamenei. The bombing of Natanz, Fordow, Isfahan. The Minab school, 160 schoolchildren and teachers. 87 hospitals. 25 pharmaceutical plants. 410 water supply facilities. The naval siege. The frozen assets. The seven conditions on the table and the word "surrender" used by Rezaei.

RUSSIA. The 2014 coup in Kyiv. Minsk II signed 12 February 2015 and endorsed by UNSC Resolution 2202 then described by Poroshenko, Merkel, and Hollande as a stall. The Istanbul track of April 2022 closed by Boris Johnson, confirmed by Yulia Mendel and David Arakhamia. The Nord Stream destruction of 26 September 2022, with the Danish and Swedish investigations closed in February 2024 without naming a party. The €210 billion at Euroclear taxed at 99.7 per cent on the windfall.

The Machinery

Sovereignty is not destroyed by tanks alone. It is destroyed by plumbing. The plumbing is documented.

The money. The Bank Recovery and Resolution Directive, amended by Directive (EU) 2026/806 and the CMDI package of April 2026. The bail-in order: shareholders, then subordinated creditors, then senior creditors, then uninsured depositors above €100,000. The BRRD does not require a parliamentary vote in a crisis. The currency is being made programmable through the digital euro, preparation phase since 2023, legislative proposal June 2023.

The identity. eIDAS 2.0 requires every EU member state to offer a digital identity wallet by the end of 2026. ID2020 was co-founded with seed money from Microsoft, the Rockefeller Foundation, Accenture, and Gavi, the alliance Gates founded. Aadhaar in India enrolled 1.4 billion and has been exported to 23 countries including six in Africa. DigiLocker holds the documents. UPI holds the payments.

The law that exempts the state. India's DPDP Act 2023, Section 17, permits the central government to exempt its own instrumentalities from the entire privacy law by executive notification. Rule 23 allows the government to seek data from companies without informing the individual. The Data Protection Board was not constituted as of April 2026. The surveillance powers began immediately. The protections do not begin until 13 May 2027.

The framework. UN Agenda 2030, adopted 25 September 2015, with 17 Sustainable Development Goals. SDG 16 is the hook: "peace, justice and strong institutions" is the language under which surveillance, digital identity, and predictive policing are funded as institution-building.

The doctrine. The WEF's "Known Unknowns," its Global Risks Report, its Strategic Intelligence maps, and the Great Reset of June 2020 — all published. Cyber Polygon ran in July 2020 and July 2021; the European Parliament's own record confirms the 9 July 2021 simulation of a "cyber pandemic."

The privatised perception layer. ICANN sits in Los Angeles under contract to the US Department of Commerce. Nine of the thirteen root server identities are on US soil. The undersea cables that carry roughly 99 per cent of intercontinental data are owned by consortia dominated by Google, Meta, Microsoft, Amazon. DARPA funded the ARPANET and TCP/IP. In-Q-Tel, the CIA's venture arm, funded Palantir. Microsoft holds the JWCC contract for the Pentagon's warfighting cloud. Azure Chaos Studio is a first-party tool that can deliberately take servers down and log the event as a resilience drill.

The Three Questions

Read what the document does, not what it promises.

QUESTION ONE: WHO HOLDS THE SWITCH?

Every document that promises a service also creates a control point. Ask who can turn it off.

The digital identity wallet promises convenience. The control point is the certificate authority that issues and revokes credentials. Revoke the credential and the citizen cannot bank, travel, or access healthcare.

The CBDC promises efficiency. The control point is the issuer. The issuer can program the money: restrict where it is spent, condition when it expires, freeze it entirely.

DORA, NIS2, and the Cyber Resilience Act promise security. The control points are the reporting obligations and the third-party risk register. The register is a list of every vendor whose failure can take down a financial entity. The regulator holds the list.

The FAA's BNATCS promises modernisation. The control point is the Common Automation Platform and the SMART AI tool awarded $875 million over 12 years to Air Space Intelligence. Three days before the 13 November 2026 ground stop, the AI tool went live at all 22 regional centres. The legacy system went offline. GAO-26-107992 had already warned of "severe airspace disruptions." The disruption happened.

QUESTION TWO: WHO PAYS WHEN IT FAILS, AND WHO IS PROTECTED?

Every framework has a loss allocation. Find it.

The BRRD allocates the loss to the depositor above €100,000, after the shareholders and the bondholders. The state and the banks are protected. The depositor is the buffer.

The 1851 Limitation of Liability Act caps a shipowner's liability at the post-casualty value of the hull. The victims of the American Heritage collision in the Mississippi share a capped fund. The insurer pays the cap. The owner is protected.

The US-Ukraine Reconstruction Investment Fund, signed 30 April 2025, gives the United States a 50 per cent share of revenue from newly issued Ukrainian extraction licences, with no security guarantee and no reconstruction obligation. The collateral is claimed before the settlement. The investor is protected.

QUESTION THREE: WHO IS EXCLUDED FROM THE ROOM?

Every framework describes who is inside. The answer is in who is outside.

The Makkah Pact of 7 August 2026 protects the territorial integrity of Saudi Arabia, Pakistan, and Turkey. It contains no clause on Gaza, no clause on the Golan, and no mechanism to confront the entity. The exclusion is the policy.

The Doha channel runs through Qatari mediators whose capital hosts Al Udeid (25.12°N 51.32°E), CENTCOM's forward headquarters. The US has no ambassador in Tehran. The Vance letter was read and left unanswered. The address is empty.

The EU was told by Medinsky in Abu Dhabi: "We did not communicate with the European representatives. We do not really understand in what capacity they are here." The EU paid €130 billion in security assistance, €90 billion in loans, and €210 billion immobilised at Euroclear. The EU has no chair at the table.

At COP31, Iran's president presented an invoice for 1.5 million tons of emissions from strikes on Asaluyeh and the Tehran storage tanks, under UNFCCC Article 4 and Rio Principle 16, both signed by the states that did the bombing. The framework was written by the accused. The invoice is being served inside it.

The Bill

Iraq 2003: CPA Order No. 2, 400,000 soldiers dismissed, the state dissolved, ISIS produced. 5 January 2020: parliament voted the forces out. They stayed.

Libya 2011: Resolution 1973. Gaddafi killed 20 October 2011. Slave markets documented 2017.

Yugoslavia 1999: bombing without Council authorisation. Seven entities. Milošević died in tribunal custody.

Venezuela 2026: Maduro removed. Delcy Rodríguez installed. Oil revenue in US Treasury custodial accounts. Citgo sold for $5.9 billion**. **$7 billion in PDVSA assets frozen. 31 tonnes of gold at the Bank of England.

Cuba: embargo since 1962. UN vote 130–17, the 34th consecutive rejection.

Iran 2026: the Leader assassinated. Minab, 160 children and teachers. 87 hospitals. 25 pharmaceutical plants. 410 water facilities. The naval siege. The seven conditions. "Surrender."

Russia: Minsk II endorsed by Resolution 2202 and called a stall by its own signatories. Istanbul 2022 closed by Johnson, confirmed by Mendel and Arakhamia. Nord Stream destroyed, the investigations closed without a name. €210 billion at Euroclear.

The machinery: BRRD bail-in above €100,000. eIDAS 2.0 wallet by end of 2026. ID2020. Aadhaar in 23 countries. DPDP Act Section 17. Agenda 2030, SDG 16. Cyber Polygon, 9 July 2021, per the European Parliament's record. ICANN in Los Angeles. Nine of thirteen root servers in the US. In-Q-Tel → Palantir. Microsoft JWCC. Azure Chaos Studio. BNATCS, SMART, $875 million, 22 centres, GAO-26-107992, the 13 November ground stop.

The three questions: who holds the switch, who pays when it fails, who is excluded from the room.

The bill is being paid in dissolved armies, capped liability funds, and a depositor bail-in written into EU law, and the receipt is a stack of public documents, orders, resolutions, directives, audits, and summit communiqués that describe the architecture in plain language while promising something else entirely.

Thousands of U.S. judges who broke laws or oaths remained on the bench
In the past dozen years, state and local judges have repeatedly escaped public accountability for misdeeds that have victimized thousands. Nine of 10 kept their jobs, a Reuters investigation found – including an Alabama judge who unlawfully jailed hundreds of poor people, many of them Black, over traffic fines.

By MICHAEL BERENS and JOHN SHIFFMAN in MONTGOMERY, ALABAMA Filed June 30, 2020, noon GMT
Judge Les Hayes once sentenced a single mother to 496 days behind bars for failing to pay traffic tickets. The sentence was so stiff it exceeded the jail time Alabama allows for negligent homicide.

Marquita Johnson, who was locked up in April 2012, says the impact of her time in jail endures today. Johnson’s three children were cast into foster care while she was incarcerated. One daughter was molested, state records show. Another was physically abused.

“Judge Hayes took away my life and didn’t care how my children suffered,” said Johnson, now 36. “My girls will never be the same.”

Fellow inmates found her sentence hard to believe. “They had a nickname for me: The Woman with All the Days,” Johnson said. “That’s what they called me: The Woman with All the Days. There were people who had committed real crimes who got out before me.”

In 2016, the state agency that oversees judges charged Hayes with violating Alabama’s code of judicial conduct. According to the Judicial Inquiry Commission, Hayes broke state and federal laws by jailing Johnson and hundreds of other Montgomery residents too poor to pay fines. Among those jailed: a plumber struggling to make rent, a mother who skipped meals to cover the medical bills of her disabled son, and a hotel housekeeper working her way through college.

Hayes, a judge since 2000, admitted in court documents to violating 10 different parts of the state’s judicial conduct code. One of the counts was a breach of a judge’s most essential duty: failing to “respect and comply with the law."

Despite the severity of the ruling, Hayes wasn’t barred from serving as a judge. Instead, the judicial commission and Hayes reached a deal. The former Eagle Scout would serve an 11-month unpaid suspension. Then he could return to the bench.

Until he was disciplined, Hayes said in an interview with Reuters, “I never thought I was doing something wrong.”

This week, Hayes is set to retire after 20 years as a judge. In a statement to Reuters, Hayes said he was “very remorseful” for his misdeeds.

Community activists say his departure is long overdue. Yet the decision to leave, they say, should never have been his to make, given his record of misconduct.

“He should have been fired years ago,” said Willie Knight, pastor of North Montgomery Baptist Church. “He broke the law and wanted to get away with it. His sudden retirement is years too late.”

Hayes is among thousands of state and local judges across America who were allowed to keep positions of extraordinary power and prestige after violating judicial ethics rules or breaking laws they pledged to uphold, a Reuters investigation found.

Judges have made racist statements, lied to state officials and forced defendants to languish in jail without a lawyer – and then returned to the bench, sometimes with little more than a rebuke from the state agencies overseeing their conduct.

Recent media reports have documented failures in judicial oversight in South Carolina, Louisiana and Illinois. Reuters went further.

In the first comprehensive accounting of judicial misconduct nationally, Reuters identified and reviewed 1,509 cases from the last dozen years – 2008 through 2019 – in which judges resigned, retired or were publicly disciplined following accusations of misconduct. In addition, reporters identified another 3,613 cases from 2008 through 2018 in which states disciplined wayward judges but kept hidden from the public key details of their offenses – including the identities of the judges themselves.

All told, 9 of every 10 judges were allowed to return to the bench after they were sanctioned for misconduct, Reuters determined. They included a California judge who had sex in his courthouse chambers, once with his former law intern and separately with an attorney; a New York judge who berated domestic violence victims; and a Maryland judge who, after his arrest for driving drunk, was allowed to return to the bench provided he took a Breathalyzer test before each appearance.

The news agency’s findings reveal an “excessively” forgiving judicial disciplinary system, said Stephen Gillers, a law professor at New York University who writes about judicial ethics. Although punishment short of removal from the bench is appropriate for most misconduct cases, Gillers said, the public “would be appalled at some of the lenient treatment judges get” for substantial transgressions.

Among the cases from the past year alone:

In Utah, a judge texted a video of a man’s scrotum to court clerks. He was reprimanded but remains on the bench.

In Indiana, three judges attending a conference last spring got drunk and sparked a 3 a.m. brawl outside a White Castle fast-food restaurant that ended with two of the judges shot. Although the state supreme court found the three judges had “discredited the entire Indiana judiciary,” each returned to the bench after a suspension.

In Texas, a judge burst in on jurors deliberating the case of a woman charged with sex trafficking and declared that God told him the defendant was innocent. The offending judge received a warning and returned to the bench. The defendant was convicted after a new judge took over the case.

“There are certain things where there should be a level of zero tolerance,” the jury foreman, Mark House, told Reuters. The judge should have been fined, House said, and kicked off the bench. “There is no justice, because he is still doing his job.”

Judicial misconduct specialists say such behavior has the potential to erode trust in America’s courts and, absent tough consequences, could give judges license to behave with impunity.

“When you see cases like that, the public starts to wonder about the integrity and honesty of the system,” said Steve Scheckman, a lawyer who directed Louisiana’s oversight agency and served as deputy director of New York’s. “It looks like a good ol’ boys club.”

That’s how local lawyers viewed the case of a longtime Alabama judge who concurrently served on the state’s judicial oversight commission. The judge, Cullman District Court’s Kim Chaney, remained on the bench for three years after being accused of violating the same nepotism rules he was tasked with enforcing on the oversight commission. In at least 200 cases, court records show, Judge Chaney chose his own son to serve as a court-appointed defense lawyer for the indigent, enabling the younger Chaney to earn at least $105,000 in fees over two years.

In February, months after Reuters repeatedly asked Chaney and the state judicial commission about those cases, he retired from the bench as part of a deal with state authorities to end the investigation.

Tommy Drake, the lawyer who first filed a complaint against Chaney in 2016, said he doubts the judge would have been forced from the bench if Reuters hadn’t examined the case.

“You know the only reason they did anything about Chaney is because you guys started asking questions,” Drake said. “Otherwise, he’d still be there.”

Bedrock of American justice

State and local judges draw little scrutiny even though their courtrooms are the bedrock of the American criminal justice system, touching the lives of millions of people every year.

The country’s approximately 1,700 federal judges hear 400,000 cases annually. The nearly 30,000 state, county and municipal court judges handle a far bigger docket: more than 100 million new cases each year, from traffic to divorce to murder. Their titles range from justice of the peace to state supreme court justice. Their powers are vast and varied – from determining whether a defendant should be jailed to deciding who deserves custody of a child.

Each U.S. state has an oversight agency that investigates misconduct complaints against judges. The authority of the oversight agencies is distinct from the power held by appellate courts, which can reverse a judge’s legal ruling and order a new trial. Judicial commissions cannot change verdicts. Rather, they can investigate complaints about the behavior of judges and pursue discipline ranging from reprimand to removal.

Few experts dispute that the great majority of judges behave responsibly, respecting the law and those who appear before them. And some contend that, when judges do falter, oversight agencies are effective in identifying and addressing the behavior. “With a few notable exceptions, the commissions generally get it right,” said Keith Swisher, a University of Arizona law professor who specializes in judicial ethics.

Others disagree. They note that the clout of these commissions is limited, and their authority differs from state to state. To remove a judge, all but a handful of states require approval of a panel that includes other judges. And most states seldom exercise the full extent of those disciplinary powers.

As a result, the system tends to err on the side of protecting the rights and reputations of judges while overlooking the impact courtroom wrongdoing has on those most affected by it: people like Marquita Johnson.

Reuters scoured thousands of state investigative files, disciplinary proceedings and court records from the past dozen years to quantify the personal toll of judicial misconduct. The examination found at least 5,206 people who were directly affected by a judge’s misconduct. The victims cited in disciplinary documents ranged from people who were illegally jailed to those subjected to racist, sexist and other abusive comments from judges in ways that tainted the cases.

The number is a conservative estimate. The tally doesn’t include two previously reported incidents that affected thousands of defendants and prompted sweeping reviews of judicial conduct.

“If we have a system that holds a wrongdoer accountable but we fail to address the victims, then we are really losing sight of what a justice system should be all about.”

Arthur Grim, retired judge

In Pennsylvania, the state examined the convictions of more than 3,500 teenagers sentenced by two judges. The judges were convicted of taking kickbacks as part of a scheme to fill a private juvenile detention center. In 2009, the Pennsylvania Supreme Court appointed senior judge Arthur Grim to lead a victim review, and the state later expunged criminal records for 2,251 juveniles. Grim told Reuters that every state should adopt a way to compensate victims of judicial misconduct.

“If we have a system that holds a wrongdoer accountable but we fail to address the victims, then we are really losing sight of what a justice system should be all about,” Grim said.

In another review underway in Ohio, state public defender Tim Young is scrutinizing 2,707 cases handled by a judge who retired in 2018 after being hospitalized for alcoholism. Mike Benza, a law professor at Case Western Reserve University whose students are helping identify victims, compared the work to current investigations into police abuse of power. “You see one case and then you look to see if it's systemic,” he said.

The review, which has been limited during the coronavirus pandemic, may take a year. But Young said the time-consuming task is essential because “a fundamental injustice may have been levied against hundreds or thousands of people.”

‘Special rules for judges’

Most states afford judges accused of misconduct a gentle kind of justice. Perhaps no state better illustrates the shortcomings of America’s system for overseeing judges than Alabama.

As in most states, Alabama’s nine-member Judicial Inquiry Commission is a mix of lawyers, judges and laypeople. All are appointed. Their deliberations are secret and they operate under some of the most judge-friendly rules in the nation.

Alabama’s rules make even filing a complaint against a judge difficult. The complaint must be notarized, which means that in theory, anyone who makes misstatements about the judge can be prosecuted for perjury. Complaints about wrongdoing must be made in writing; those that arrive by phone, email or without a notary stamp are not investigated, although senders are notified why their complaints have been summarily rejected. Anonymous written complaints are shredded.

These rules can leave lawyers and litigants fearing retaliation, commission director Jenny Garrett noted in response to written questions.

“It’s a ridiculous system that protects judges and makes it easy for them to intimidate anyone with a legitimate complaint,” said Sue Bell Cobb, chief justice of the Alabama Supreme Court from 2007 to 2011. In 2009, she unsuccessfully championed changes to the process and commissioned an American Bar Association report that offered a scathing review of Alabama's rules.

In most other states, commission staff members can start investigating a judge upon receiving a phone call or email, even anonymous ones, or after learning of questionable conduct from a news report or court filing. In Alabama, staff will not begin an investigation without approval from the commission itself, which convenes about every seven weeks.

By rule, the commission also must keep a judge who is under scrutiny fully informed throughout an investigation. If a subpoena is issued, the judge receives a simultaneous copy, raising fears about witness intimidation. If a witness gives investigators a statement, the judge receives a transcript. In the U.S. justice system, such deference to individuals under investigation is extremely rare.

“It’s a ridiculous system that protects judges and makes it easy for them to intimidate anyone with a legitimate complaint.”

Sue Bell Cobb, former chief justice of the Alabama Supreme Court

“Why the need for special rules for judges?” said Michael Levy, a Washington lawyer who has represented clients in high-profile criminal, corporate, congressional and securities investigations. “If judges think it’s fair and appropriate to investigate others for crimes or misconduct without providing those subjects or targets with copies of witness statements and subpoenas, why don’t judges think it’s fair to investigate judges in the same way?”

Alabama judges also are given an opportunity to resolve investigations confidentially. Reuters interviews and a review of Alabama commission records show the commission has met with judges informally at least 19 times since 2011 to offer corrective “guidance.” The identities of those judges remain confidential, as does the conduct that prompted the meetings. “Not every violation warrants discipline,” commission director Garrett said.

Since 2008, the commission has brought 21 public cases against judges, including Hayes, charging two this year.

Two of the best-known cases brought by the commission involved Roy Moore, who was twice forced out as chief justice of the Alabama Supreme Court for defying federal court orders.

Another Alabama justice fared better in challenging a misconduct complaint, however. Tom Parker, first elected to the state’s high court in 2004, pushed back when the commission investigated him in 2015 for comments he made on the radio criticizing the U.S. Supreme Court's decision legalizing gay marriage.

Parker sued the commission in federal court, arguing the agency was infringing on his First Amendment rights. He won. Although the commission had dropped its investigation before the ruling, it was ordered to cover Parker’s legal fees: $100,000, or about a fifth of the agency’s total annual budget.

In 2018, the people of Alabama elected Parker chief justice.

These days, Parker told Reuters, Alabama judges and the agency that oversees them enjoy “a much better relationship” that’s less politically tinged. “How can I say it? It’s much more respectful between the commission and the judges now.”

text:
TEXAS DEMOCRATS’ FIRST PRIORITY: KILL ICE DEALS AND SHIELD ILLEGALS

On the very first day Texas lawmakers could pre-file bills for the 90th Legislature, San Antonio Democrats Rep. Trey Martinez Fischer and Sen. José Menéndez dropped House Bill 123 and Senate Bill 99. Their goal is simple: repeal the 2025 law that forces county sheriffs who run jails to sign 287(g) agreements with ICE.

That law, Senate Bill 8, passed under Republican control and signed by Governor Greg Abbott, requires those sheriffs to enter formal partnerships so local officers can help identify and process illegal aliens already in custody. It also created state grants to help cover the cost. Hundreds of Texas sheriffs have already complied or are under the December 1, 2026 deadline to do so. The new Democratic bills would wipe out the mandate, let sheriffs cancel existing agreements with written notice, shut off new grant money, and dismiss any pending attorney general lawsuits meant to enforce the rule.

This is not a quiet technical cleanup. It is the opening move after Democrats flipped the Texas House and statewide offices, including the governorship. With the regular session set to start in January 2027, they are signaling that reducing local cooperation with federal immigration enforcement is at the top of the list. The bills would not stop every voluntary partnership, but they would remove the statewide requirement and the financial incentive, handing blue-leaning counties an easy off-ramp.

Supporters of the original law argue it simply puts Texas sheriffs on the same page with federal officers when criminal suspects in local jails turn out to be removable aliens. Critics of the repeal say the practical effect is to make it harder for ICE to take custody of people already booked on state charges, effectively restoring sanctuary-style friction in the largest counties. Texas already leads the nation in 287(g) agreements; these bills aim to reverse that momentum right as enforcement has expanded under the current federal administration.

The filings came with statements about “meaningful change” and working with “constituents and advocates.” What they do not emphasize is that the people most directly affected by weaker jail-to-ICE handoffs are the Texans who live next to the criminal illegal aliens those agreements help remove. With the Senate still in Republican hands, the bills face long odds, but the priority is clear: the first item of business is to loosen the state’s grip on local immigration enforcement.

🇮🇷🇵🇰|#Islamabad: Hegseth says "don't talk about the law to those who wield a sword"; Iran’s Foreign Minister replies, "The one who wields the sword ends up being beheaded."

November 16, 2026, Islamabad. The 30th Meeting of the Council of Ministers of the Economic Cooperation Organization (ECO). Standing at the podium, Foreign Minister Araghchi began by thanking his colleagues who had "spoken with one voice to forcefully condemn the aggression against the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the Islamic Republic of Iran, as well as the war waged against it"—and offered condolences for the martyred leader, Seyyed Ali Khamenei.

He then outlined three key pillars: strengthening connectivity, expanding regional trade, and developing energy cooperation.

💥 These three points are not merely an "agenda"; they are a "detour" (an alternative route).

Strengthening connectivity: With the West having severed financial messaging systems, academic exchanges, and air links, the ten ECO member states must establish their own channels for communication and settlement.

Expanding regional trade: The Strait of Hormuz is closed; Red Sea shipping routes are disrupted; access to SWIFT is cut off. What remains are land routes spanning Central, South, and West Asia utilizing Pakistan’s borders, Turkey’s corridors, and Iran’s railways.

Developing energy cooperation: While Iran’s oil exports are blocked, natural gas, electricity, and petrochemical products can still flow to neighboring countries via pipelines, power grids, and overland routes. The ECO provides the framework for this.

Araghchi did not say, "We are under sanctions." Instead, he spoke of the need to "strengthen connectivity, trade, and energy." Both statements describe the same reality, but the latter offers a solution.

🎯 Hegseth’s sword and the Roman who lost his head

U.S. Secretary of Defense Hegseth reposted a video by Rubio on X, adding the comment: "Stop talking about the law to those who wield a sword."

Araghchi’s response did not rely on a mere "condemnation."  He drew upon history:

“These words were spoken by a Roman leader. His military campaign despite his numerical superiority ended in a crushing defeat. After fleeing the battlefield, he was beheaded.”

“Those who cannot remember the past are condemned to repeat it.”

That Roman was Pompey. The year was 48 BC; the setting, the Battle of Pharsalus. Pompey’s forces outnumbered Caesar’s, and he was certain of victory. He overlooked a crucial fact: Caesar’s legions were battle-hardened veterans of a decade-long campaign in Gaul, whereas Pompey’s troops were newly recruited, poorly trained, and lacked shared combat experience.

The result: a catastrophic defeat for Pompey. He fled to Egypt, hoping to find sanctuary. But Ptolemy XIII of Egypt, seeking to curry favor with Caesar, had Pompey beheaded, placed the head in a basket, and delivered it to Caesar.

Hegesias once remarked, “Do not speak of the law to a man who holds a sword.” Araghchi’s point is this: that sword-wielding Roman ultimately met his end by the blade not by the law, but by the hand of another man with a sword. Yet, this second man understood something Pompey did not: he knew when to sheathe his blade.

“Those who cannot remember the past are condemned to repeat it.” This is no mere rhetorical flourish; it is a direct warning to Hegesias. Look at America’s interventions in Afghanistan, Iraq, Libya, and Vietnam. Time and again, the U.S. believed the “sword” could solve its problems. Time and again, it was proven wrong. Time and again, it was forced to withdraw, leaving nothing but ruins in its wake.

Araghchi is saying: You are now in Iran, repeating the very same mistake. Only this time, your sword has grown dull. Fifty-six MQ-9 drones have been shot down; bases in eight different countries have been struck; an E-3 aircraft has been destroyed; an F-35 has signaled an emergency (squawk 7700); and aircraft carriers have been forced to retreat from the Red Sea. In the midterm elections, the American people have said “no.”  

📜 Assessment by the ECO Secretary-General: Iran’s Resistance Signifies “Prestige,” Not “Weakness”

At the meeting, ECO Secretary-General Asad Majeed Khan remarked:

“The ECO has successfully maintained the continuity of interaction and communication among its member states, ensuring that regional security developments do not affect the internal relations of the organization.”

“I commend the Islamic Republic of Iran for its resilience in the face of an imposed war, and I acknowledge the pivotal role Iran has played in supporting the organization’s endeavors and achieving its objectives.”

“Resilience:” this term is not an expression of “sympathy”; it is an acknowledgment. A nation surrounded by war, sanctions, blockades, and assassinations is not viewed within the ECO framework as an entity “in need of rescue.” Rather, it is a core member state that actively supports the organization’s efforts and the realization of its goals.

The statement that “regional security developments have not affected the internal relations of the organization” serves as a confirmation. The region is embroiled in conflict; the Strait of Hormuz faces the threat of closure, and U.S. military bases have come under fire. Yet, the ten member states of the ECO continue to convene, discussing trade, communications, and energy. War has not halted regional cooperation; it has merely altered the urgency with which such cooperation is pursued.

⚔️ Baghaei and the Pakistani Foreign Secretary: Bilateral Engagement within the ECO Framework

On the sidelines of the ECO meeting, Foreign Ministry Spokesperson Baghaei met with Pakistan’s Foreign Secretary, Sajjad Haider. Both sides “expressed appreciation for their shared commitment to developing Iran-Pakistan relations” and emphasized “collaborative efforts to promote regional security and stability.”

Just weeks ago, Pakistan had closed its border with Iran—a move that triggered an LPG crisis, leaving many households without cooking gas. Following a visit to Tehran by General Munir, the border was reopened. Now, Baghaei is in Islamabad, shaking hands with the Pakistani Foreign Secretary.

This is more than mere “diplomatic protocol”; it is a reaffirmation following the reopening of the border. The border is open, but trade volumes must be restored, and the flow of LPG must resume. The ECO framework provides the institutional structure to facilitate this exchange.  The meeting between Baghaei and Haider served as the first bolt tightened within that framework.

🔻 A Day in Islamabad

Araghchi: Three pillars; connectivity, trade, and energy. My gratitude to those colleagues who condemned the aggression.

☠️Hegseth: "Do not speak of the law to those who wield the sword."
🇮🇷Araghchi: That Roman who wielded the sword, he ended up beheaded. Those who cannot remember the past are condemned to repeat it.
ECO Secretary-General: Commending Iran’s resilience. Iran is a core member.
Baghaei and Haider: Reaffirming cooperation following the reopening of the borders.

This is not merely a "meeting"; it is a "framework." Eight months into the war, the ECO is no mere "talking shop," it is an alternative regional order. Its member states span Central, South, and West Asia. Its agenda focuses on connectivity, trade, and energy. Its function is to ensure that, even under blockade, Iran retains access to routes, markets, and partners.

As for Hegseth’s "sword," it finds no audience in the ECO’s meeting hall. Those present know the fate of Pompey; they know that a "sword" might win a single battle, but it cannot win a war. And Iran is fighting a war not with a sword, but through connectivity, trade, energy, and resilience.

Long live Iran. Long live the ECO. Long live the Resistance. Long live the Axis of Resistance.

A socialist republic is a sovereign nation that operates under a republican form of government and maintains a socialist economic and political system.

Key Characteristics
• Republican Governance: The country lacks a monarch and is organized as a public matter (res publica), where leaders are chosen by representatives or the populace.
• Socialist Economy: Major means of production, resources, and key industries are publicly, collectively, or state-owned rather than privately controlled.
• Constitutional Commitment: The state’s foundational laws explicitly pledge allegiance to socialist principles or the transition toward socialism.

Political Structures
• Marxist–Leninist Models: Many historical and current socialist republics (such as the former Soviet republics or modern one-party states) feature a dominant communist or Marxist-Leninist party guiding the state apparatus.
• Democratic & Multi-Party Models: Some nations incorporate constitutional references to socialism or democratic socialism while operating within multi-party parliamentary frameworks.

Examples
• Current Examples: Countries such as the Socialist Republic of Vietnam formally designate themselves as socialist republics.
• Historical Examples: The Soviet Union (Union of Soviet Socialist Republics) and its constituent republics (such as the Socialist Republic of Croatia or Socialist Republic of Slovenia).

A socialist state, socialist republic, or socialist country is a sovereign state constitutionally dedicated to the establishment of socialism. This article is about states that refer to themselves as socialist states, and not specifically about communist states that refer to themselves as socialist states. It includes information on liberal democratic states with constitutional references to socialism as well as other state formations that have referred to themselves as socialist.

Constitutional references to socialism
See also: Liberal democratic constitutions with references to socialism
A number of countries that make references to socialism in their constitutions are not communist states. In most cases, these are constitutional references to the building of a socialist society and political principles that have little to no bearing on the structure and guidance of these country's machinery of government and economic system. The preamble to the 1976 Constitution of Portugal states that the Portuguese state has, as one of its goals, opening "the way to socialist society".[1] Another broad example is that of Slovenia, which defines itself as a "state governed by the rule of law and a social state".[2] Algeria, the Congo, India, and Sri Lanka have directly used the term socialist in their official constitution and name. Croatia, Hungary, and Poland directly denounce "Communism" in their founding documents in reference to their past regimes.[i]

In these cases, the intended meaning of socialism can vary widely and sometimes the constitutional references to socialism are left over from a previous period in the country's history. In the case of many Middle Eastern states, the term socialism was often used in reference to an Arab socialist/nationalist philosophy adopted by specific regimes, such as that of Gamal Abdel Nasser and that of the various Ba'ath parties. Examples of countries directly using the term socialist in their names include the Democratic Socialist Republic of Sri Lanka and the Socialist Republic of Vietnam, while a number of countries make references to socialism in their constitutions, but not in their names. These include India[3] and Portugal. In addition, countries such as Belarus, Colombia, France, Russia, and Spain use the varied term social state, leaving a more ambiguous meaning. In the constitutions of Croatia, Hungary, and Poland, direct condemnation is made to the respective past socialist regimes.[4] The autonomous region of Rojava, which operates under the principles of democratic confederalism, has been described as a socialist state.[5]

Washington had stopped funding the UN Support Office for Somalia (UNSOS), which provides vital logistics to African Union troops.

Without UNSOS, the African Union's military campaign in Somalia was unlikely to be able to continue.
The Al-Qaeda-linked Al-Shabaab group has been fighting the Somali government for two decades.
Despite the AU mission, the militants still control large parts of central Somalia.
US officials had cited frustration with the Somali government's slow progress against Al-Shabaab and the country's persistent political chaos.
Washington has stressed that the renewed backing is not an open-ended commitment.
It is urging Somalia and the African Union to plan more sustainable regional security arrangements for the future.
The move brings relief to Mogadishu and to the troop-contributing nations of the African Union mission.

The Simpsons Writer Who Predicted Trump's Presidency Launches His Own 2028 White House Bid
Dan Greaney, who wrote the infamous 2000 'Simpsons' episode that mentioned a "President Trump," announced his own campaign for president as a "progressive Republican"
By Meredith Kile  Published on May 26, 2026 04:20PM EDT
The Simpsons writer who "predicted" Donald Trump's presidency is making his own run for the White House decades later.

Dan Greaney, a longtime writer and producer on the Emmy-winning animated series, announced his candidacy on Tuesday, May 26, describing himself as "a progressive Republican in the tradition of Abraham Lincoln and Teddy Roosevelt."

Greaney's campaign announcement video plays up his fame within the Simpsons fandom as the seemingly clairvoyant creative who penned the prescient 2000 episode "Bart to the Future." In the episode, Lisa Simpson is depicted as the first straight female president of the United States in a flash-forward, begrudging the "budget crunch" she's been left by her predecessor, "President Trump."

Dressed in a robe and a wizard's costume wig alluding to how some have called him "The Prophet," Greaney, 61, "predicts" political despair from the current Republican Party.

"Trump, Vance, the billionaires, careerists, and cowards in both parties have turned their backs on [the United States],” he says. “It’s money, power, and security for them, but not for you."

"In America, the government is supposed to work for everyone. Democracy for all, accountability for all, prosperity for all. We must restore this," he continued. "I'd love to help, but I'm not a lawyer. I’m just a self-proclaimed prophet… who went to law school, graduated, passed the bar... Wait! I am a lawyer!”

Greaney then transforms into a clean-cut politician to present his candidacy, which he says is centered on "rejecting the counsels of despair."

"His platform includes restoring democratic norms alongside progressive policies such as universal healthcare and the Green New Deal, unified under the campaign’s central idea of building an America that works for all," reads a press release from Greaney's campaign.

It may surprise some that Greaney is running as a Republican. But the four-time Emmy winner, who has also written for The Office and Borat, admits to "having occasionally voted Republican." His campaign says his candidacy is "an effort to engage Americans across ideological lines, including within the Republican base," as well as "an attempt to bridge entrenched divisions and to speak to a broader sense of shared national purpose."

Greaney concluded his campaign announcement cheekily, with a reference to his infamous reputation: “As to what happens next…we’ll just have to wait and see. You will, at least. I actually do know how it turns out."

Prior to Trump's first election in 2016, Greaney opened up about writing "Bart to the Future" 16 years earlier. In an interview with The Hollywood Reporter, he explained that the storyline was less about predicting the unlikely campaign and subsequent victory, and more of a "warning to America" about its already-spiraling political culture.

"The important thing is that Lisa comes into the presidency when America is on the ropes. What we needed was for Lisa to have problems that were beyond her fixing, that everything went as bad as it possibly could, and that’s why we had Trump be president before her," he recalled. "That just seemed like the logical last stop before hitting bottom. It was pitched because it was consistent with the vision of America going insane."

While he couldn't have foreseen the political future while writing the episode or when the storyline came to fruition, Greaney seemed to be correct in his somewhat apathetic 2016 assessment that the shocking coincidence of "Bart to the Future" would not lead to any widespread political change.

“I am tickled we are getting all this attention, but I don’t think it’s going to trigger this well-awaited reevaluation of my episode that I was hoping for,” he said at the time. “The Simpsons has always kind of embraced the over-the-top side of American culture … and [Trump] is just the fulfillment of that.”

Around the same time, Greaney also spoke with The Washington Post, offering a bit bleaker of a perspective that may have evolved over the years to fuel his latest political motivations.

Of Trump, Greaney told the Post, "He seems like a Simpsons-esque figure — he fits right in there, in an over-the-top way. But now that he’s running for president, I see that in a much darker way."

"He seemed kind of lovable in the old days, in a blowhard way," the writer continued, adding that he "never" would have predicted Trump's actual campaign and did not believe, as of the interview's May 2016 publication, that the reality star-turned-politician had a chance to win the White House.

He wondered wryly if the brand of counter-culture comedy that The Simpsons has relied on for decades gave rise to the anti-establishment that ultimately spawned the Trump presidency. "I blame the culture of comedy," Greaney said at the time. "We seem to have blown it up."

Greaney is one of the first to officially declare his candidacy for 2028, especially within the Republican Party, where the presumed frontrunners are members of the current administration.

The top two GOP contenders are thought to be Vice President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio, the latter of whom placed third in the 2016 GOP presidential primaries that Trump ultimately won.

The U.S. Constitution outlines the structure, powers, and responsibilities of the Senate primarily in Article I, with key modifications added by later amendments.

Composition and Election
Equal Representation: Each U.S. state is represented by two Senators, regardless of its population or size.
Terms: Senators serve six-year terms, and each Senator has one vote.
Staggered Elections: Senate seats are divided into three classes so that approximately one-third of the Senate is elected every two years.
Direct Election: Originally, Senators were chosen by state legislatures, but the Seventeenth Amendment (ratified in 1913) CHANGED THIS SO VOTERS ELECT THEM DIRECTLY.
Vacancies: If a Senate seat becomes vacant, the governor of that state may make a temporary appointment or call a special election, depending on state law.

Representative democracy, also known as indirect democracy or electoral democracy, is a type of democracy where elected delegates represent a group of people, in contrast to direct democracy.[1] Nearly all modern Western-style democracies function as some type of representative democracy: for example, the United Kingdom (a unitary parliamentary constitutional monarchy), Germany (a federal parliamentary republic), France (a unitary semi-presidential republic), and the United States (a federal presidential republic).[2] Unlike liberal democracy, a representative democracy may have de facto multiparty, free and fair elections, but may not have a fully developed rule of law and additional individual and minority rights beyond the electoral sphere.[3]

Representative democracy places power in the hands of elected representatives. Political parties often become central to this form of democracy if electoral systems require or encourage voters to vote for political parties or for candidates associated with political parties (as opposed to voting for individual representatives).[4] Some political theorists (including Robert Dahl, Gregory Houston, and Ian Liebenberg) have described representative democracy as polyarchy.[5][6]

Representative democracy can be organized in different ways including both parliamentary and presidential systems of government. Elected representatives typically form a legislature (such as a parliament or congress), which may be composed of a single chamber (unicameral), two chambers (bicameral), or more than two chambers (multicameral). Where two or more chambers exist, their members are often elected in different ways.

Australian Mining

Global Commodity Rankings

Australia holds some of the world's largest reserves and is a leading producer of several key minerals.

#1 Producer: Iron Ore, Bauxite, Lithium, Rutile, and Zircon.

#1 Reserves: Iron Ore, Gold, Lead, Nickel, Rutile, Uranium, and Zinc.

#2 Producer: Gold, Alumina, and Manganese.

Key Mining Hubs & Major Projects

Western Australia: The nation's "engine room," producing 98% of Australia's iron ore and 60% of its gold. Major sites include the Pilbara (iron ore) and the Super Pit in Kalgoorlie (gold).

Queensland: A global leader in metallurgical coal (Bowen Basin) and silver/lead production (Cannington mine).

South Australia: Home to Olympic Dam, which contains the world's largest single uranium deposit and significant copper and gold reserves.

Major Players

The sector is dominated by several multinational giants and significant domestic players:

BHP: Often ranked as Australia's most valuable company; major interests in iron ore, copper, and coal.

Rio Tinto: A world leader in iron ore (Pilbara) and aluminum.

Fortescue (FMG): Primarily focused on iron ore and rapidly expanding into green energy.

Hancock Prospecting: Australia's largest private mining company, led by Gina Rinehart, the nation's wealthiest person.

South32: Spun out of BHP; manages a diversified portfolio including manganese, silver, and nickel.

2026 Trends & Developments

Critical Minerals Push: The government has introduced a $23 billion package to support domestic processing and manufacturing of critical minerals to reduce global reliance on single-country supply chains.

Uranium Rally: Prices exceeding US$100/lb have sparked renewed interest in Australian prospects like the Kalkaroo project.

M&A Activity: Major merger talks continue between giants like Rio Tinto and Glencore as they seek to consolidate copper exposure for the EV market.

Workforce Challenges: The Minerals Council of Australia is currently calling for migration reforms to address a significant "skills crunch" in the sector.

text:
In 2021, Texas suffered the worst energy infrastructure failure in state history, following three severe winter storms in February. At least 246 people were killed as a result of the disruptions, which led to food, water, heat and electricity shortages.

If energy officials had had more time to prepare for the storms, for example by bringing in more trucks of natural gas to disrupted areas, damage from the event could have been mitigated. Unfortunately, weather forecasts beyond two weeks are notoriously unreliable, making for a tighter window for energy operators, farmers, and emergency response officials around the globe.

A new technique by a team including researchers at MIT significantly improves weather forecasting beyond two weeks. The researchers developed a machine-learning model that learns to correct errors in existing forecasting models to improve their output over the two-to-six-week time frame. When applied to a gold-standard forecasting model, it doubled forecasting accuracy over that time frame, placing first in a prominent international forecasting competition.

In a new paper in Nature, the researchers describe their approach and show how it enables forecasts that for the first time beat climatologic averages between two and six weeks.

“Not only does this do better on time averaged forecasts for this range, which is already very useful for farmers and members of the energy industry trying to match supply with demand, but it also improves predictions of extreme weather events, whether it’s flooding or cold spells or something else,” co-author and MIT Research Scientist Judah Cohen says. “It’s really important to predict both, but extreme events might be the most impactful part of this for society.” 

Joining Cohen on the paper are lead authors Hannah Guan, a Harvard College undergraduate; Soukayna Mouatadid, a University of Toronto postdoc; Genevieve Flaspohler SM ’18, PhD ’22; Paulo Orenstein, an associate professor at Brazil’s National Institute for Pure and Applied Mathematics; Jeremy Berman of the data company DTN; Jakob Schloer and Joshua Talib, researchers with the European Center for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts; and Alex Lu, Haiyu Dong, Jonathan Weyn, Zekun Ni, and Lester Mackey, all researchers at Microsoft.

Longer forecasts

In the 1970s, longtime MIT Professor Edward Lorenz came up with the idea of chaos theory to describe how tiny changes in initial weather conditions lead to completely different outcomes.

“He came up with this theoretical two-week limit where beyond that, we just can’t predict weather because the noise in the system grows so much that it overwhelms any signal you start with,” Cohen says. “That had a strong influence on the field that may have held people back from exploring forecasting beyond the two-week range. I never really believed that completely. In theory the atmosphere can create an infinite number of patterns, but it likes to fall into these favorite patterns over and over again. Once one thing happens, I think you can predict the domino that will fall after that, and the domino that will fall after that.”

Today, the best weather forecasts come from either dynamical models, which numerically simulate how the atmosphere and oceans evolve over time, or artificial intelligence models, which learn to make predictions from historical weather data. AI models have shown improvements in predicting weather at short ranges, but they’re even worse than dynamical models at longer time ranges.

Cohen, who is based in the MIT Department of Civil and Environmental Engineering, focuses on forecasting weather two to six weeks in advance, which is known as subseasonal forecasting. “That range is referred to as the ‘predictability desert,’ because in the short range you can capitalize on the initial conditions in the climate system and the atmosphere, and on the longer term you have these slow, varying boundary forces, like the super El Niño everyone’s focused on this winter,” Cohen says. “The subseasonal range can’t take advantage of either of those. In most cases forecasting in the subseasonal ranges is no different than going to a casino and rolling the dice.”

Cohen credits his co-author Lester Mackey, whom he has been collaborating with for more than a decade, with the initial idea of using machine learning to reduce errors in forecasting models.

“We built this wrapper — Lester calls it postprocessing,” Cohen says. “We know AI models have a lot of errors, so we thought maybe we can quantify those errors and remove them.”

While other forecasting systems do more simplistic error correction, the research team’s postprocessing layer uses AI to learn from a forecasting system’s mistakes based on historic data and shifts its forecasts. In that time range, forecasters use so-called probabilistic forecasts, where the likelihood of a range of possibilities if given.

“As more forecasts and data become available, our model adaptively improves its correction,” Cohen says.

To build the model, the researchers used MIT Engaging, a supercomputing cluster hosted by MIT’s Office of Research Computing and Data, but the resulting model does not require a supercomputer to run.

To put their model to the test, last year the research team submitted three models that included their post-processing layer to the European Center for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF), which is considered the best forecasting center in the world. Each season ECMWF holds forecasting competitions between models.

The submission that won first place combined ECMWF’s forecasting model with another, and then applied the postprocessing correction on top. That approach ended up doubling the original model’s predictive power in the subseasonal range. For the first time, the model offered an improvement over relying on climatologic averages.

“Up until now, no one had been able to show a model predicts weather better than long term averages for these subseasonal forecasts,” Cohen says. “They’ve pretty much all been worse than that — you could literally flip a coin and do better. People have questioned if it’s even worth investing in models at all for this time range. We consistently beat climatology averages with our models.”

The model also showed a statistically significant improvement in the ability to predict extreme weather.

“That’s one of the more important findings, because it’s so difficult to accomplish,” Cohen says. “When the ECMWF developed their own, non-AI, error-correction to their model, it got worse at predicting extreme weather. I think that’s because traditional error, or bias, correction is always trying to get to the mean, whereas extreme weather is on the fringe of probabilities.”

Preparing for disaster

In the Nature paper, the team showed their technique could be used to improve land forecasts in most regions across the globe. They also applied their bias correction technique to other models and showed it improved those as well, putting even lesser models on par with the ECMWF’s forecasts.

“What’s nice about our model is it’s an add-on wrapper,” Cohen explains. “We used it with the ECMWF’s dynamical model because that was considered the best, but it can be used with any model. It even improves models that are already bias corrected using another AI algorithm. So it shows a robust improvement. And it’s open source and low cost.”

Cohen says the meteorological office for the Republic of Kenya has already reached out about implementing the model to improve forecasting of the annual monsoon season to improve agricultural yields this winter. He hopes other groups will also use the model.

“This could help you decide when to fertilize around rain, when there’s a freeze coming to protect crops during winter harvests, or help you avoid droughts,” Cohen says. “It could also be useful for energy and emergency management. I’ve talked to energy officials who say, ‘If I’m told two days before that an ice storm’s coming, I don’t have enough time, but if I had two weeks, that could be enough to make adequate preparations.”

The work was supported, in part, by the U.S. National Science Foundation, the Carlos Chagas Filho Foundation for Research Support, and the European Union.
