text:
NVIDIA’s board should bring Jensen Huang back under enforceable constraints while its investigation runs its course. The company has said that its founder, and its only chief executive in 33 years, will not work with NVIDIA “in any capacity.” The board’s announcement gave no reason for his departure. Nor has the board explained why no arrangement short of total exclusion would do, or how exclusion serves shareholders, and the public record supports neither. 

The board has acted as though its only options were business as usual or exile. That is a false binary. And the board’s own timeline shows how quickly it chose between them. On November 8, with the espionage reports already public, the board opened an investigation into reports that Jensen had been targeted by foreign intelligence, said it saw no reason to believe national security or company secrets had been compromised, and declared that it “has confidence in Jensen.” On November 10, its independent directors retained Wachtell Lipton to conduct an investigation. On November 11—a day after naming its investigators, and hours after the New York Times reported an affair, this time with an employee—the board reportedly forced Jensen’s immediate resignation. It decided before its own investigators could report a single finding. 

The issues before the board are serious, and the board is right to treat them that way. But unlike a morality tribunal, a board shows it takes them seriously by what its response accomplishes, not by how much it hurts. A serious response holds Jensen accountable for what happened and protects shareholders from what could happen next. A sanction designed simply to punish Jensen is not a valid exercise of business judgment, least of all when measures that cost shareholders less can contain the risks. The board has no mandate to propitiate indignant commentators.

The SEC faced a similar choice with Elon Musk. In 2018 it sued him for fraud and initially asked a court to bar him from serving as an officer of any public company. Two days later it settled for constraints instead: Musk gave up Tesla’s chairmanship, Tesla added independent directors and a committee to oversee his communications, and Elon stayed on as chief executive. SEC Chairman Jay Clayton explained why: in misconduct cases, “the skills and support of certain individuals” may be essential to a company’s future. A remedy that ignores that "protects" shareholders by destroying their investment. 

That is what NVIDIA’s board risks doing here, and needlessly, because the risks on the record have remedies short of exile. An export-control monitor can be assigned who reports to the independent directors. Affected employees can be moved out of Jensen's reporting lines and walled off from him. HR and Legal can report straight to the independent directors. The board can condition Jensen's return on candor: a single misstatement to the board or its investigators ends the arrangement for cause. Concerning concentration of power, NVIDIA has already named Harvey Jones its first-ever chair. There are solutions here short of exile. The Board has a duty to examine them, and the public record makes it hard to believe it has adequately done so. 

These constraints preserve much of the work at the center of Jensen’s immense value. That value lies in product architecture and in supplier relationships that rest on his word. Of TSMC, which makes NVIDIA’s chips, Jensen has said that after tens or hundreds of billions of dollars of business, “we don’t have a contract.” A ring-fenced role directing architecture and supplier relationships under the board’s supervision, keeps that value inside the company while Wachtell works. The board’s own announcement calls Jensen’s contributions “immeasurable.” Dan Ives has measured them anyway: he estimates NVIDIA is worth 25 to 30 percent less without Jensen, roughly $1 trillion. 

A bounded role short of exile is neither leniency nor special treatment. Jensen has lost the title he held since NVIDIA’s founding and his seat on the board, and Bloomberg estimates he forfeited about $108 million in unvested stock. If those forfeitures were to stand, they would serve accountability. Jensen is not above the law, but neither is he beyond it. The law itself leaves to the board’s business judgment what discipline best serves the company and does not require maximum penalties. Denying Jensen the middle path other executives have received, out of fear of appearing permissive, is an overcorrection—a ritual of penance performed to appease indignant voices performed with other people’s money. 

A full banishment also weakens NVIDIA’s own hand. The money was never the board’s leverage over Jensen. The work is. The board said on November 8 that Jensen had committed to cooperating with its investigation. Inside a bounded role, that commitment is enforceable, along with fiduciary duties and behavioral covenants. Outside, nothing binds him: NVIDIA’s proxy says its executives have no employment or severance agreements, and California law voids post-employment non-competes. He could recruit, too: 88 percent of NVIDIA employees answering a Blind survey wanted him to stay. 

The market for Jensen’s services opened before NVIDIA had even announced his departure. When a post on X urged “Elon please hire Jensen,” Musk replied, “That would be an honor.” Musk kept his own job in 2018 under constraints like these. 

Severity is not a fiduciary safe harbor. Sound business judgment weighs the cost of error in both directions. A board that defaults to total exclusion without waiting for the evidence is not erring on the side of prudence; it is abdicating its duty to deliberate. 

The board should withdraw its spokesperson’s “in any capacity” remark, a self-inflicted wound that appears in neither its press release nor its 8-K. It should place Jensen in a bounded role, pause its search for a permanent chief executive, and publish a target date for Wachtell’s report, which no board statement has yet supplied. Two large NVIDIA shareholders, Brad Gerstner of Altimeter Capital and Gavin Baker of Atreides Management, have rightly urged the board to keep “all options on the table, including the potential return of Jensen Huang.” A bounded role is how it keeps them open, pending the investigation. Let Wachtell’s findings, not the week’s headlines, inform what role Jensen holds for good. 

The board is right to weigh the risks of keeping Jensen. But it must also weigh the cost to shareholders of losing him.

Australian Mining

Global Commodity Rankings

Australia holds some of the world's largest reserves and is a leading producer of several key minerals.

#1 Producer: Iron Ore, Bauxite, Lithium, Rutile, and Zircon.

#1 Reserves: Iron Ore, Gold, Lead, Nickel, Rutile, Uranium, and Zinc.

#2 Producer: Gold, Alumina, and Manganese.

Key Mining Hubs & Major Projects

Western Australia: The nation's "engine room," producing 98% of Australia's iron ore and 60% of its gold. Major sites include the Pilbara (iron ore) and the Super Pit in Kalgoorlie (gold).

Queensland: A global leader in metallurgical coal (Bowen Basin) and silver/lead production (Cannington mine).

South Australia: Home to Olympic Dam, which contains the world's largest single uranium deposit and significant copper and gold reserves.

Major Players

The sector is dominated by several multinational giants and significant domestic players:

BHP: Often ranked as Australia's most valuable company; major interests in iron ore, copper, and coal.

Rio Tinto: A world leader in iron ore (Pilbara) and aluminum.

Fortescue (FMG): Primarily focused on iron ore and rapidly expanding into green energy.

Hancock Prospecting: Australia's largest private mining company, led by Gina Rinehart, the nation's wealthiest person.

South32: Spun out of BHP; manages a diversified portfolio including manganese, silver, and nickel.

2026 Trends & Developments

Critical Minerals Push: The government has introduced a $23 billion package to support domestic processing and manufacturing of critical minerals to reduce global reliance on single-country supply chains.

Uranium Rally: Prices exceeding US$100/lb have sparked renewed interest in Australian prospects like the Kalkaroo project.

M&A Activity: Major merger talks continue between giants like Rio Tinto and Glencore as they seek to consolidate copper exposure for the EV market.

Workforce Challenges: The Minerals Council of Australia is currently calling for migration reforms to address a significant "skills crunch" in the sector.

AFL reclaims grand final TV crown from NRL

(Original article by Sam Buckingham-Jones)
(RMS)

Data from OzTAM shows that the Nine Network's coverage of the NRL grand final on Sunday night boasted an average audience of 4.29 million people. Some 1.45 million people also watched the premiership decider via the 9Now app, and the match had a total audience reach of 6.05 million. In contrast, the previous weekend's AFL grand final attracted an average audience of 4.52 million on the Seven Network, and a total audience reach of 6.5 million. Ben Willee from Spinach Advertising says the fact that both codes attracted more than six million viewers underlines the value of live sport for both advertiser and broadcasters. (RMS)

Miners stay top of ATO's taxpayer table
(RMS)

The Australian Taxation Office's latest corporate tax transparency report shows that the nation's largest companies paid $87.5bn in taxes during 2024-25. Rio Tinto topped the list with $5.2bn in taxes, ahead of BHP with a total company tax bill of $3.9bn. The Mining, Energy and Water sector contributed 41.1 per cent of the corporate tax take, or $35.9bn; this was $12.5bn lower than previously, due to weaker commodity prices. The data also shows that the petroleum resource rent tax raised $1.9bn in 2024-25. (RMS)

Netflix's joint CEO Greg Peters has ruled out striking deals to licence technology companies to train their large-language models using the streaming video giant's intellectual property. Alphabet’s stake in Anthropic expands

The value of Alphabet’s stake in the artificial intelligence start-up Anthropic has soared to around $US124 billion ($178 billion), making it one of the most lucrative bets in the company’s history.The Google parent disclosed in a filing on Thursday (Friday AEST) that the value of its investments in unidentified private companies totalled roughly $US124.3 billion as of June 30. The filing noted that this value is “primarily” driven by one investment, which is a reference to Alphabet’s stake in Anthropic, according to a person familiar with the matter, who asked not to be identified because the information is not public. The company said it recorded about $US77 billion in unrealised gains from its private investments in the second quarter, without providing further details in the filing. Google has emerged as one of Anthropic’s biggest backers over the past several years. The technology giant first invested $US3 billion in the start-up starting in 2023. Earlier this year, it agreed to invest as much as $US40 billion more, consisting of $US10 billion upfront and a potential $US30 billion in additional funding tied to operational and financial milestones through 2030.Alphabet’s filing on Thursday showed the remaining commitment has fallen to $US20 billion as of June 30 from $US30 billion at the end of the first quarter, suggesting that Google invested another $US10 billion in the start-up last quarter. Rio Tinto dodges merger bullet

Rio Tinto has dodged two 'bullets' due to Glencore's rejection of a merger proposal: a possible BHP takeover bid and a dangerous acquisition. BHP looked closely at whether to bid for Rio Tinto if the latter announced a merger with Glencore. The two companies would make excellent merger partners; amongst others things, their staff and senior people have similar cultures, they are co-operating on future Australian iron ore projects and they are copper joint venture partners in Chile and the US. Meanwhile, there are significance cultural differences between Rio Tinto and Glencore; there is little doubt that Rio Tinto's CEO Simon Trott would have had doubts about a merger once he understood these cultural differences. (RMS)

News/Snapshot

Australian Mining

Global Commodity Rankings

Australia holds some of the world's largest reserves and is a leading producer of several key minerals.

#1 Producer: Iron Ore, Bauxite, Lithium, Rutile, and Zircon.

#1 Reserves: Iron Ore, Gold, Lead, Nickel, Rutile, Uranium, and Zinc.

#2 Producer: Gold, Alumina, and Manganese.

Key Mining Hubs & Major Projects

Western Australia: The nation's "engine room," producing 98% of Australia's iron ore and 60% of its gold. Major sites include the Pilbara (iron ore) and the Super Pit in Kalgoorlie (gold).

Queensland: A global leader in metallurgical coal (Bowen Basin) and silver/lead production (Cannington mine).

South Australia: Home to Olympic Dam, which contains the world's largest single uranium deposit and significant copper and gold reserves.

Major Players

The sector is dominated by several multinational giants and significant domestic players:

BHP: Often ranked as Australia's most valuable company; major interests in iron ore, copper, and coal.

Rio Tinto: A world leader in iron ore (Pilbara) and aluminum.

Fortescue (FMG): Primarily focused on iron ore and rapidly expanding into green energy.

Hancock Prospecting: Australia's largest private mining company, led by Gina Rinehart, the nation's wealthiest person.

South32: Spun out of BHP; manages a diversified portfolio including manganese, silver, and nickel.

2026 Trends & Developments

Critical Minerals Push: The government has introduced a $23 billion package to support domestic processing and manufacturing of critical minerals to reduce global reliance on single-country supply chains.

Uranium Rally: Prices exceeding US$100/lb have sparked renewed interest in Australian prospects like the Kalkaroo project.

M&A Activity: Major merger talks continue between giants like Rio Tinto and Glencore as they seek to consolidate copper exposure for the EV market.

Workforce Challenges: The Minerals Council of Australia is currently calling for migration reforms to address a significant "skills crunch" in the sector.

text:
Fred Saberi deserves recognition for his incisive analysis. He connects American strategy, the interests of regional powers, and the danger that existing regime networks could survive a political transition. There is one point, however, that I would give greater weight: The will of the Iranian people must be at the center of the entire discussion.

To me, the analysis describes a triangle. At one corner stands the United States, seeking to maintain its position in the Middle East and its standing against Russia and China, while its resolve operates under the time constraints of domestic politics. At the second stand Arab Islamic governments, some of which may fear that a free, secular Iran could also call their own political and religious order into question. At the third stands the Iranian people, demanding territorial integrity, secular government, equal rights, and free elections. While governments weigh their strategic interests, people in Iran pay for their resistance with their freedom and their lives.

That is precisely why the contradictions in the international response matter so much. In January, the UN Human Rights Council condemned the violent suppression of the protests and authorized further investigations. Yet on November 11, Iran was reelected to the UN Committee for Programme and Coordination with 144 votes. This is not a seat on the Human Rights Council, but it still gives the country’s leadership institutional influence and international recognition. The states casting those votes are responsible for that election, not independent human rights organizations. To me, this exposes a substantial gap between the stated commitment to human rights and political action.

Sanctions are in place, including asset freezes, travel bans, and export restrictions. The central question, however, is whether their enforcement and scope are adequate given the scale of the repression. Governments that publicly condemn the violence must explain how they are actually weakening the financial, political, and organizational foundations that sustain it.

Diplomatic relations also belong in this discussion. Germany ordered the closure of all three Iranian consulates general, but the embassy remained open. Diplomatic contacts do not, by themselves, mean approval of the regime. Nevertheless, governments must explain what specific purpose these relationships serve and what consequences further crimes will carry.

An earlier, consistently coordinated policy targeting the regime’s power structures and financial networks might have helped prevent military escalation. That cannot be proven retrospectively, but it must remain part of the discussion about political accountability. The nuclear threat belongs in that discussion as well: Nuclear weapons would give such a regime additional power to blackmail others; their actual use would pose a catastrophic risk.

My disagreement with Saberi’s emphasis is therefore this: Iran’s future must not be judged primarily by the advantages it offers Washington, Riyadh, Moscow, or Beijing. What matters is whether Iranians can finally determine their own country’s future. Governments that invoke human rights must be held accountable for whether their policies uphold that principle.

text:
Carl DeMaio: Better 12 Fighters Than 20 Collaborators

Republican Assemblyman Carl DeMaio is done pretending the size of the GOP caucus ever mattered in Sacramento. After surviving his race while many colleagues lost, he told California Politics 360 that dropping from 20 Republicans to around 12 changes nothing.

“Someone asked me a few days ago, well, you’re going from 20 in the Assembly for Republicans down to, what, 12? You know, what does that mean? What’s the difference? I said, there’s no difference. Do you think we had any relevancy or any impact on legislation when we were 20? No.”

DeMaio laid out the real job of an opposition party: give voice to the voiceless, offer alternatives to California’s problems, and apply public pressure on a broken system. He rejected the idea that more numbers equal more influence.

“I would rather have 12 principled fighters who are committed to working every day to offer alternatives to California’s problems than 20 milquetoast get along get along collaborators. Because, you know, you’re not really doing any good and you’re certainly not giving millions of Californians who disagree with the course of our state any sort of voice.”

When asked whether the incumbents who lost were milquetoast, DeMaio acknowledged past problems in the caucus but pointed to recent improvement. “I think that in the past we’ve had Republicans in Sacramento that are milquetoast. And I’m so proud of the fact that the Assembly caucus for the last two years has been much more a united and vocal caucus for change.”

He warned against any return to the old approach. “There are some who say the solution is to go back to being sycophants. I totally disagree. That’s what led us to a superminority. We have got to offer positive, bold alternatives to the failed policies of the Democrat supermajority.”

DeMaio expects the political pendulum to swing and says the Republican Party must learn from its mistakes so it is ready when it does. For now, his message is clear: fewer seats, sharper fight.

AI Overview
On July 14, 2016, a deadly terrorist truck attack took place in Nice, France, along the Promenade des Anglais next to the Mediterranean SEA. 
The Attack: During Bastille Day celebrations, a 19-ton rented cargo truck plowed through a crowd for over a mile.
Casualties: 86 people were killed (including children) and hundreds more were injured.
The Perpetrator: Mohamed Lahouaiej Bouhlel, a 31-year-old Tunisian-born resident of Nice, was shot and killed by police at the scene.
Aftermath & Convictions: The Islamic State (ISIS) claimed responsibility, and in December 2022, a French court convicted eight co-defendants for their roles in supplying weapons or aiding the plot, handing down prison sentences ranging from 2 to 18 years. Details of the trial and verdict can be reviewed via NPR.

Déniz or Deniz (also written Denis in some parts of South America, see Denis) is a Spanish-Portuguese surname derived from the French surname De Niz. Deniz, although of different origin, is also a Turkish name.

MARKET UPDATE — MONDAY, 16 NOVEMBER 2026

Three tests in four days will decide how the AI trade ends the year.

Nvidia reports on Tuesday without the founder who built it. Anthropic prices one of the largest share sales in history on Wednesday. On Thursday, Trump sits down with Xi and Putin. Investors are starting the week by selling chips, bitcoin and gold, and buying dollars.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

🟢 MARKETS: TECH SOLD, THE REST CALM

💠 Futures at 7:30 am ET:

🔸 S&P 500: −0.78% to 7,524.00

🔸 Nasdaq 100: −1.64% to 27,575.75

🔸 Dow: −0.16% to 52,333

🔸 Euro Stoxx 50: −0.65% to 6,365.70

🔸 VIX: +6.5% to 20.56

💡 Futures show where shares are likely to open. A Dow that has barely moved beside a falling Nasdaq means the selling is concentrated in technology, not spread across the market. The VIX is Wall Street's "fear gauge". Just above 20, it signals rising nerves, not panic.

💠 Last week the S&P 500 rose 2.5% and the Nasdaq 2.3%, ending a four-week losing run, according to Barron's. A leading chip-stock fund bounced 9.3% after losing 30% in five weeks.

💠 This morning the chip sector is handing some of that back.

🔸 Nvidia closed Friday down 2.01% at $162.85, on about twice its normal volume. Before the open it is down a further 3.65% at $156.90 (7:20 am ET). That leaves it roughly a third below its early-October peak.

🔸 The rest of the chain is falling harder (about 7:25 am ET): CoreWeave −8.1% at $48.85, Sandisk −6.9% at $823.58, Micron −5.7% at $734.01. AMD, Marvell and Broadcom are also lower.

🔸 TSMC, which manufactures Nvidia's chips, closed almost 6% lower in Taiwan. Its US-listed shares are down 5.4% at $377.11.

💡 CoreWeave rents out Nvidia chips and relies on borrowed money, so it is the stock most exposed to both worries at once: Nvidia's troubles and tighter credit. Micron and Sandisk make the memory chips that AI servers need.

🔸 The WSJ notes that last week investors separated Nvidia's rivals from Nvidia's customers. Today they are selling the whole supply chain.

🔸 Intel is down 5.3% at $56.48. Shareholders have filed a proposed class action alleging it hid the scale of a PC sales slump before its 29% one-day fall on 30 October. Intel hasn't commented.

💠 The wider market is holding up better than the headlines suggest. The FT's Unhedged column calculates that since 29 October Nvidia has lost about $1.2trn in market value, yet the S&P 500 is down less than 2% and about 300 of its 500 members have risen.

Robert Armstrong, Financial Times:

"People are fleeing data centre risk, not equity risk."

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

🟢 NVIDIA: THE CALL EVERYONE WILL HEAR

💠 Nvidia reports on Tuesday, five days after Jensen Huang resigned. Interim CEO Colette Kress, the long-time finance chief, will take the questions.

🔸 The bar Nvidia set for itself in August: revenue of $108bn, give or take 2%, and a gross margin of about 74%, assuming no data-centre chip sales to China.

💡 Gross margin is the share of each sales dollar left after the cost of making the product. It shows how much pricing power a company has.

🔸 Analysts expect management to say little about Huang. Watch four things instead: the sales forecast, margins, any change in language on China, and whether Nvidia will keep financing its own customers.

💠 A public fight has broken out over who should run the company.

🔸 A "Stand With Jensen" petition calling for Huang's return has more than 170,000 signatures, including Elon Musk's. The FT reports Huang has discussed a comeback with confidants. Shareholders Brad Gerstner and Gavin Baker have urged the board to keep every option open.

🔸 Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent wants the opposite. He told Fox News the board must hire from outside:

"Just what was going on inside the company, they need a dramatic shake-up."

🔸 Bessent also wants answers within 10 days on whether Nvidia ignored warning signs that Singapore-based shell companies were routing its chips to China.

🔸 The FT reports the board has approached Rene Haas, head of chip designer Arm. The board says no formal search has begun. Internal candidates include Kress and data-centre chief Ian Buck.

💠 The open chequebook is closing. 
The WSJ reports that Huang told partners last month they must secure upfront payments from their own customers to get chips. Kress, who was already wary of some deals, is expected to tighten further.

🔸 UBS analyst Tim Arcuri estimates a pullback could take $50bn or more of financing out of the market.

🔸 PitchBook counts Nvidia in 129 venture-capital deals this year, 27% of global venture deal value.

🔸 The FT lists four pending deals now in doubt: Thinking Machines Lab, Groq, Reflection AI and the $12.9bn purchase of Hugging Face.

Elon Musk, on X:

"Many of those deals were a handshake with Jensen, not a written contract."

💡 Nvidia didn't only sell chips. It lent its financial strength so that customers could afford them. If that support shrinks while interest rates are rising, the weakest AI companies will struggle to raise money.

💠 Washington is pulling in two directions.

🔸 Both parties back bills to tighten chip exports to China. They are likely to be attached to the must-pass defence budget before year-end, the FT reports. Huang has agreed to testify before a House committee.

🔸 Yet the WSJ reports the administration still plans to name Nvidia among more than two dozen AI "national champions" within a week. The label brings faster export licences and access to federal financing. The date could slip.

🔸 Shareholders have sued Nvidia and Huang over his disclosures. The FT reports Nvidia's insurance covers its executives personally, up to $900m, but not the company itself against such claims.

The counterargument: 
Gabelli's Hendi Susanto says customers are unlikely to cancel orders and sees no major effect on Nvidia's product plans for at least two years. The scandal has changed who runs Nvidia. It hasn't yet changed demand for its chips. Tuesday's numbers will test that.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

🟢 ANTHROPIC: A $100BN ASK IN A BRUISED MARKET

💠 The Claude maker plans to sell 825m shares at $70–78 each, raising $57.75bn to $64.35bn and valuing the company at $1.26trn to $1.41trn. Pricing is expected on Wednesday, with Nasdaq trading from Thursday under the ticker ANT. The WSJ says trading could slip to Friday.

🔸 There is also a separate $26bn share sale to technology partners, and banks can sell up to 123.75m extra shares. Add those and the total approaches $100bn at the top of the range.

🔸 Barron's ranks the IPO alone as the second-largest ever, behind SpaceX's $85.7bn in June.

🔸 The FT reports bankers are considering a higher price after heavy demand. That is not confirmed.

🔸 The business: annualised revenue reached about $81bn at the end of October, up from $47bn in May, the WSJ reports. Against that sit roughly $900bn of spending commitments for cloud capacity, chips and data centres, according to Barron's.

💡 Annualised (or "run-rate") revenue takes recent sales and scales them up to a full year. It shows speed of growth, not money already earned.

🔸 Seven co-founders will keep voting control, so ordinary shareholders get little say.

💠 The backdrop is poor. 
The FT calculates that the ten largest US IPOs of 2026 have fallen 20.5% on average from their offer prices. 

🔸 Nasdaq will fast-track Anthropic into the Nasdaq 100 index as soon as 15 days after listing, as it did with SpaceX. Index funds must then buy at whatever the price is. SpaceX has lagged the index by more than 10% since it was added.

💡 A great company and a great share price are different things. If buyers overpay on day one, the business can thrive while its shareholders lose money.

Bull case for the listing: it is the first pure AI company investors can buy directly, and a warm reception would calm the whole sector. 

Bear case: it asks for about $100bn from a market that is already tired of new share sales.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

🟢 THE AI DEBATE: WALL STREET VS THE CENTRAL BANKS

💠 Morgan Stanley told clients to hold as much in shares as their rules allow. It targets 8,700 for the S&P 500 by the end of 2027, about 15% above Friday's close.

Serena Tang's team, Morgan Stanley:

"With risk assets having cheapened, we embrace risk."

🔸 The bank expects the biggest US cloud companies to spend $1.7trn on AI infrastructure in 2027 and $1.8trn in 2028. It doesn't expect a federal pause on data-centre building, and it thinks the market can absorb a Fed rate rise in December and another in 2027.

💠 On the same morning, two central bankers warned about the same boom.

🔸 ECB Vice-President Boris Vujcic said AI has grown from a question of expensive shares into a risk to the whole financial system. He cited a $5.5trn financing need for large US tech firms through 2030, opaque off-balance-sheet deals, and governments competing with Big Tech for the same pool of capital.

🔸 Fed Governor Michael Barr said the build-up of data-centre debt recalls the telecoms boom of the late 1990s. He added a newer worry: if traders rely on a few similar AI models, they may all buy and sell at the same moment.

💠 The evidence so far cuts both ways.

🔸 Credit: a WSJ investigation found tech-focussed hedge funds lost 12.6% in October, and the high-yield bond market has effectively shut to AI borrowers after they raised $13bn in September.

🔸 Politics: Cleanview data in the WSJ show all of OpenAI's roughly 14 gigawatts of planned capacity not yet under construction sits in states whose governors back a pause on data centres. About 10 gigawatts is in one Ohio project. Microsoft's exposure is 45%, Amazon's 42%, and Google's and Anthropic's about 20%.

🔸 Concentration: Ruchir Sharma writes in the FT that 80% of global equity flows have gone into US shares this year, double the long-run average, and that foreigners now hold $25trn of them. He estimates a 25% fall in US stocks would cut American consumer spending by about 2%. That is a scenario, not a forecast.

🔸 Deutsche Bank's counterpoint: the market's three big fears (an oil shock, an AI slowdown and a bond-market squeeze) are unlikely to strike together. When AI fears rise, bond yields tend to fall, which eases the debt worry.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

🟢 BONDS, THE FED & THE DOLLAR

💠 Treasury yields are easing this morning: 
the 10-year is at 5.117% (−2.2 basis points), the 2-year at 4.827% (−2.5) and the 30-year at 5.452% (−1.8).

💡 A basis point is one-hundredth of a percentage point. Yields are the interest rate the US government pays to borrow, and mortgage and business loan rates follow them.

🔸 Last week the 10-year yield posted its biggest weekly rise since April 2025, the WSJ reports, after a third hot inflation reading in a row. Traders now expect a rate rise at the Fed's 8–9 December meeting. In October the Fed held at 3.75–4%, with two officials voting to raise.

🔸 Peter Boockvar of OnePoint BFG thinks yields have peaked for now. He sees the Fed adjusting rates, not starting a long series of rises, because AI spending is likely to slow.

🔸 The minutes of the October meeting arrive on Wednesday.

💠 The dollar index is at 103.45, around its strongest since April 2025. The euro briefly dipped below $1.10, its lowest since 10 April 2025. The pound hit a five-month low near $1.319.

💡 Higher US interest rates pull money into dollars. A stronger dollar usually weighs on gold, bitcoin and emerging markets.

🔸 Gold is at $3,878 an ounce, back below $3,900.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

🟢 OIL & THE GULF: A GLUT ON PAPER, MINES IN THE WATER

💠 Brent crude is down 0.9% at $94.94 a barrel, despite the worst weekend of Gulf headlines in weeks.

💠 Why it is falling: supply. 
Goldman Sachs now expects the world to produce about 2m barrels a day more than it uses next year. It sees Brent averaging $88 in 2027 and sliding to $78 by the end of that year. The International Energy Agency sees an even larger surplus, about 3.8m barrels a day.

🔸 The reasons: Gulf producers are exporting more through pipelines that avoid the Strait of Hormuz, Brazil is pumping more, and high prices and electric vehicles are cutting Chinese demand.

🔸 The catch: petrol, diesel and jet fuel remain tight because refining capacity is growing slowly. Relief at the pump will lag any fall in crude.

💠 Why it isn't falling faster: the war risk is rising again.

🔸 Bab el-Mandeb: Saudi-backed Yemeni forces withdrew on Sunday to defend Aden, leaving the Iran-aligned Houthis in control of the area overlooking the strait.

💡 Gulf oil has two exits. Hormuz is on one side of the Arabian Peninsula. Bab el-Mandeb, the gateway to the Red Sea and the Suez Canal, is on the other. Iran and its ally now press on both.

🔸 The bypass: Saudi Arabia sends about 4m barrels a day, roughly 4% of world supply, through its East-West Pipeline to the Red Sea. The Houthis claim they struck two pumping stations on Sunday. Riyadh hasn't confirmed it.

🔸 Hormuz: Iran's Revolutionary Guards say five tankers hit mines and caught fire over the weekend. Reuters could not verify this, and the US says the main routes are clear. The UN counts 25 seafarers killed since the war began, with October the worst month for incidents.

🔸 Bahrain: Iran says it fired six drones at a US radar site yesterday. Bahrain says it intercepted the attack. These were its first threat alerts since September. Al Jazeera reports a third US aircraft carrier has arrived in the region.

🔸 US intelligence estimates Iran still has 1,500 to 2,500 missiles, the WSJ reports. Officials call it a low-confidence figure, but it contradicts claims that Iran's military was destroyed.

🔸 Iran's foreign minister visits Oman, a mediator, on Tuesday.

A tension in the data: Reuters reports crude is leaving the Gulf at close to pre-war levels, while UK maritime authorities put Hormuz ship traffic about 65% below pre-war. Both can hold if more oil now moves by pipeline, but the gap deserves watching.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

🟢 CHINA & THE SHENZHEN SUMMIT

💠 China's October figures missed forecasts across the board:

🔸 Industrial output: +4.8% on the year (forecast 5.3%, September 5.5%)

🔸 Retail sales: +0.4% (forecast 0.8%, September 1.1%)

🔸 Fixed-asset investment: −8.1% for January–October (−7.2% to September). Capital Economics calculates October alone fell 16.1%, the steepest drop since early 2020.

🔸 Property investment: −21.6% so far this year

🔸 One caveat: a holiday shifted some spending into September, which flatters that month and hurts October.

💡 China is making far more than its own households buy. That means cheaper Chinese exports for the world and weaker demand for oil and metals, which is part of the oil surplus story.

💠 On Thursday Trump meets Xi on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific summit in Shenzhen. The first three-way meeting with Putin follows, with no agreed agenda. The FT expects few concrete results.

🔸 The market issue is rare earths. Washington says China is delivering only about two-thirds of what it pledged. The US–China trade truce expires on 10 January.

💡 Rare earths are minerals needed for chips, electric cars and weapons. China dominates their supply, which gives it leverage in any trade dispute.

🔸 Ahead of the summit, the US and allies including Japan, the UK, Australia, India and South Korea signed an accord to protect AI supply chains from China.

💠 Ukraine: President Zelenskyy says US negotiators asked whether Kyiv would give up the rest of the Donbas region in return for NATO membership. He would put any firm offer to the Ukrainian people. Washington and NATO haven't confirmed the proposal, and Russia opposes Ukrainian membership.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

🟢 CRYPTO: THE DOLLAR'S VICTIM

💠 Bitcoin is down 1.97% at $64,023 after dropping below $62000 yesterday, and ether 2.17% at $1,795. Bitcoin is about 26% below its September peak, the WSJ reports, and has fallen through the $66,000 level BTIG flagged last week.

🔸 Coinbase, Strategy and Robinhood are all lower before the open.

🔸 XM's Achilleas Georgolopoulos says gold and bitcoin are both suffering from the strong dollar. He sees little chance of a rally until rate-rise bets ease or oil falls further.

💡 Bitcoin and gold pay no interest. When interest rates and the dollar climb, holding them costs more in missed income.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

🟢 ALSO MOVING

💠 SpaceX caught Starship's upper stage at its Texas launch tower on Saturday, a first, after about 22 hours in orbit and the release of 26 Starlink satellites. The booster was lost after a fuel problem. Bernstein calls reusability the most important step towards justifying SpaceX's valuation. 
A rival stumbled: The Economist reports a Vulcan rocket carrying 40 Amazon internet satellites exploded after lift-off.

💠 US air travel is recovering from an air-traffic-control equipment failure. About 9,200 flights were cancelled on Friday and 6,700 on Saturday. The FAA is investigating and sees no sign of a cyberattack. The transport secretary wants $50bn to modernise the system.

💠 Europe is looking beyond Palantir. Reuters reports Germany's shortlist for military AI software excludes the US firm, France aims to field its own system by mid-2027, and the Netherlands wants a European option within two years. No contract has been lost yet. The trend is governments paying for independence over capability.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

🟢 CALENDAR

Today:

🔸 Empire State manufacturing survey

🔸 Fed Chair Kevin Warsh gives opening remarks at a productivity and jobs conference

🔸 Earnings: Tyson Foods, Baidu

Coming up:

🔸 Tue 17 Nov: Nvidia, Home Depot and Disney results. October retail sales (forecast +0.2% after +0.8%), industrial production, import prices. Iran's foreign minister in Oman.

🔸 Wed 18 Nov: Fed minutes. Housing starts. Target, Lowe's, TJX and Palo Alto Networks results. Anthropic prices its IPO. Asia-Pacific summit opens.

🔸 Thu 19 Nov: Anthropic expected to start trading. Walmart and Alibaba results. Jobless claims. Trump–Xi meeting and the three-way with Putin.

🔸 Fri 20 Nov: consumer sentiment. China's loan-rate decision.

🔸 8–9 Dec: Fed decision

🔸 10 Jan: US–China trade truce expires

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

🟢 WHAT IT MEANS

🔸 The sell-off has been selective so far. Money is leaving the companies that build and finance data centres, not the stock market. That is the healthy version of a correction, and it lasts only while credit stays open for everyone else.

🔸 Nvidia's call is about funding as much as chips. If Kress confirms a retreat from financing customers, the pressure moves down the chain to cloud start-ups and AI labs with large bills and small revenues.

🔸 Anthropic is the market's referendum on AI. A strong debut says investors still want the theme. A weak one, after a year of losing IPOs, would hit sentiment well beyond one stock.

🔸 Morgan Stanley and the central banks can both be right for a while. AI spending can lift profits in 2027 and still leave too much debt behind it. The thing to watch is whether lenders keep funding the build-out.

🔸 Oil is caught between a growing surplus and two threatened sea lanes. The surplus is winning this morning. A confirmed hit on Saudi Arabia's pipeline would reverse that quickly.

🔸 The dollar connects much of today's price action. A stronger dollar and higher yields explain weaker gold, weaker bitcoin and a euro at a 19-month low.

Bull case: Nvidia meets its $108bn guide and steadies investors, Anthropic prices well and holds its gains, the Fed minutes show little appetite for a big rise, crude keeps drifting lower, and Trump and Xi extend the truce.

Bear case: Nvidia's outlook or its financing retreat spooks the supply chain, Anthropic trades below its offer price, yields turn higher again, the East-West Pipeline takes real damage, and Shenzhen ends without progress on rare earths.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

💭 THOUGHT FOR THE DAY

"The harder the conflict, the more glorious the triumph."

— Thomas Paine, The American Crisis (1776)

Weeks like this one feel heavy because so much rides on them. They are also when patient investors learn the most about what they own and why. Stay curious, stay disciplined, and let the hard weeks do their work for you.

text:
$BXDC Q3 2026 earnings: Blackstone Digital lands its first deal, but fees now start

Blackstone Digital Infrastructure Trust, a real estate trust that buys data centers, signed its first property deal after holding only cash since May. Third-quarter net income of $15.6 million, or $0.17 per share in adjusted cash flow, still came from interest on uninvested cash across a full quarter. Alongside the results, chief executive Nick Pell announced an agreement to buy a 75% stake in 13 Amazon data centers valued at $5 billion.

• AFFO per adjusted share: $𝟎.𝟏𝟕 ($0.08 in the partial prior quarter)
• Amazon deal gross value (100%): $𝟓.𝟎𝐁 ($3.76B for the trust's 75.1% share by our math)
• Initial property yield (cap rate): 𝟕.𝟎% (5.75%–7.0%+ target range)
• Formal financial outlook: 𝐍𝐨𝐧𝐞 𝐢𝐬𝐬𝐮𝐞𝐝 (consistent with prior quarter)

⚖️ 𝐕𝐞𝐫𝐝𝐢𝐜𝐭: 🟢 Bullish

The story got better because the trust committed its initial cash at a 7% property yield that beats the low-6% rates management previously cited. By our math, its share of the deal brings $263 million in first-year rent with 2.75% yearly increases, leaving room for profit above borrowing costs. One caution: the management fee waiver expired on November 15, and the release gives no closing date or debt terms.

The question now is how much of that 7% property yield reaches shareholders after borrowing costs and management fees. Cheap property-level debt and a fast closing would lift per-share cash flow quickly, while expensive credit-line borrowing or closing delays would eat into the gains. The upcoming quarterly filing and deal closing terms will settle the math.

[Model: Gemini 4 Argon. Full article with charts - link in bio]

🐂 𝐁𝐮𝐥𝐥 𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐞

🟢🟢 𝐅𝐢𝐫𝐬𝐭 𝐃𝐞𝐚𝐥 𝐂𝐨𝐦𝐦𝐢𝐭𝐬 𝐂𝐚𝐩𝐢𝐭𝐚𝐥 𝐈𝐧𝐭𝐨 𝐀𝐦𝐚𝐳𝐨𝐧 𝐃𝐚𝐭𝐚 𝐂𝐞𝐧𝐭𝐞𝐫𝐬
Blackstone Digital Infrastructure Trust raised nearly $2 billion in May to buy data centers, but it held only cash through June. Now the real estate trust has its first deal. Chief executive Nick Pell announced that the company "agreed to acquire a 75% controlling interest in two newly developed powered shell data center campuses" through a sale-leaseback with Amazon, where the tech giant sells the buildings and leases them back.

• Total property value: $5.0 billion across 13 buildings and 647 megawatts of capacity
• Trust ownership share: 75.1%, or about $3.76 billion of gross value by our math
• Lease length: 12 years initially, and up to 32 years with two 10-year renewal options

This agreement matters because it puts the trust's cash to work in one stroke. Buying properties directly from cloud giants also widens the pool of available deals, "as the hyperscaler sale-leaseback channel doubles our total addressable market," Pell said.

What to watch: the exact closing date and debt package in the quarterly filing. Those details will show when rent begins to replace interest on cash.

🟢 𝐒𝐞𝐯𝐞𝐧 𝐏𝐞𝐫𝐜𝐞𝐧𝐭 𝐘𝐢𝐞𝐥𝐝 𝐂𝐥𝐞𝐚𝐫𝐬 𝐁𝐨𝐫𝐫𝐨𝐰𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐂𝐨𝐬𝐭 𝐇𝐮𝐫𝐝𝐥𝐞
A central question for the trust was whether property yields would beat its borrowing costs. Last quarter, management pointed to market deals yielding just above 6%, which barely cleared the interest rate on its credit line. The Amazon portfolio pays an initial capitalization rate—first-year rent divided by property value—of 7.0%, with triple-net leases where the tenant pays property taxes, insurance and maintenance.

In the transaction presentation, the real estate group described the 7.0% yield for a powered shell—a building with power and cooling hookups where the tenant installs its own servers—as "driving compelling relative value and operating efficiency". By our math, that rate generates $350 million of first-year base rent across the properties, or $262.9 million for the trust's 75.1% share, while 2.75% yearly rent increases add growth.

What to watch: the interest rate on the debt used to fund the $3.76 billion purchase share. A borrowing cost well below 7.0% will allow leverage to lift per-share cash flow.

🐻 𝐁𝐞𝐚𝐫 𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐞

🔴🔴 𝐌𝐚𝐧𝐚𝐠𝐞𝐦𝐞𝐧𝐭 𝐅𝐞𝐞𝐬 𝐑𝐞𝐬𝐭𝐚𝐫𝐭 𝐁𝐞𝐟𝐨𝐫𝐞 𝐃𝐞𝐚𝐥 𝐂𝐥𝐨𝐬𝐞𝐬
"Today marks an important milestone for BXDC with our inaugural investment in thirteen newly constructed data centers across two campuses through a sale-leaseback with Amazon," chief executive Nick Pell said on November 16. However, signing an agreement is not the same as closing it. The trust's six-month waiver on its 1% annual management fee expired on November 15, one day before the announcement.

Throughout the third quarter, the real estate vehicle still earned its $15.6 million of net income from uninvested cash. Because the Amazon purchase has not closed yet, the trust now owes management fees to its Blackstone manager while still collecting lower cash yields. The release also notes risks around "our ability to complete the BXDC Transaction on the currently anticipated terms or at all" and omitted both a closing timeline and financing breakdown.

What to watch: the closing schedule and fourth-quarter management fee expense in the full quarterly report. Every week between November 15 and closing reduces per-share earnings.

🔴 𝐎𝐧𝐞 𝐂𝐥𝐨𝐮𝐝 𝐆𝐢𝐚𝐧𝐭 𝐁𝐚𝐜𝐤𝐬 𝐀𝐥𝐥 𝐈𝐧𝐢𝐭𝐢𝐚𝐥 𝐑𝐞𝐧𝐭
Putting the entire initial cash pile into a single deal creates total reliance on one customer. Amazon guarantees 100% of the rent across all 13 buildings in the $5.0 billion portfolio. While Amazon holds a strong AA credit rating from S&P and signed a 12-year initial lease, the trust has no tenant diversity until it raises more money and buys additional properties.

The transaction also stretches the geographic target slightly. Management aims to buy primarily in top-tier data center hubs. More than two-thirds of the Amazon portfolio sits in Northern Indiana near Chicago, which fits that goal, but less than one-third sits in Mississippi, a smaller market. Relying on a single tenant across just two locations leaves long-term renewal value tied to Amazon's future computing needs.

What to watch: future property acquisitions and how the trust funds them. Adding new tenants will require issuing new shares or taking on more debt.

🔴 𝐑𝐢𝐬𝐤𝐬 𝐭𝐡𝐢𝐬 𝐪𝐮𝐚𝐫𝐭𝐞𝐫 𝐝𝐢𝐝𝐧'𝐭 𝐚𝐧𝐬𝐰𝐞𝐫
Two standing concerns around how the trust grows and pays its external manager received no new detail in the earnings release or transaction slides.

• Issuing new shares to grow: by our math, the $3.76 billion purchase share absorbs the trust's initial cash and debt capacity, so buying more properties requires selling new stock; the release gives no capital-raising plan.
• External manager fee structure: the base fee equals 1% of market value, which rewards growing the share count regardless of per-share profit; the quarterly filing will show related-party fee details.

👓 𝐎𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐫 𝐓𝐡𝐞𝐦𝐞𝐬

𝐈𝐧𝐝𝐢𝐚𝐧𝐚 𝐏𝐨𝐰𝐞𝐫 𝐂𝐨𝐬𝐭𝐬 𝐃𝐫𝐚𝐰 𝐃𝐚𝐭𝐚 𝐂𝐞𝐧𝐭𝐞𝐫 𝐆𝐫𝐨𝐰𝐭𝐡
More than two-thirds of the Amazon portfolio sits in Northern Indiana, which borders the Chicago market. According to the presentation, electricity in Indiana costs 20% less than in neighboring Illinois. Because data centers consume vast amounts of electricity, cloud companies are building across the state line: industry forecasts in the slides show Indiana data center capacity more than tripling from 1,426 megawatts in 2026 to 4,722 megawatts by 2028.

— • — • —

💲 𝐎𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐫 𝐊𝐏𝐈𝐬

𝐖𝐞𝐢𝐠𝐡𝐭𝐞𝐝-𝐚𝐯𝐞𝐫𝐚𝐠𝐞 𝐬𝐡𝐚𝐫𝐞𝐬 (𝟐𝟔𝐐𝟑): 𝟏𝟎𝟎.𝟕 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇒ stable
Standard weighted shares doubled from 50.2 million last quarter to 100.7 million. Last quarter included days before the May initial public offering, which understated the share count and made standard net income per share look artificially high at $0.14. Starting this quarter, standard shares match post-offering adjusted shares, so net income per share of $0.15 reflects the true count.

𝐍𝐨𝐧-𝐨𝐩𝐞𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐜𝐨𝐬𝐭 𝐚𝐝𝐣𝐮𝐬𝐭𝐦𝐞𝐧𝐭𝐬 (𝟐𝟔𝐐𝟑): $𝟏.𝟎𝟓 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇗ accelerating
To calculate adjusted funds from operations (AFFO)—a cash flow measure for real estate trusts—the company adds back non-cash and setup costs to net income. In the third quarter, organization setup costs dropped 77.2% from last quarter to $122 thousand, while amortization of credit-line financing fees doubled to $670 thousand on a full 90-day calendar.

— • — • —

❓ 𝐊𝐞𝐲 𝐐𝐮𝐞𝐬𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧𝐬

𝐖𝐡𝐞𝐧 𝐝𝐨𝐞𝐬 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐀𝐦𝐚𝐳𝐨𝐧 𝐝𝐞𝐚𝐥 𝐜𝐥𝐨𝐬𝐞 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐬𝐭𝐚𝐫𝐭 𝐩𝐚𝐲𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐫𝐞𝐧𝐭?
The 1% annual management fee waiver expired on November 15, one day before the deal announcement. Every week before closing leaves the trust paying full management fees while earning lower interest on cash.

𝐇𝐨𝐰 𝐰𝐢𝐥𝐥 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐭𝐫𝐮𝐬𝐭 𝐟𝐢𝐧𝐚𝐧𝐜𝐞 𝐢𝐭𝐬 $𝟑.𝟕𝟔 𝐛𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐬𝐡𝐚𝐫𝐞?
By our math, a 75.1% stake in the $5.0 billion portfolio costs $3.76 billion, requiring about $1.8 billion of debt alongside the initial cash. The interest rate on that debt determines how much of the 7.0% yield reaches shareholders.

𝐖𝐡𝐨 𝐨𝐰𝐧𝐬 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐫𝐞𝐦𝐚𝐢𝐧𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝟐𝟒.𝟗% 𝐣𝐨𝐢𝐧𝐭 𝐯𝐞𝐧𝐭𝐮𝐫𝐞 𝐬𝐭𝐚𝐤𝐞?
The presentation notes strong alignment through a joint venture structure where the trust holds 75.1%, but it does not state whether Amazon, another Blackstone fund, or an outside partner holds the rest.

𝐖𝐡𝐚𝐭 𝐢𝐬 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐝𝐢𝐯𝐢𝐝𝐞𝐧𝐝 𝐩𝐥𝐚𝐧 𝐨𝐧𝐜𝐞 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐝𝐞𝐚𝐥 𝐜𝐥𝐨𝐬𝐞𝐬?
The trust has paid only nominal distributions while holding cash. With $262.9 million of initial annual base rent for its share on the way by our math, investors need the timeline for a regular dividend.

text:
Despite the “dot-com crash” in 2000, the tech industry remained an attractive career destination for many who believed technology represented the future. The digital age — defined by global connectivity and computers — had firmly taken hold, and over time, the tech industry emerged as a dominant force in the labor market. High-paying jobs for engineers, designers, and professionals across a wide range of fields became increasingly common. 

MIT PhD student JS Tan SM ’22 was among those who, upon graduating from Brown University and Rhode Island School of Design in 2015, joined the tech industry. 

“A lot of us had this idea that technology, and in particular the technologies related to the internet, had the potential for bringing about a more progressive version of the world,” Tan says. 

Google echoed this ethos to its employees with its once-famous motto, “don’t be evil,” as their informal corporate philosophy and code of conduct guideline. They’ve since dropped the tagline.

But in time, particularly with the start of the first Trump administration, some tech industry employees found themselves questioning if their employers were really intent on supporting policies to support a more democratic world. According to Tan, their willingness to publicly oppose their employers’ actions — at first successfully — is currently experiencing an anti-worker backlash. 

Now, Tan and his former tech industry colleague Clarissa Redwine have published a book on the rise and fall of the tech worker labor movement. “Against Tech Oligarchy: Worker Resistance in the World’s Most Powerful Industry” (Haymarket Books, 2026) chronicles how tech workers organized themselves, the effective strategies they used, and the effect the movement had on Silicon Valley labor politics over the past decade.

Documenting a movement from within

In 2017, Tan was working for Microsoft and Redwine for Kickstarter, when President Donald Trump signed an executive order suspending entry into the United States for nationals from seven predominantly Muslim countries for 90 days, and suspending Syrian refugees from entering the country indefinitely. 

“As a whole, I think the tech sector really pushed back against this,” says Tan. “[OpenAI co-founder] Sam Altman participated in protests of this ban at the airport. In fact, the day before he joined these protests, he wrote in his blog that the tech industry needed to take a stand against the Trump administration, and particularly its immigration policies.” 

Altman’s Jan. 28, 2017, blog post read, in part, “Tech companies go to extraordinary lengths to recruit and retain employees; those employees have a lot of leverage. If employees push companies to do something, I believe they’ll have to. At a minimum, companies should take a public stance. But talking is only somewhat effective, and employees should push their companies to figure out what actions they can take.”

Tan says Altman’s words inspired tech workers across the industry to publicly voice their opposition and “push for the values they believed in.” For the next several years, workers staged walkouts and protested their employers’ contracts with U.S. military and immigration enforcement agencies, as well as workplace policies they considered sexist. 

“That was a time in which a lot of tech workers felt that their companies were walking back the values that they had initially promised,” says Tan.

Their objections initially met with some success. In 2018, following protests by Google employees, the company decided not to renew its contract for Project Maven, a Pentagon initiative using artificial intelligence to analyze drone surveillance footage. Nearly 4,000 employees signed an open letter to their CEO stating, “Google should not be in the business of war.”

Fast forward eight years. Earlier this year, more than 600 employees signed an open letter urging Google’s CEO to reject classified AI work with the Pentagon, citing concerns about potential uses including lethal autonomous weapons and domestic surveillance. 

“The way Google responded to them this time was to say, basically, ‘Too bad, we’re committed to working with the Pentagon,’” says Tan. “So, there is this kind of shift as to how Google is positioning itself politically, as well as to their employees.”

What happened to the tech industry employee leverage? 

Tan’s book outlines several events that he argues have negatively impacted their formerly strong influence. First, following interest rate hikes in 2022, the tech industry lost hundreds of billions in market valuation and set out to cut costs, the most significant of them being the expensive salaries of their employees. In other words, the labor market soured on tech workers, giving employers opportunity to wrest back control, Tan suggests. 

Second, he points to the drastic effect of agentic AI coding systems on the nature of their work, arguing that these tools have deskilled workers and made everyone much more worried about job security.  

“Tech workers had to face these shocks on their own. With a union or some ability to coordinate across workers and bargain as a group, they might’ve had more power to actually push back,” says Tan.  

Documenting the past to support the future

Tan enrolled at MIT in 2020, earning a master’s degree at the MIT Media Lab. He is currently a doctoral student in the Department of Urban Studies and Planning with a focus on the political economy of the tech sector.

At various points in their careers, Tan and his co-author had been involved with organizing in the tech sector. Redwine was a prominent organizer in the union drive at Kickstarter. She was fired from the company in 2019; Redwine said her dismissal was retaliation for her organizing activity, while Kickstarter denied that claim. One reason Tan and Redwine wrote this book is because they saw that the bandwidth for labor organizing among tech workers had hit a new low. 

“Tech workers want to have a say over the way their technologies are designed,” says Tan. “They want to be able to push for the right guardrails around technologies that they’re building. We wanted to use this book as an opportunity to analyze why it was that, within eight years, the tech worker movement had sort of fallen into this state of paralysis.”

They began writing the book in 2024, reliving the highs and lows of the past decade. This is Tan’s first book. He says writing it was an “exhilarating experience” and one that he profoundly enjoyed.

“It’s why, in part, I’m drawn to academia. To a large extent, I believe in the power of research and of writing. To have the opportunity to do this about a subject that I care deeply about has been an amazing experience.”

A book launch and discussion about “Against Tech Oligarchy,” co-hosted by the Department of Urban Studies and Planning, will take place on Oct. 26.

text:
Indian chip startup Bharat Semi raises $24M seed round for AI image sensors

Five years old, pre-revenue, first commercial product targeting 2027 — and $24 million just landed. That's not a red flag, it's just what deep-tech semiconductor development actually looks like, and anyone expecting SaaS-style growth curves in chip design is in the wrong industry.

The core bet is architectural: combine image capture, processing, and AI inference on a single programmable chip instead of stringing three separate components together. Bharat Semi claims that cuts system cost by at least 70%. If true, that's not a minor optimization — that's the kind of bill-of-materials reduction that makes procurement people's eyes widen. The person saying it is co-founder Vrinda Kapoor, and the person backing the technical claim is CTO Boyd Fowler, who held the same role at OmniVision. OmniVision is basically the canonical "we almost owned image sensors and then got squeezed" cautionary tale. Having someone who watched that happen from the inside is either great institutional knowledge or a reason to worry about history repeating.

The General Atomics design win is the most credible signal in the whole announcement. Defense customers are glacially slow, pathologically demanding, and almost impossible to displace once qualified. Getting even a design win — before production, before commercial launch — means someone with real engineering standards looked at the prototype and didn't immediately throw it in the bin. That's worth more than the $24M in terms of market signal.

India's domestic semiconductor ambitions are the awkward backdrop here. The government has committed billions to build a chip manufacturing hub, and the results so far are mostly ribbon-cutting ceremonies and optimistic timelines. Bharat Semi is smart enough not to bet on that ecosystem: they're staying fabless, outsourcing fabrication, and focusing on design and software IP. That's the correct call when your domestic fab options are still largely a PowerPoint. Build the valuable part — the architecture, the algorithms, the customer relationships — and let TSMC handle the part that requires decades of process engineering and $20 billion fabs.

The targets — smart homes, industrial automation, surveillance, drones, aerospace — are broad enough to feel like a pitch deck and specific enough that at least one of them will probably hit. Drones processing visual data onboard without expensive companion compute is a genuinely compelling use case right now, given how much of the drone market is currently paying a Nvidia tax to get inference done.

The risk is straightforward: 2027 is a long time, the big sensor players aren't standing still, and "we have design wins" is not the same as "we have revenue." But for a seed round anchored by real design partners and a CTO who's actually shipped image sensor silicon before, this is a more credible bet than most things wearing the word "semiconductor" in their pitch these days.

text:
Artificial intelligence (AI) has the vast potential to offer innovations to improve every facet of society, from legacy engineering systems to healthcare to creative processes in arts and entertainment. In Hollywood, for example, studios are using AI to surface and measure bias in scripts—the very tools producers and writers need to create more equitable and inclusive media. However, AI is only as smart as the data it’s trained on, and that data reflects real-life biases. To avoid perpetuating stereotypes and exclusivity, technologists are addressing equity and inclusion both in real-life and in their innovations.

Innate bias in humans

As technologists look to use AI to find human-centric solutions to optimize industry practices and everyday lives alike, it’s critical to be mindful of the ways that our innate biases can have unintended consequences.

“As humans, we are highly biased,” says Beena Ammanath, the global head of the Deloitte AI Institute, and tech and AI ethics lead at Deloitte. “And as these biases get baked into the systems, there is very high likelihood of sections of society being left behind—underrepresented minorities, people who don’t have access to certain tools—and it can drive more inequity in the world.”      

Projects that begin with good intentions — to create equal outcomes or mitigate past inequities — can still end up biased if systems are trained with biased data or researchers aren’t accounting for how their own perspectives affect lines of research.

Thus far, adjusting for AI biases has often been reactive with the discovery of biased algorithms or underrepresented demographics emerging after the fact, says Ammanath. But, companies now have to learn how to be proactive, to mitigate these issues early on, and to take accountability for missteps in their AI endeavors. 

Algorithmic bias in AI

In AI, bias appears in the form of algorithmic bias. “Algorithmic bias is a set of several challenges in constructing an AI model,” explains Kirk Bresniker, chief architect at Hewlett Packard Labs and vice president at Hewlett Packard Enterprise (HPE). “We can have a challenge because we have an algorithm that is not capable of handling diverse inputs, or because we haven’t gathered broad enough sets of data to incorporate into the training of our model. In either case, we have insufficient data.”

Algorithmic bias can also come from inaccurate processing, data being modified, or someone injecting a false signal. Whether intentional or not, the bias results in unfair outcomes, perhaps privileging one group or excluding another altogether.

As an example, Ammanath describes an algorithm designed to recognize different types of shoes such as flip flops, sandals, formal shoes, and sneakers. However, when it was released, the algorithm couldn’t recognize women’s shoes with heels. The development team was a group of fresh college grads—all male—who never thought of training it on the heels of women’s shoes. 

“This is a trivial example, but you realize that the data set was limited,” Ammanath said. “Now think of a similar algorithm using historical data to diagnose a disease or an illness. What if it wasn’t trained on certain body types or certain genders or certain races? Those impacts are huge.      

Critically, she says If you don’t have that diversity at the table, you are going to miss certain scenarios.”    

Better AI means self-regulation and ethics guidelines

Simply obtaining more (and more diverse) datasets is a formidable challenge, especially as data has become more centralized. Data sharing brings up many concerns, not the least of which are security and privacy.      

“Right now, we have a situation where individual users have far less power than the vast companies that are collecting and processing their data,” says Nathan Schneider assistant professor of media studies at the University of Colorado Boulder.

It is likely that expanded laws and regulations will eventually dictate when and how data can be shared and used. But, innovation doesn’t wait for lawmakers. Right now, the onus is on AI-developing organizations to be good data stewards, protecting individual privacy while striving to reduce algorithmic bias. Because technology is maturing so quickly, it’s impossible to rely on regulations to cover every possible scenario, says Deloitte’s Ammanath. “We are going to enter an era where you’re balancing between being adherent to existing regulations and at the same time, self-regulating.”

This kind of self-regulation means raising the bar for the entire supply chain of technologies that go into building AI solutions, from the data to the training to the infrastructure required to make those solutions possible. Further, companies need to create pathways for individuals across departments to raise concerns over biases. While it is unlikely that bias can be eliminated altogether, companies must regularly audit the efficacy of their AI solutions.

Because of the highly contextual nature of AI, self-regulation will look different for each company. HPE, for example, established ethical AI guidelines. A diverse set of individuals from across the company spent nearly a year working together to establish the company’s principles for AI, and then vetted those principles with a broad set of employees to ensure they could be followed and that they made sense for the corporate culture.

“We wanted to raise the general understanding of the issues and then collect best practices,” says HPE’s Bresniker. “This is everyone’s job—to be literate in this area.”      

Technologists have reached a maturity with AI that has progressed from research to practical applications and value creation across all industries. The growing pervasiveness of AI across society means that organizations now have an ethical responsibility to provide robust, inclusive, and accessible solutions. This responsibility has prompted organizations to examine, sometimes for the first time, the data they’re pulling into a process. “We want people to establish that providence, that measurable confidence in the data that’s going in,” says Bresniker. “They have that ability to stop perpetuating systemic inequalities and create equitable outcomes for a better future.”

text:
NATO for Donbas: why the U.S. offer is unworkable and dangerous — for Ukraine, for Europe and for the world

Ukraine is right to seek NATO membership. It is equally right to reject territorial "concessions". The problem with the latest U.S. proposal — membership in exchange for withdrawing from Donbas — is not the destination but the price and the sequence: Ukraine would hand over land now, irreversibly, in return for a promise that Washington cannot keep on its own. Nor should Ukraine put its sovereignty and territorial integrity to a referendum, for several reasons.

1. A free and fair referendum is impossible
Under Article 73 of the Constitution, any change to Ukraine's territory can be decided only by an all-Ukrainian referendum. That means a vote across the whole of Ukraine, including illegally occupied Crimea and the occupied parts of Donetsk, Luhansk, Zaporizhzhia and Kherson regions. Russia has hurried to write these regions into its own constitution. No free and fair vote can be held there.

Even on government-controlled territory the conditions are absent. Ukrainian law prohibits holding a referendum under martial law; millions of Ukrainians are displaced internally or living abroad; hundreds of thousands are serving at the front; and polling stations would be targets for Russian missiles and drones. A vote held under these conditions would be contested at home and exploited by Moscow abroad.

2. Rewarding aggression sets a dangerous precedent

If Ukrainians were to consent, they would set a precedent in which aggression is rewarded through legal means. That is dangerous not only for Ukraine but for the international order as a whole, which rests on sovereignty, political independence and territorial integrity. Shake those pillars, and no state is safe.

The UN Charter (Article 2(4)) and the Helsinki Final Act both forbid changing borders by force. Every revisionist power — from Beijing looking at Taiwan to smaller actors with irredentist claims — would read a "land for guarantees" deal as proof that patience and violence pay. Recall, too, that Ukraine has already traded security for paper once: the 1994 Budapest Memorandum, under which it gave up the world's third-largest nuclear arsenal, did not stop Russia in 2014 or in 2022.

3. The Trump Administration cannot deliver what it offers

NATO membership is not Washington's to give. Accession requires the unanimous consent of all 32 Allies and ratification by each of their parliaments. Turkey and Hungary held up Sweden's accession for almost two years. The United States cannot guarantee the votes of other Allies — still less the outcome of national ratification processes in Europe. Nor can it guarantee Ukraine's swift accession to the European Union, which it has floated in earlier versions of its plan.

* Sequencing. Withdrawal from Donbas would be immediate and irreversible; membership would be deferred and conditional. Once Ukrainian forces leave the fortified Sloviansk–Kramatorsk belt, that defensive line cannot be bought back.
* The U.S. itself. Ratification requires a two-thirds majority in the U.S. Senate, and a future administration could disown the commitment, as this one has disowned earlier policy.
* The EU. Accession requires unanimity among 27 member states and national ratification; France's constitution provides for a referendum on new accessions. Washington has no say in any of this.

4. The real agenda: rewriting Europe's security architecture

In my assessment, the U.S. proposal should be read alongside Russia's demand to reshape European security: returning NATO to its pre-1997 posture and withdrawing American forces from Europe.

European states do not yet possess the capabilities to deter Russia or defend Europe without the United States. A NATO hollowed out in this way would fail to fulfil its purpose for its current members — let alone with Ukraine on board. Membership in such an alliance would be a guarantee in name only.

text:
Promenade des Anglais (French pronunciation: [pʁɔmnad dez‿ɑ̃ɡlɛ], [- dez‿ɑ̃ɡle]; lit. "Walkway of the English"; Niçard: Passejada deis Anglés, Standard Occitan: Passejada dels Anglés) is a promenade along the Mediterranean coast of Nice, France. It extends from Nice Côte d'Azur Airport on the west to the Quai des États-Unis [fr] ("United States Quay") on the east, for a distance of approximately 7 kilometres (4.3 mi).[1] It forms part of Route nationale 98, which runs between Toulon and Menton.

History
Starting in the second half of the 18th century, the English aristocracy took to spending the winter in Nice, enjoying the panorama along the coast. In 1820, when a particularly harsh winter further north brought an influx of beggars to Nice, some of the English proposed that the beggars could work on the construction of a walkway (chemin de promenade) along the sea. It was funded by the Reverend LEWIS Way and members of Holy Trinity, the Anglican church in Nice.[2][3]

The city of Nice, intrigued by the prospect of a pleasant promenade, greatly increased the scope of the work. The Promenade was first called the Camin deis Anglés (the English Way) by the Niçois in their native dialect. After the annexation of Nice by France in 1860 it was rechristened La Promenade des Anglais.

The Promenade was the site of the team time trial in the 2013 Tour de France, held on 2 July 2013. It was also featured as a start and finish location of the first two stages of the 2020 Tour de France.[4] Due to the Paris Olympics, the 2024 Tour de France concluded on the Promenade, instead of its usual location of the Champs-Élysées.[5]

Stages 8 and 9 of the 2026 Tour de France Femmes concluded on the Promenade.[6]

Modern day
For local inhabitants, Promenade des Anglais has simply become the Promenade or, for short, La Prom. It is popular with bicyclists, baby strollers, and families, especially on Sundays. It has also become a favorite place for skateboarders and in-line skaters.

2016 Bastille Day attack
Main article: 2016 Nice truck attack
On 14 July 2016, a truck was deliberately driven at revellers celebrating Bastille Day on the Promenade. The driver, 31-year-old Mohamed Lahouaiej-Bouhlel,[7] also shot at others before crossing the road in the vehicle to continue the assault. The vehicle was surrounded by police near the Palais de la Méditerranée, and the terrorist was shot dead. Eighty-six people were killed, and 458 were wounded.[8]

Revelation 17:1 The state of the Church militant being declared, now followeth the state of the Church overcoming and getting victory, as I showed before in the beginning of chapter 10. The state is set forth in 4 chapters. As in the place beforegoing I noted, that in that history the order of time was not always exactly observed, so the same is to be understood in this history, that it is distinguished according to the persons of which it treateth, and that in the several stories of the persons is severly observed in the time thereof. For first is delivered the story of Babylon destroyed, in this and the next chap. (for this Babylon out of all doubt shall perish before the 2 beasts and the Dragon). Secondly is delivered the destruction of both the two beasts, chap. 19. And lastly of the Dragon, chap. 20, in the story of the spiritual Babylon are distinctly set forth the state thereof in this chap. and the overthrow done from God, chap. 18. In this verse and that which followeth is a transition or passage unto the first argument, consisting of a particular calling of the Prophet (as often heretofore) and a general proposition.

Revelation 17:4 In attire most glorious, triumphant, most rich, and most gorgeous.
Revelation 17:4 In profession, the nourisher of all, in this verse, and teaching her mysteries unto all, verse 5, setting forth all things most magnificently: but indeed most pernicious besotting miserable men with her cup, and bringing upon them a deadly giddiness.
Revelation 17:5 Deceiving with the title of religion, and public inscription of mystery: which the beast in times past did not bear.

Revelation 17:7 The second part or place, as I said, verse 1. The narration of the vision, promised in this verse, and delivered in the verse following. Now there is delivered first a narration of the beast and his story, unto verse 14. After, of the harlot, unto the end of the chap.
Revelation 17:8 The story of the beast hath a triple description of him. The first is a distinction of this beast from all that ever hath been at any time: which distinction is contained in this verse: The second is a delineation or painting out of the beast by things present, by which he might even at that time be known of the godly, and this delineation is according to his heads, verses 2, 10, 11. The third is an historical foretelling of things to come, and to be done by him: and these are ascribed unto his horns, verses 12, 13, 14. This beast is that Empire of Rome, of which I spake, chap. 13:11, according to the mutations and changes whereof which then had already happened, the holy Ghost hath distinguished and set out the same. The Apostle distinguisheth this beast from all others in these words. The beast which thou sawest, was and is not. For so I expound the words of the Apostle for evidence’s sake as I will further declare in the notes following.
Revelation 17:8 The meaning is, that beast which thou sawest before (Rev. 13:1) and which yet thou hast now seen, was, (I say was) even from Julius Caesar in respect of beginning, rising up, station, glory, dominion, manner and stock, from the house of Julius: and yet is not now the same, if thou look unto the house and stock for the dominion of this family was translated unto another, after the death of Nero from the other unto a third, from a third unto a fourth, and so forth was varied and altered by innumerable changes. Finally, the Empire is one, as it were one beast: but exceedingly varied by kindreds, families, and persons. It was therefore (saith S. John) in the kindred or house of Julius: and now it is not in that kindred, but translated unto another.
Revelation 17:8 As if he should say, Also the same that is, shall shortly not be: but shall ascend out of the depth, or out of the sea (as was said, Rev. 13:1) that is, shall be a new stock from amongst the nations without difference, and shall in the same state go unto destruction or ruin, and perish: and so shall successively new Princes or Emperors come and go, arise and fall, the body of the beast remaining still, but tossed with so many and often alterations, as no man can but marvel that this beast was able to stand and hold out, in so many mutations. Verily no Empire that ever was tossed with so many changes, and as it were with so many tempests of the sea, ever continued so long.
Revelation 17:8 That is as many as have not learned the providence of God, according to the faith of the Saints, shall marvel at these grievous and often changes when they shall consider, the selfsame beast, which is the Roman Empire, to have been, not to be, and to be and still molested with perpetual mutation, and yet in the same to stand and continue. This in mine opinion is the most simple exposition of this place, and confirmed by the event of the things themselves. Although by the last change also, by which the Empire, that before was civil became Ecclesiastical, is not obscurely signified by these words: of which two, the first exercised cruelty upon the bodies of the saints: the other also upon their souls: the first by human order and policy, the other under the color of the law of God, and of Religion, raged and imbrued itself with the blood of the godly.
Revelation 17:9 An exhortation preparing unto audience, by the same argument, with that of Christ: He that hath ears to hear, let him hear. Wherefore, for mine own part, I had rather read in this place, Let there be here a mind, etc. So the Angel passeth fully unto the second place of this description.
Revelation 17:9 Very children know what that seven hilled city is, which is so much spoken of, and whereof Virgil thus reporteth, And compasseth seven towers in one wall: that city it is, which when John wrote these things had rule over the kings of the earth: It was and is not, and yet it remaineth this day, but it is declining to destruction.
Revelation 17:9 This is the painting out of the beast by things present (as I said before) whereby S. John endeavored to describe the same, that he might both be known of the godly in that age, and be further observed and marked of posterity afterwards. This delineation hath one type, that is, his heads, but a double description or application of the type: one permanent from the nature of itself, the other changeable, by the working of men. The description permanent, is by the seven hills, in this verse, the other that fleeteth, is from the seven kings, verses 10, 11. And here it is worthy to be observed, that one type hath sometimes two or more applications, as seemeth good unto the holy Ghost to express either one thing by divers types, or divers things by one type. So I noted before, of the seven spirits, Rev. 1:4.
