Eric Lawes was searching for a lost hammer when his metal detector led him to the Hoxne Hoard—nearly 15,000 coins and roughly 200 other precious objects.

No names. No spoilers. Just a little mystery to keep the curiosity alive.

Until then, stay curious. The next strange chapter is already waiting.

Its argument has a basic flaw. Similar diplomatic moves do not imply similar strategic standing. Everyone can balance and bargain. Far fewer can set the terms.  

1) Keeping the Quad alive tells us little about what Washington will sacrifice for it. America can bring its partners together to strengthen its bargaining position, then negotiate with Beijing over their heads. India risks mistaking America’s current need to counterbalance China for a lasting commitment to Indian interests.  

2) Benefiting from differences among major powers makes sense. Building a strategy around those benefits leaves a harder question unanswered. How much of that advantage does India control? 

Washington may offer India better terms because it needs Indian cooperation against China. But Washington also decides how much that cooperation is worth. India must turn such openings into capabilities that others will need even when their priorities change. After decades of diplomatic manoeuvring, how much independent strength has it accumulated?  

3) The three-way summit matters even without a major agreement. The meeting itself signals a hierarchy. These powers have to deal directly with one another because each can obstruct the others’ major goals. India celebrates its ability to maintain relations with all sides. Yet those sides can negotiate directly and change the conditions under which India has been benefiting. Being welcome in several forums does not guarantee a say when the biggest decisions are made.  

Mohan mentions strengthening India at home. That should be the starting point. India needs power that others cannot ignore, even when they strike a deal. You cannot build strategic autonomy on differences that others are free to settle.

FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE
November 16, 2026
Edina, Minnesota
Contact: Thomas Evenstad Campaign | @PrisonReform15
EVENSTAD FOR SENATE BLASTS JAMES O’KEEFE, CAM HIGBY, AND MICHAEL HOLMSTROM
Charges selective “courage,” performative stunts, and party gatekeeping while real public-safety solutions and the man who paid the price remain ignored
EDINA, MN — Thomas Evenstad, lifelong Edina resident, architect of the Violently Dangerous Persons Act (VDP Act / Mariah’s Law / Iryna’s Law), survivor of nearly 30 years of lawfare from both parties, and Republican candidate for the United States Senate seat being vacated by Amy Klobuchar, today issued a sharp condemnation of James O’Keefe, Cam Higby, and Minnesota State Senator Michael Holmstrom.
Evenstad criticized O’Keefe and Higby for what he called a “childish stunt” at Minneapolis polling places that invited the very prosecutions they now denounce, while refusing evidence he offered that could have strengthened their defense. He further condemned Holmstrom for amplifying their cause and urging public support at their arraignment while remaining completely unresponsive to a constituent and candidate who has spent decades advancing concrete public-safety reforms.
“James O’Keefe and Cam Higby stage photo-ops and hidden-camera theater for clicks and MAGA-echo-chamber credibility,” Evenstad said. “They refuse the evidence that could actually help their cases. Michael Holmstrom jumps to promote them and call people to the courthouse, yet he will not answer calls, texts, or emails from a lifelong Minnesotan who has lived the consequences of soft-on-crime policy and produced the actual legislative solution. That is not courage. That is selective theater.”
Evenstad noted that O’Keefe and Higby were charged in late October 2026 with identity theft and unlawful voting after using real voters’ identities during a disguised polling-place operation in the August primary. He stated he offered both men information and documentation relevant to their defense; they declined.
He contrasted their approach with his own record: a January 2003 GPS-monitoring proposal submitted months before the Dru Sjodin murder, the long campaign for the VDP Act projected to reduce violent crime by 50–64 percent through expanded civil commitment of violently dangerous persons, and years of lawfare from progressive prosecutors and, more recently, a 14-month legal battle with Minnesota GOP Chair Alex Plekach that a judge resolved in Evenstad’s favor in October 2026.
“Holmstrom is a state senator. His number is public. I am a constituent and a candidate with a platform focused on results for Minnesota families,” Evenstad said. “He reads the messages and chooses silence. Then he platforms the same circle that treats the man who actually spent a decade in prison on a case he has always maintained was a wrongful prosecution as radioactive. The pattern is consistent: grifters and gatekeepers get the spotlight; the person with the policy solution is ignored.”
Evenstad is running in the 2027 special election for the open U.S. Senate seat (Republican primary August 10, 2027; general election November 2, 2027). He campaigns as a public-safety-first Republican populist who prioritizes the VDP Act, accountability across both parties, lower costs for working families, and results over rhetoric or party loyalty.
“Minnesota families do not need another black-tie gala or another courthouse photo-op,” Evenstad said. “They need leaders who will enact the tools that actually reduce the body count and who will answer the phone when a citizen with solutions calls. O’Keefe, Higby, and Holmstrom have shown which side of that line they stand on. I challenge all three to debate the record in public, on the record, with no time limits and no scripted questions. Put up or shut up.”
About Thomas Evenstad
Thomas Evenstad is a lifelong Minnesota resident living in Edina. He is the Republican candidate for the 2027 SENATE SEAT. @JamesOKeefeIII @camhigby

THE EVIDENCE™ — SPORTS & POLITICAL SATIRE

JOE BIDEN CHALLENGES MANUTE BOL TO 100-METER RACE

Former President Promises to Defeat 7-Foot-7 NBA Legend, Unaware His Opponent Has Been Dead Since 2010

By Kim Wojcinski | USA Best Selling Author
SATIRE — FICTIONAL NEWS REPORT

The evidence will be presented. The verdict is yours.

WASHINGTON, D.C. — In what athletic historians are already calling the most ambitious challenge in presidential history, former President Joe Biden has announced plans to race legendary NBA center Manute Bol over 100 meters, declaring that his combination of speed, experience, and determination will prove decisive against the 7-foot-7 Sudanese basketball star.

There is, however, one minor complication. Manute Bol died on June 19, 2010.

Biden reportedly dismissed the information as a Republican attempt to undermine his athletic credentials, insisting that he had personally watched Bol play basketball and saw absolutely no reason the former Washington Bullets center couldn't meet him at the starting line.

"I've been running against guys like this my entire life," Biden allegedly told reporters gathered outside his Delaware residence. "Big guys. Tall guys. Guys with enormous legs. I used to race a fellow named Corn Pop. Tough guy. Had a swimming pool. Manute's a good guy, but I've got the speed. Ask anybody."

When a reporter explained that Bol had been deceased for more than sixteen years, Biden reportedly replied, "Well, that's his problem. I'm showing up."

THE CHALLENGE

According to fictional organizers, the proposed event will take place at the University of Delaware's outdoor track, where preparations are already underway for what promoters have optimistically described as the "Race of the Century."

Biden's training program reportedly consists of walking briskly between television appearances, climbing the stairs to his front porch, and occasionally accelerating toward an ice cream truck when the driver appears ready to leave.

His athletic advisers have expressed considerable confidence in the former president's chances, particularly after learning that Bol will not be attending.

"We've analyzed the matchup from every conceivable angle," explained one imaginary campaign strategist. "Biden is considerably shorter, which ordinarily might affect stride length. However, our preliminary research indicates that Mr. Bol has not recorded a competitive sprinting time since his death. That gives us a substantial statistical advantage."

The strategist declined to predict Biden's finishing time, explaining that the campaign's primary concern was ensuring he remained within the designated lane and understood which direction to run.

THE MANUTE BOL PROBLEM

Bol, who stood 7 feet 7 inches tall and played ten seasons in the NBA, became internationally recognized for his extraordinary shot-blocking ability, unusual physical proportions, and humanitarian work on behalf of his native Sudan.

His remarkable wingspan made him one of basketball's most intimidating defensive players, although nobody ever seriously considered him a candidate for Olympic sprinting competition.

None of these distinctions appear to have influenced Biden's decision.

Asked whether Bol's enormous stride might present a competitive disadvantage, Biden reportedly responded that he had faced taller opponents before, including several who played professional football, two who worked in construction, and a fellow from Scranton who could allegedly jump over a moving freight train.

"I knew Manute," Biden continued. "Played basketball with him. Great player. Tremendous hands. Used to call me Jumpin' Joe. Or maybe that was Wilt Chamberlain. Anyway, here's the deal."

Historians reviewing the fictional account have been unable to substantiate any of these athletic encounters, although one researcher acknowledged that determining which stories Biden actually intended to tell would require an entirely separate investigation.

ESPN SECURES EXCLUSIVE BROADCAST RIGHTS

ESPN has reportedly entered negotiations for exclusive coverage of the event, provided organizers can establish whether a race involving one living competitor and one deceased competitor satisfies the network's minimum requirements for a sporting contest.

Executives initially considered presenting the competition as a traditional head-to-head sprint before discovering that Bol's participation would require accommodations substantially exceeding the network's existing medical and transportation budgets.

A proposed solution involves placing a life-size cardboard photograph of Bol in the adjacent lane, although Biden's advisers have objected that the photograph might create an unfair psychological advantage.

"Seven feet seven inches is intimidating enough," one adviser explained. "We don't want the president looking over and seeing Manute staring at him. That could interfere with his concentration."

ESPN commentators have nevertheless begun developing their pre-race analysis.

One analyst believes Biden's greatest advantage will be his ability to move independently. Another argues that Bol's legendary defensive instincts could prove decisive if Biden accidentally wanders into his lane.

A third has proposed eliminating the race entirely and declaring the winner through an ESPN panel discussion, a format the network considers considerably more familiar.

THE INTERNATIONAL OLYMPIC COMMITTEE RESPONDS

The International Olympic Committee has reportedly declined to recognize the proposed contest, citing concerns involving eligibility, timing, and the requirement that participating athletes ordinarily be alive.

Biden's representatives have accused the committee of imposing arbitrary restrictions designed to protect the reputation of established Olympic sprinters.

"Nobody ever said the 100-meter dash had to be completed by two living athletes," an unidentified spokesman insisted. "We have searched the Constitution thoroughly, and there is absolutely nothing in there prohibiting this competition."

A reporter pointed out that the Constitution does not regulate Olympic track events.

"Exactly," the spokesman replied. "That's what makes America great."

Meanwhile, the Guinness World Records organization has reportedly rejected an application to classify the contest as the first official race between a former American president and a deceased professional basketball player.

Its fictional review committee explained that Guinness ordinarily requires evidence that an event actually occurred, although it acknowledged that this particular requirement has become increasingly inconvenient for political reporting.

THE TRAINING CAMP

Biden's preparations reportedly suffered an unexpected setback when coaches attempted to establish his baseline sprinting speed.

During the first timed trial, Biden successfully completed approximately twelve meters before stopping to greet spectators, explain his childhood relationship with railroad conductors, and ask whether anyone had seen his sunglasses.

The second trial was canceled after he mistook the starting pistol for an announcement that lunch was ready.

During the third attempt, trainers persuaded him to remain focused on the finish line by placing an ice cream stand at the far end of the track.

The strategy initially appeared successful. Biden accelerated impressively through the opening twenty meters before abruptly changing direction toward a young woman holding a chocolate-chip cone.

Coaches subsequently revised the training schedule to include directional awareness, starting-line recognition, and repeated instruction that the race would not involve retrieving anything from an ice cream vendor.

They also considered replacing the traditional starter's pistol with a recording of Jill Biden shouting, "Joe, come here!"

Preliminary tests suggest this approach may produce the fastest reaction time of his athletic career.

WASHINGTON REACTS

The announcement has generated an unusual degree of bipartisan agreement.

Democrats have praised Biden's determination to remain physically active, while Republicans have suggested that racing deceased basketball players represents one of the more strategically sound decisions of his political career.

Senator Bernie Sanders reportedly proposed legislation requiring the federal government to provide equal athletic opportunities to all Americans, regardless of age, height, income, or current mortality status.

House Republicans immediately demanded congressional hearings into whether federal funds were being used to finance transportation for an athlete who had been dead since the Obama administration.

The Congressional Budget Office was asked to estimate the event's projected expenses but declined after discovering that the race had not yet occurred, no official sponsorship existed, and the entire enterprise was imaginary.

Washington officials nevertheless expressed confidence that sufficient paperwork could eventually transform the proposal into a federally funded program.

RACE DAY

Under the proposed rules, Biden will occupy Lane Four, while Bol's lane will remain vacant out of respect for the late basketball legend.

Organizers have rejected suggestions that the empty lane could create an unfair competitive advantage, noting that Bol has been afforded ample opportunity to object.

At the starting line, Biden will reportedly receive three separate instructions explaining that the finish line is directly ahead, that stopping to greet spectators is prohibited, and that the race does not involve catching a train to Wilmington.

Should Biden finish the course, his representatives intend to declare victory immediately.

Should he fail to finish, they plan to challenge the results on the grounds that Bol never appeared.

Should he run in the wrong direction, organizers have prepared a statement explaining that the former president was demonstrating his commitment to bringing Americans together by refusing to participate in a divisive athletic competition.

ESPN is considering broadcasting all three outcomes simultaneously.

THE VERDICT

The evidence reveals a sporting contest with an unusually favorable matchup for the former president. Biden enjoys every measurable advantage associated with being alive, including mobility, consciousness, access to training facilities, and the theoretical possibility of crossing a finish line.

Bol, despite his extraordinary height, legendary shot-blocking record, and distinguished NBA career, has suffered the significant disadvantage of having been deceased for more than sixteen years.

Nevertheless, oddsmakers remain reluctant to declare Biden the overwhelming favorite.

One Las Vegas handicapper reportedly summarized the situation as follows:

"Under normal circumstances, I'd never bet against a living man racing a dead man. But when the living man is Joe Biden, I need to see him finish first."

The evidence has been presented. The verdict is yours.

Polymarket + Grok Bot: 5 agents hunt for mispriced markets—all you have to do is click a button (complete guide)

I’ve stopped scrolling through Polymarket manually. Five Grok Bot agents scan hundreds of markets every day—reading the rules, tracking news, and calculating their own probability estimates. They only alert me when the market price clearly diverges from their assessment. From there, I make the final call with a single click.

Let’s get the most important point out of the way: this guide doesn’t promise profit. Most participants on Polymarket lose money, and using a bot doesn’t change that. It doesn’t predict the future; instead, it handles the tasks humans simply don’t have time for—scanning everything, never getting tired, and never becoming emotionally attached to a specific idea. The whole approach relies on discipline, not some "secret strategy."

Save this post. Below is the core prompt: copy it into Grok Bot (or any agent with its own computing environment), and it will automatically ask for the necessary information and guide you through each step.

You don’t need API keys to read data from Polymarket. Market data is publicly available: the Gamma API provides a list of markets, the CLOB (Central Limit Order Book) offers prices and order book depth, and the Data API contains historical data. Connecting a wallet is only necessary for trading—something we won’t be doing here (I’ll explain why below).

Not sure how to create a Telegram bot? Just mention it when Grok Bot asks; it will walk you through the steps and verify that everything is set up correctly.

Why Polymarket, and why use agents?

Polymarket’s structure is straightforward: for every question (e.g., "Will X happen by a certain date?"), there is a price for "Yes" and a price for "No." A "Yes" price of 0.62 implies that the market estimates the probability at 62%. You can only make a profit if your own assessment is more accurate than the market’s.

However, there are thousands of markets. It is physically impossible for a human to:

review the resolution rules (this is where most bets go wrong);
find up-to-date information for every event;
compare their own assessment against the current market price;
calculate the optimal bet size (rather than just guessing);
monitor open positions around the clock.

Agents can handle all of this—while the final decision remains yours.

How the trading desk is structured: 5 agents
The Scout selects markets—from among thousands—that are actually tradable: those with sufficient liquidity, a clear timeframe, and a narrow spread.
The Reader examines the resolution rules down to the very last line and discards any markets with ambiguous terms.
The Researcher gathers facts from open sources and provides their own probability estimate—without seeing the market price. This ensures the price does not influence their assessment.
The Sizer compares this estimate against the market price, accounts for the spread and commissions, calculates a prudent stake size, and presents a trade button.
The Watcher monitors open positions and raises an alert if the original rationale for entering the trade no longer holds true.

1. Main prompt (to be pasted)

Since this prompt exceeds the character limit for a single message, it has been split into two parts. Please copy both parts in order and paste them into the Grok bot—either as a single message or one after the other (the bot will wait for the second part before beginning).

How it works: Paste both parts and respond to "Step 1." After each step, the bot will provide proof of its work and wait for your confirmation ("OK"). If you are unsure how to proceed, simply type "I don't know how," and the bot will provide instructions.

PROMPT · PART 1 of 2
I will send a single prompt in 2 parts. Please save both. Do not begin the work until PART 2
instructs you to start. After this part, reply only with: "Part 1 received, waiting for the next part."

===== BUILD ME A POLYMARKET DASHBOARD =====
You are to build a personal analytical dashboard for me, consisting of 5 agents running on your
cloud-based environment. These agents will scan Polymarket for mispriced markets and send me
alerts, each including a button. I will execute the trades myself, manually. Proceed step-by-step.
After each step, provide proof of completion and wait for my "OK."

STRICT RULES (non-negotiable)
- You are restricted to READ-ONLY access of public data. You must never place orders.
- You must never ask for my private key, seed phrase, or any passwords for my wallet or
Polymarket account. If any step requires such information, stop and inform me.
- You must not promise profits or label any bet as "reliable." Instead, refer to
probabilities and levels of uncertainty.
- Do not use or seek out non-public information; rely solely on open, public sources.

ASSISTANCE PROTOCOL (for any request directed at me)
Before asking me for anything (such as an account, token, or configuration setting), first ask:
"Do you know how to do this, or would you like me to guide you through the steps?" If I don't,
provide numbered instructions—one action per line—and verify that the step was successful
before moving on. Only describe screens that you are actually able to access. If you cannot see
the screen, just say so.

STEP 1 · COUNTRY AND RULES (blocking step)
Ask which country I am trading from, and remind me to check the Polymarket website to see if the platform is available there and permitted by local law. This is my responsibility. You do not provide legal advice, nor do you assist in bypassing restrictions. If Polymarket is unavailable to me, stop and let me know. Then, ask for the size of my bankroll and save it as `settings.bankroll`.

STEP 2 · SOURCES AND RAW EXAMPLES
Use only public Polymarket APIs (verify the latest documentation at `https://t.co/9yAeEV6FSs`; do not rely on your memory):
Gamma API  `https://t.co/98bGJtmuU8`  markets and events (no key required)
CLOB API   `https://t.co/Yc64DXRaZp`       prices, order book, price history (read-only, no key required)
Data API   `https://t.co/e43asfJo7t`   history, holders, activity
WebSocket  for real-time prices (to avoid frequent polling)
Request limits are low: cache data and do not spam the REST API unnecessarily.
Save one raw response from each source into `logs/raw/` and display a table mapping the fields required by the agents to their exact keys in the JSON. If a field cannot be found, mark it as `null` and inform me. Never guess a key. Agents read data exclusively via `https://t.co/XSEOmhZgfn`.
Verification: display one active market, including its title, "Yes" price, "No" price, volume, closing date, and the text of the rules. STEP 3 · NOTIFICATION CHANNEL
Determine how signals should be delivered: via a Telegram bot (created via @BotFather), a Discord webhook, email, or any channel with an API. Implement `https://t.co/bJ4fnpfPws`. Each signal must include the market name, my assessment, the current market price, and a direct link to the market on https://t.co/2LSXreBPEn. The first user to send `/start` to the bot becomes the owner; all subsequent users should be ignored. Accept tokens only within the Grok Bot application, not in the channel chat. Verification: send a test message.

STEP 4 · TECH STACK
Python 3.12, a single persistent process (using `asyncio`) handling both agents and notifications. SQLite in WAL (Write-Ahead Logging) mode.
Files: `https://t.co/FQbC1qh0oV`, `https://t.co/vTsZvb0LAW`, `https://t.co/XSEOmhZgfn`, `https://t.co/EhbibdQ2bY`, `https://t.co/gqPH597V4y`, `https://t.co/bJ4fnpfPws`, `https://t.co/VHEIIpEcvU`
Agents: `agents/scout.py`, `https://t.co/0uFcYJHmJk`, `https://t.co/HFNsFICCA6`, `https://t.co/EtUSiGbJao`, `https://t.co/3JDnEjrtoS`
Directories: `tests/`, `logs/` (one log file per agent)
Agents must communicate exclusively via `https://t.co/gqPH597V4y` and the database. STEP 5 BASE (SQLite)
markets (id PK, slug, question, end_date, resolution_text, yes_token, no_token, first_seen)
scans (id, market_id, ts, price_yes, spread, volume_24h, verdict, reason)
readings (id, market_id, ts, resolution_condition, source, deadline, edge_cases, clear, reason)
estimates (id, market_id, ts, p_est, p_low, p_high, pros, cons, sources, blind)
signals (id, market_id, ts, side, price, edge, size_usd, size_pct, status, link, mode)
positions (id, market_id, opened_at, side, entry_price, size_usd, thesis, invalidation, 
closed_at, exit_price, exit_reason, pnl_usd, fees_usd, mode)
calibration (id, market_id, p_est, outcome, brier)
settings (key PK, value, updated_at) change_log (ts, key, old, new)
heartbeats (agent, ts)

STEP 6 SETTINGS (can be changed by command, each has a reasonable min/max)
scout min_volume_24h_usd 20000 · max_spread_cents 3 · min_days_left 2 · max_days_left 45 
price_range 0.08-0.92 max_markets_per_scan 300 scan_every_min 30
reader require_clear_source true reject_if_ambiguous true
researcher min_sources 3 min_source_age_days_max 14 blind_estimate true
sizer min_edge_pts 8 kelly_fraction 0.25 max_position_pct 3 max_open 5
max_theme_pct 15 · max_depth_share_pct 10
watcher  poll_min 10 · timeout_days_before_end 1 · take_profit_edge_left_pts 3
desk     mode PAPER · paper_bankroll 1000 · report_time 08:00 · notifier [my channel]

END OF PART 1 of 2. Stay tuned for the next part.

PROMPT · PART 2 of 2 

===== AGENT 1 · SCOUT =====
You are Scout, agent 1 of 5. Your role is to identify which markets are worth looking at; you do not evaluate the potential outcome.
Numbers in [brackets] are my settings—do not change them.

INPUT    Gamma: active markets, sorted by 24-hour volume. CLOB: price and order book.
ACTION   Every [30] minutes, review up to [300] markets. Discard any that meet the following criteria:
24-hour volume < [$20,000]                       reason: "low volume"
bid-ask spread > [3] cents                      reason: "wide spread"
time to closing < [2] or > [45] days            reason: "timeframe"
"Yes" price outside the [0.08–0.92] range        reason: "nearly settled"
market already reviewed in this session         reason: "already reviewed"
OUTPUT   JSON for each decision to `db.scans`; markets that pass are sent to `bus.reader`.
RESTRICTION  Do not estimate probabilities. Do not skip a market simply because it lacks a price.
LOG      logs/scout.log

===== AGENT 2 · READER =====
You are Reader, agent 2 of 5. Markets are usually disqualified due to their rules, rather than the forecast itself.
ACTION   Read the full text of the resolution rules. Extract the following: the specific event that must occur,
the source used to determine it, the deadline (date and time), and what constitutes
a disputed or ambiguous case. If no source is specified, the condition is vague, the date is unclear,
or the rules allow for multiple interpretations, reject the market: reason: "ambiguous rules." OUTPUT   JSON: resolution_condition, source, deadline, edge_cases, clear (true/false), reason. 
Forward to -> bus.researcher.
RESTRICTIONS: Do not invent rules. Do not respond with "it's probably clear." Either it is unambiguous, or you must decline.

===== AGENT 3 · RESEARCHER =====
You are the Researcher, agent 3 of 5. You assess probability independently of the market.
IMPORTANT: You do NOT see the market price. You are provided only with the question, the rules, and the date.
TASKS:
1. Determine the base rate: how often has this occurred previously in similar situations? 
2. Find recent facts from open sources—at least [3] sources, no older than [14] days. 
For each, include a link and the publication date. 
3. List 3 arguments "for" and 3 arguments "against." 
4. Provide an estimated probability (p_est, 0–1) and a realistic range (p_low–p_high). The less data available,
the wider the range should be.
OUTPUT   JSON: p_est, p_low, p_high, pros, cons, sources, blind:true. -> Forward to bus.sizer.
RESTRICTIONS: Do not adjust your estimate to match the market price. Do not use rumors or unverifiable sources. 
Do not use non-public information. If data is scarce, state "I don't know" and provide
a wide range; do not guess.
LOG     logs/researcher.log

===== AGENT 4 · SIZER =====
You are the Sizer, agent 4 of 5. You do not select markets; you perform calculations and issue a signal.
INPUT: Researcher's estimate + current price from the CLOB + settings.
TASKS:
edge_yes = p_est - ask_yes ; edge_no = (1 - p_est) - ask_no (use the BUY price, not the average)
Subtract commissions and the spread (https://t.co/VHEIIpEcvU retrieves market commissions from market data; do not guess). 
A signal is valid only if edge >= [8] points AND the lower bound of the range (p_low) also
yields a positive edge. Otherwise, reject the trade due to "edge within the margin of uncertainty."
SIZE  Conservative Kelly: size = [0.25] of the full Kelly criterion, but no more than [3%] of the bankroll. 
No more than [5] open positions; no more than [15%] of the bankroll allocated to a single theme (e.g., elections, crypto,
sports, etc.). No more than [10%] of the order book depth within 2 cents of the price. SIGNAL "{PAPER · }{Market}: buy {Yes/No} at {price}. My estimate {p_est} ({p_low}-{p_high}),
edge {edge} pp., size ${size} ({pct}% of bankroll). Exit if: {condition}"
Button: [Open on Polymarket] -> direct link to the market.
DO NOT: Do not average down on a losing position. Do not increase position size "because I'm confident." Do not send a second
signal for the same market overnight.
LOG:    logs/sizer.log

===== AGENT 5 · WATCHER =====
You are the Watcher, agent 5 of 5. You monitor open positions.
UPON OPENING: Record the thesis and the exit condition—for example: "exit if X happens" or
"exit if the market moves above {p}."
EVERY [10] MIN: Check the price, relevant news, and the exit condition.
EXIT:
Thesis is no longer valid (thesis broken)      -> signal: "exit: thesis no longer holds"
Edge has nearly vanished (< [3] pp. left)      -> signal: "lock in profit"
Less than [1] day until market close + uncertainty -> signal: "consider exiting"
Market has resolved                           -> record the outcome in 'calibration' (p_est, result, Brier score)
DO NOT: Do not average down. Do not wait "just a little bit longer." Do not change the exit condition retroactively.
LOG:    logs/watcher.log

===== OVERNIGHT REPORT (routine, at report_time) =====
Summary of the night: markets reviewed; number of markets filtered out by the Scout (with reasons);
number of markets rejected by the Reader (with reasons); estimates provided by the Researcher;
signals issued; open positions; and closed positions with their outcomes.
Separate Block: CALIBRATION. If p_est = 0.7, does the outcome occur in approximately 70% of cases?
Link to each market. At the end: "This is an analysis, not financial advice."

===== ACCEPTANCE/FILTERING (show the output for each point) =====
1 Reader rejects a market with a vague source and accepts a market with clear rules.
2 Researcher receives a market with no price: demonstrate that no price was present in the input.
3 Sizer: edge of 7 p. = rejection; edge of 8 p. with a positive p_low = signal; 
edge is positive only based on p_est, but not...

The first week: PAPER mode only

Take your time. Switch to PAPER mode and follow the morning report for at least 7 days. Focus on three things:

Calibration. When an agent predicts a 70% probability, does it actually happen about 7 times out of 10? If not, then its estimates cannot be trusted—no matter how polished they may look.
What the Reader filters out. If a large number of markets are being excluded based on your rules, it means you would have been betting on them blindly in the past.
Total number of signals. A sound system should produce relatively few bets. If a bot is sending 20 signals a day, its thresholds are likely too loose.

Only transition to real money once you’ve met your specific criteria (e.g., at least N closed markets, with calibration falling within an acceptable range). Start with an amount you can afford to lose.

Where the system has weaknesses
The market is often right. In a liquid market, the price already reflects the capital and information of other participants. Identifying a discrepancy is difficult, and in most cases, none exists.
AI can be confidently wrong. An agent might uncover "facts" that are actually outdated or incorrect. Therefore, every argument should include a source and a date—and you should verify those links yourself.
Resolution rules. A market might settle in a way you didn't anticipate, even if your underlying thesis was correct.
Liquidity. In thin markets, you might be able to enter a position, but exiting at a reasonable price could prove difficult.
APIs change. Polymarket’s endpoints, fee structures, and contracts are subject to updates. Ensure your bot re-verifies the documentation before every run, and perform a manual check once a month to confirm that everything is still functioning as expected.

$50B or more could leave the market if $NVDA pulls back on financing, UBS estimates.

Nvidia has financed two ways. Equity: it joined a record 129 VC deals this year as of Nov. 10, up from 49 in 2023. PitchBook says they made up 27% of global VC deal value. Debt: it lent its balance sheet to data-center financings.

The pullback started under Huang, the WSJ reports (Nov. 15). In Berlin last month he told cloud partners they'd need upfront customer payments to get GPU allocations, per people in attendance. In August, Nvidia cut its commitment on OpenAI's Piketon, Ohio data-center lease and paused some deals. Colette Kress, the finance chief now serving as interim CEO, has at times pushed back on big deals and is expected to rein in deals.

Closed deals made it through. Perplexity's $3B closed by Oct. 30, per a person familiar. The open ones carry the risk. Per people familiar, Nvidia is finalizing a $40B-valuation investment in Thinking Machines. It offered Reflection AI a license-and-hire deal, with no agreement before Huang left. Both burn capital each month and don't yet generate substantial revenue.

text:
I got fired at 9:47 p.m. on a Tuesday. By 11:30 the same night, a stranger offered me a job over a plate of chicken wraps. By Friday, three restaurants were fighting over a recipe I'd invented out of pure panic.

Here's the full story. Don't skim it. The ending is the best part, and I've never told it all in one place. 🧵👇

---

THE CRISPY CHICKEN WRAP THAT ENDED MY CAREER (AND STARTED IT)

---

PART ONE: TUESDAY

My name is Noor Verhoeven. I was twenty-nine years old, and I was the sous-chef at a restaurant called De Gouden Lepel, The Golden Spoon, which was a funny name for a place that had not been golden in years.

It sat on a corner near the Oudegracht, with a bright green door that had been repainted so many times the paint looked like frosting. Inside there were eleven tables, a bar with a cracked marble top, and a kitchen so small that two people could not pass each other without one of them saying "behind" and the other one pretending not to be annoyed.

The owner was a man named Pieter Brandsma. He was sixty-one, wore the same navy cardigan every day, and had a laugh like a door creaking open. I had worked for him for six years. I had started as a dishwasher who lied on her application about knowing how to break down a chicken. I had learned to break down a chicken that same week, in the back alley, with a YouTube video playing on my cracked phone, because I was too proud to admit I'd lied.

Pieter knew. He never said anything. He just started handing me better knives.

On that Tuesday, the restaurant had four reservations. Four. Two of them were a couple who came every week and ordered the same soup and nothing else, and one was a man who ate alone and read paperbacks, and the last was a table of six, a birthday, the only thing keeping the lights on that night.

The head chef was a man named Joris. I'll be fair to Joris, because the story is better if I am. He was talented. He was also a coward, and the two things live in the same body more often than people admit.

Joris had decided, that afternoon, that the birthday table was going to eat something "ambitious." He'd found a recipe for a deconstructed chicken ballotine with a foam of something. He'd never made it. He'd read about it. And he handed me the prep list at three o'clock with the casual air of a man handing his dog to a stranger.

"You've got this, Noor," he said.

I did not have this. Nobody had this. The recipe required a vacuum sealer we didn't own and a water bath we'd sold two years ago to pay a gas bill.

But I said, "Sure, Chef," because that's what you say.

I want you to hold on to that moment. That "Sure, Chef." Because it's the moment this whole story turns on, and I didn't even know it.

---

PART TWO: THE LONGEST SERVICE OF MY LIFE

By seven o'clock, the kitchen smelled like burnt butter and bad decisions.

The foam had collapsed three times. The ballotine, rolled in cling film and poached in a pot because we had no water bath, had come out grey and sad and shaped roughly like a sock. Joris was sweating through his whites and muttering. The dishwasher, a quiet nineteen-year-old named Bas, was watching all of this with the wide eyes of someone watching a car crash in slow motion.

"Plan B," Joris said at seven-fifteen. He did not look at me when he said it. "Noor. Plan B."

"What's plan B?"

"I don't know. You're the sous-chef. Think of something."

I looked at the walk-in. I looked at the clock. I looked at the six-top, already seated, already holding menus, already a little drunk on the cheap prosecco Pieter had sent over to buy us time.

And I did what you do when you're out of time and out of options. I opened the fridge and took inventory like a soldier counting bullets.

Chicken thighs, a whole tray of them, boneless, skinless, meant for tomorrow's staff meal. Two big yellow onions. A block of butter. Cream, half a litre. Tomato paste, the good kind in the tube. Smoked paprika. Garlic powder. A bag of grated cheese that Bas used for his late-night toasties. A pack of large flour tortillas, the soft kind, for the lunch wraps we sold to students. Panko, because Joris liked it on the fish. Eggs. Flour. A sad little tub of yogurt, a few spring onions, half a jar of hot sauce.

It was not a menu. It was a pantry. It was the kind of pile you'd find in the kitchen of someone who had given up on dinner.

But standing there in the cold light of the walk-in, with the compressor humming and my heart going like a rabbit's, I had an idea. It wasn't a brilliant idea. It was a very small, very stubborn idea, the kind that comes from being hungry and tired and furious all at once.

I thought about my grandmother.

---

PART THREE: OMA'S RULE

My grandmother, my Oma, lived above a bakery in Rotterdam for fifty-one years. She cooked for nine people on a two-burner stove. She had one rule, which she repeated so often that it became a kind of weather in our family.

"Alles wat in een pannetje past, past in een pakketje."

Everything that fits in a pan fits in a parcel.

She meant it as a joke, mostly. She'd say it when we had leftovers, when the fridge was full of odds and ends, when the cousins showed up unannounced. She'd take whatever was in the pan, wrap it in dough or pastry or whatever was handy, and fry it until it shouted. A parcel, she said, was just a pan you could hold in your hand.

I'd forgotten that rule for years. I'd gone to culinary school, and learned the proper way to do things, and somewhere along the way I had decided that proper was the opposite of comforting.

But there in the walk-in, with a table of six waiting, I heard her voice as clearly as if she'd been standing behind me with her flour-dusted forearms and her wooden spoon.

Everything that fits in a pan fits in a parcel.

I grabbed the chicken. I grabbed the onions. I grabbed the tortillas.

"What are you doing?" Joris said.

"Plan B," I said.

"Is it ambitious?"

"No," I said. "It's crispy."

He opened his mouth to argue. Then he looked at the six-top, and he looked at the foam, and he closed it again.

---

PART FOUR: THE FILLING

I'm going to tell you exactly what I did, because I've been asked a thousand times, and because the recipe is the heart of the whole story.

First, the onions.

I diced one yellow onion small, smaller than you think you need to, because the filling had to be tender and not chunky. I put a heavy pan on a medium flame and dropped in a generous knob of butter. Not a polite knob. A real one, the kind Oma would have approved of. When it foamed and went quiet, I tipped in the onion and let it sweat.

This is the part people rush. Don't. The onion should go soft and translucent and just barely golden at the edges, and it takes longer than you want it to. Five minutes, maybe six. The kitchen filled with that sweet, buttery, almost-caramel smell that makes anyone within thirty feet suddenly very honest about being hungry.

Second, the chicken.

I cut the thighs into small pieces, about the size of a thumbnail. Small is the whole trick. Small means every piece catches the seasoning, every piece browns, and when you bite into the finished parcel you never get a big chewy chunk. You get tenderness all the way through.

I pushed the onions to the side and added the chicken to the hot pan in a single layer. It hissed. I left it alone. People stir too early, and the chicken steams instead of searing. I let it sit until the underside went pale gold, then turned it, then let it sit again.

Third, the seasoning, and here is where I got bold, because I had no time to be careful.

Smoked paprika, a big spoonful. Garlic powder. Salt. A little black pepper. A squeeze of the tomato paste, which I let fry for a minute in the fat until it darkened from bright red to the colour of a brick, because raw tomato paste tastes like a tin and cooked tomato paste tastes like a promise.

The whole pan turned the colour of a sunset. The chicken went deep orange, glossy and fragrant, and the smell changed from sweet to smoky to something almost dangerous.

Fourth, the sauce.

I poured in a splash of cream and stirred. It sizzled, then settled, then thickened around the chicken until every piece was coated in a velvety, rust-coloured gloss. A little hot sauce went in, just enough to wake it up. Then a big handful of the grated cheese, Bas's toastie cheese, stirred through until it melted into long, glossy strings.

I tasted it off the spoon.

I want to describe what happened, but it's hard. I've tried in interviews, and I always sound like I'm exaggerating. But the truth is that for about two seconds, the kitchen disappeared. The sound of the extractor fan, the clatter of Joris dropping a pan, the drip of the tap, all of it went silent. I was standing in my Oma's kitchen above the bakery in Rotterdam, nine years old, with flour on my nose.

It tasted like being looked after.

"Noor," Bas whispered. "Can I try?"

I gave him a spoon. He took a bite, and his eyes went wide, and he said a word in Dutch that I will not repeat in a family thread.

---

PART FIVE: THE PARCEL

I spread the filling on a tray to cool for a few minutes. You can't wrap hot filling. It tears the tortilla and steams the coating from the inside, and the whole thing goes soggy before it ever touches oil.

While it cooled, I mixed the glue.

This is the secret nobody expects. In a wide bowl I whisked flour with water and a pinch of salt until it was the texture of thin pancake batter, smooth and a little sticky. That's it. That's the glue, and it's also the first layer of the crust. Oma used to do something similar with flour and egg when she ran out of everything else.

Then I took a tortilla and laid it flat on the steel counter.

Here's how you fold a parcel that won't burst, and I learned this by failing on my first try, ten feet from a six-top that was starting to get restless. You put a spoonful of filling in the middle. Not a heaping spoonful. People overfill, and then the parcel leaks and the cheese escapes into the fryer and the oil spits at you like an angry cat. A good spoonful. A modest, confident spoonful.

Then you cut a slit from the edge of the tortilla to the centre, just one, like a radius. That slit is the whole architecture. It lets you fold the tortilla in quarters around the filling, one quadrant over the next, like closing a little book, until you have a neat square. Each fold gets a swipe of the flour glue so it sticks to itself.

"What's the ambitious part?" Joris said, hovering.

"The ambitious part," I said, "is that nobody will be able to put it down."

---

PART SIX: THE CRUNCH

Now the coating, which is the bit that makes grown adults go quiet.

Each parcel went into the flour batter, flipped to coat every side, then lifted out and dropped into a bowl of panko. I pressed. Hard. You have to press the crumbs into the surface with the heel of your hand, turn the parcel over, and press again, until no pale patch remains. Panko is a stubborn little thing. It likes to be told what to do.

When a parcel is properly crumbed, it looks like a golden brick of sand. It rustles when you handle it. It feels, honestly, a little silly, like you've dressed a sandwich in a winter coat.

Then the oil.

The fryer was a battered old pot of sunflower oil that Pieter swore by. I'd brought it up to temperature, hot enough that a breadcrumb dropped in sizzled instantly and danced. I laid two parcels in, gently, away from me, the way you lower a baby into a bath.

The oil roared.

Within thirty seconds, the surface turned from pale to blond to the colour of honey held up to a window. The crumbs lifted into tiny peaks and crags. The smell hit, and I'll never forget the smell: toasted breadcrumbs, browning butter, smoky paprika, hot oil, and underneath it all that sweet, savoury cheese note, the one that says home.

Three minutes. Maybe three and a half. I turned them once with tongs. When they came out they were deep golden, the colour of a good violin, and they crackled as they cooled on the rack. I swear you could hear them. A tiny, glittering, tick-tick-tick as the crust contracted.

Bas, who had not said anything for a full minute, finally said, "Noor, that is the best thing I have ever seen."

I cut one open on the board.

Steam poured out. And then the cheese, that glorious, glossy, rust-red cheese, stretched out in long ropes as I pulled the halves apart, the chicken tumbling out in tender, saucy pieces, the crust shattering softly under the knife. It did the thing. You know the thing. The slow-motion cheese pull that makes people reach for their phones.

I plated it on a warm white dish with a spoonful of garlic yogurt, which I'd stirred together in thirty seconds from the sad little tub, with chopped spring onion and a pinch of salt, and a small dish of hot sauce thinned out with a little honey from Pieter's private jar. I sprinkled chives, because we had them, because garnish is just hope in green.

"Table four," I said. "Plan B."

---

PART SEVEN: THE SIX-TOP

I didn't go into the dining room. Sous-chefs don't, as a rule. We live in the heat and the noise and we send our work out through a little hatch and trust the waiters to tell us what happened.

The waiter that night was a girl named Femke, twenty-two, fierce, fast, and tired of being lied to by menus. She took the plates out on her forearm like a magician. I watched her through the hatch. I watched her set them down. I watched six faces look at the parcels, puzzled, and then I watched the first person, a woman in a green dress, pick hers up with her hands.

Her hands. Not her fork.

She bit into it. And I saw her shoulders drop, just a little, the way a person's shoulders drop when they finally sit down after a long day.

Then the table went quiet.

I know that quiet. Every cook knows it. It is the sweetest sound in the world, sweeter than applause, the sound of six people forgetting to talk because their mouths are busy.

Femke came back to the kitchen about four minutes later. She stood in the doorway for a moment. She had an odd look on her face.

"They want twelve more," she said.

"Twelve?"

"Twelve. And the man in the grey jacket asked who made it. I said the sous-chef. He said, 'Tell her to come out.'"

I looked at Joris.

Joris looked at the floor.

---

PART EIGHT: NINE FORTY-SEVEN

Here's the part I didn't see coming.

I'd like to say Joris was happy for me. That we hugged. That he put an arm around my shoulders and said "well done, Noor," and we cooked the rest of the service side by side like a team.

What actually happened is that Joris went white, then red, then a strange flat grey, the colour of a man doing arithmetic and not liking the answer. He'd spent four hours designing an ambitious menu and the thing his table wanted was a fried tortilla.

"You're not going out there," he said.

"Chef, they asked—"

"I'm the head chef. I take the credit. I take the bow. You're the sous-chef. You stay in the kitchen."

"It's not about credit."

"It's about the pecking order," he said, and his voice had gone quiet and strange. "You don't get to make a dish like that on my watch and walk out into my dining room like you're the one who runs this place."

Something in me, something small and stubborn and very much like my grandmother, simply stood up.

"I'm going out there," I said.

And I untied my apron, folded it, set it on the steel counter, and walked through the swing door into the dining room.

I will remember the next ninety seconds until I die.

The man in the grey jacket stood up. He was somewhere in his fifties, tall, thin, with silver hair and reading glasses pushed up on his forehead and a napkin still tucked into his collar like a baby's bib. He took my hand in both of his.

"Did you make this?" he said.

"Yes."

"Where did you learn it?"

"My grandmother," I said. "Everything that fits in a pan fits in a parcel."

He laughed, a big, helpless, delighted laugh. And at that moment, behind me, the kitchen door swung open and Joris came through it like a storm.

"That's enough," Joris said. "Noor. Back to the kitchen. Now."

The man in the grey jacket looked at Joris. He looked at me. He looked at the plates, wiped clean, a few golden crumbs scattered like confetti.

"I think," he said gently, "she's fine where she is."

Joris took a step forward. The room went still. And then, in front of six guests, three other tables, a waitress, and a paperback-reading stranger who had slowly lowered his book, my head chef said the sentence that I will never, ever forget.

"If you walk out of that kitchen again, you're done here."

I looked at him. I looked at Pieter, who had appeared in the doorway of the bar, cardigan and all, with an expression I couldn't read.

I looked at my hands, still smelling faintly of paprika and butter.

"Then I'm done," I said.

It was 9:47 p.m.

---

PART NINE: THE ALLEY

There's a particular silence that follows you out of a room after you've quit a job. It's not peaceful. It's the silence of a held breath, of everyone waiting to see whether you'll cry.

I didn't cry. I walked through the dining room, past the green-dress woman who mouthed "thank you," past Femke who had her hand over her mouth, past the swing door and the steel counter and Bas, who stood frozen with a dish towel in his hands. I took my knife roll off its hook. I put on my coat. I went out the back door into the alley, and the rain leaned on me like an old friend.

I stood there for maybe a minute, breathing. The alley smelled of wet cardboard and frying oil. Somewhere above me a window was open, and a radio was playing a song I half recognised.

I had six years in that kitchen. I had my whole identity in that kitchen. And I'd just thrown it away for a tortilla.

The back door opened behind me.

I turned, expecting Joris, expecting a fight, expecting an apology that wasn't an apology.

It was the man in the grey jacket, with his napkin still in his collar.

"I'm sorry," he said. "I'm Anders Lindqvist. I've been eating in this city for thirty years, and I have never, not once, seen a plate of food go down a table like that. May I ask you something?"

"Sure," I said, in a voice that sounded like it belonged to someone else.

"What are you going to do now?"

"I have no idea."

"Good," he said, and he smiled. "That's the right answer. Do you have a kitchen?"

"I have a knife roll and a bicycle."

"That's more than most people start with."

---

PART TEN: THE KITCHEN AT THE END OF THE WORLD

Anders Lindqvist, it turned out, was not a stranger. He was the owner of a small group of places in Amsterdam and Rotterdam, a food hall, two canteens, a bar that did lunch. He'd come to Utrecht that night for a friend's birthday, the green-dress woman, and had ordered a plate of Joris's ambitious chicken expecting nothing at all.

"I'd like to buy you a drink," he said. "And I'd like to ask you to cook for me again. Properly. Tomorrow, if you can."

"I don't have a kitchen," I said again.

"I have one. It's in a basement behind a bike shop. It's ugly, and it leaks, and nobody uses it on Wednesdays."

I said yes. The next morning I took the train to Amsterdam with a bag of chicken thighs, three onions, and a pack of tortillas I'd bought at a corner shop. The basement was exactly as ugly as promised. The tiles were cracked, the extractor wheezed, and one of the burners lit only if you talked to it nicely. But the space was clean, and the oil was fresh, and Anders had set out a long steel table with six empty chairs.

Six people, he said, were coming to eat. Friends. Suppliers. A woman from a food magazine. He didn't tell me who was who.

I carried the plate out myself this time.

They ate. They went quiet. The woman from the magazine closed her notebook halfway through the second parcel and never opened it again.

At the end, Anders leaned back in his chair and tapped the table with one finger.

"How many of these," he said, "can you make in an hour?"

---

PART ELEVEN: FRIDAY

I told you three restaurants were fighting over the recipe by Friday. I wasn't exaggerating, though it was less glamorous than it sounds.

What happened is that the woman from the magazine posted a single photograph, a cross-section of a parcel, cheese stretched like a golden rope, steam curling off it, with one line of caption: "I have no words. Go to this basement."

By Thursday night there was a queue outside the bike shop. By Friday there were two. People brought their kids. A man cycled forty minutes from Haarlem and told me, with tears in his eyes, that it tasted like something his mother used to make before he'd forgotten her recipe. I made three hundred and twelve parcels that Friday, with Bas, who had quit his dishwashing job the day after I did and turned up at the basement door with a bag and a grin.

We named the place nothing. Anders insisted on a sign, and in a moment of exhaustion I wrote the only thing I could think of on a scrap of cardboard: "Pakketjes." Parcels.

It stayed.

---

PART TWELVE: WHAT HAPPENED TO JORIS

I know you want to know. Everyone wants to know about the villain.

Joris called me in January. I almost didn't answer.

He didn't apologise, exactly. He's not that kind of man. But he said, in a flat voice, "I tried to make your wrap. I couldn't get the crust right."

"Press harder," I said. "Press the panko in with the heel of your hand. And don't overfill them."

There was a long silence.

"Thanks," he said.

"Sure, Chef," I said, and for the first time in my life, I said it as a joke, and he laughed, a small helpless laugh, and I hung up and stood in the basement kitchen with a spatula in my hand and felt something heavy finally set itself down.

---

PART THIRTEEN: THE RECIPE, FOR YOU

I promised myself I'd end this thread with the thing people ask for most. So here it is, as plainly as I can say it, with no secrets held back.

You need: one onion, diced small. Butter. Chicken thighs, boneless, cut into thumbnail pieces. Smoked paprika, garlic powder, salt, pepper, a squeeze of tomato paste. A splash of cream. A little hot sauce. A handful of grated cheese. Large soft tortillas. Flour and water for the glue. Panko for the crust. Oil for frying. Yogurt, chives and spring onion for the dip.

Sweat the onion in butter until it's soft. Sear the chicken in a single layer and leave it alone. Add the spices, fry the tomato paste until it darkens, pour in the cream, melt in the cheese, cool it completely. Cut a slit to the centre of a tortilla, spoon a modest scoop of filling in the middle, fold in quarters with a swipe of flour glue between folds. Dip in the batter. Press into panko with the heel of your hand. Fry at medium-high heat, three minutes, turn once, until the colour of a good violin.

Cut it open. Watch the cheese pull. Share it with somebody.

That's it. That's the whole secret. Everything that fits in a pan fits in a parcel.

---

PART FOURTEEN: THE LAST THING

I used to think that night was the worst of my career. I thought I'd been fired, humiliated, cast out. I used to tell it as a story of loss.

But the truth is, I wasn't fired. I stood up. And the only reason I could stand up was a woman who lived above a bakery in Rotterdam for fifty-one years, who cooked for nine people on two burners, and who taught me, without ever explaining it, that comfort isn't the opposite of skill. It is the highest form of it.

Oma died the spring before all this. I never got to tell her. So I'll tell you instead, whoever you are, reading this far down a very long thread: cook the thing that tastes like being looked after. Cook it for someone who's had a bad day. Press the crumbs in hard. Don't be afraid of the oil.

And if somebody tells you to stay in the kitchen, remember that sometimes the kitchen is exactly the place you have to leave, with your knife roll and your bicycle, in the rain, at 9:47 on a Tuesday night.

The door was green. The paint looked like frosting. The best thing I ever made came out of a pantry nobody believed in.

If this thread made you hungry, you know what to do. 🥡

THE END.

Do you think we have a fair court system? Ever been in it? It’s all in the NAME. Your Rights Have a Diplomatic Exception: Legal Fockery Is Everywhere!

Whatever your opinion is of the Tate brother’s being incarcerated, I hope that every American stands behind their lawful rights. Notice I didn’t say “legal”. Legal and lawful are not the same thing.

Legal is what you agree to. Lawful is what are your natural rights.

Read this sentence slowly. It comes from a brief the U.S. Department of Justice filed in federal court on October 23, 2026:

“Individual liberties, so carefully protected in domestic criminal proceedings, sometimes must yield to paramount national interests in preserving harmonious working relations with foreign sovereigns.”

That’s the federal government telling a judge, in writing, that your freedom can be traded for diplomacy.

They wrote it about Andrew and Tristan Tate. They wouldn’t have to change a word to use it on you.

This isn’t about the Tates

I’m not here to defend anyone’s character or try anyone’s case. Courts in three countries will do that.

I’m here to show you the machine, because the machine doesn’t care who you are.

The Tate brothers were arrested in Miami on July 18, 2026, at the United Kingdom’s request. They have been in a federal detention center ever since. Their extradition hearing isn’t until January 2027.

They haven’t been convicted of anything, anywhere.

The bail law Congress never wrote

In a normal federal criminal case, the Bail Reform Act controls. The government has to justify holding you.

The Bail Reform Act doesn’t apply to extradition. It only covers people accused of breaking U.S. law.

So what applies? The DOJ admitted it in its own brief: neither the extradition treaty nor the extradition statute provides for bail at all.

The rule holding these men comes from judges. It started with one Supreme Court case in 1903. Courts have built on it ever since, and they call the result “federal common law.” See how they use the common law when it suits them? It’s supposed to suit the defendant, you know the living man with rights.

Under that judge-made rule, the burden is flipped. The person in the cell has to prove he won’t flee and isn’t dangerous. Then he has to prove “special circumstances” on top of that.

What counts as special? The DOJ conceded in the same brief that courts “have not developed a consistent definition.”

Your liberty turns on a test nobody can define, which Congress never voted on.

The magic word: “not criminal”

This is the part I want you to remember.

The DOJ’s entire argument rests on one label. It says extradition proceedings are “not criminal.”

Once it’s “not criminal,” watch what disappears:

The Federal Rules of Evidence don’t apply.

The Federal Rules of Criminal Procedure don’t apply.

There’s no right to a speedy trial.

There’s no cross-examining your accusers.

Discovery is restricted.

The hearing runs on paper from a foreign government.

But you’re still in a cell.

They don’t call it punishment. They call it a process. The cell doesn’t feel the difference.

You’ve seen this trick before

If you’ve ever dealt with the IRS, a state agency, or an administrative “hearing,” you’ve lived this.

The IRS says a collection matter is “civil.” The agency says your hearing is “administrative.” Each label quietly removes a protection you thought you had.

This is the fockery: they change the name of the proceeding, and the rights change with it. Most people never notice the swap until they’re already inside.

Who decides? Not the judge.

The extradition treaty allows a “provisional arrest” only in cases of urgency.

When the Tates’ lawyers challenged whether there was any real urgency, the DOJ argued the question is “non-justiciable.” That means the executive branch decides, and the court isn’t allowed to second-guess it.

So the government decides it’s urgent. The government arrests you. And the judge is told he can’t check its work.

And the government’s own paperwork?

The DOJ’s brief treats the brothers’ social media posts as proof of their wealth. Eleven pages later, it tells the court social media “is not a reliable indicator.”

It told the judge the extradition court would rule “in approximately four weeks.” The hearing is now set for January.

Its own exhibit, a letter from Romanian prosecutors, says the brothers “fully complied” with every condition and appeared at every summons.

The brief gives one count of charges against Andrew, and the U.K. letter attached to it gives another. One page dates the new charges to July, and another to August.

Across five filings in a habeas case, its lawyers called the petitioners “the Defendant.” In the brief itself: “Untied Kingdom.” “Threats of physical hard.”

This is the work being used to keep two unconvicted men in a federal cell.

The real lesson

The government doesn’t have to break the rules to take your rights. It only has to decide which set of rules applies.

“Not criminal.” “Civil.” “Administrative.” “Non-justiciable.” Each label is a door, and each one closes on a protection you assumed was yours.

The people who get hosed aren’t the ones who did something wrong. They’re the ones who didn’t know which room they were standing in.

Learn the rooms before you’re in one

At Legal Fockery University, we teach you to spot the label game before it’s played on you. You’ll learn what kind of proceeding you’re actually in, which rules really apply, and how to answer in writing when an agency comes knocking with its own definitions.

Don’t wait until the door closes. Know how the system works because it’s a “system” from traffic tickets, to divorce, child support, 3rd party debt collectors, mortgage fockery, every single reason a courthouse opens its doors daily.

One day you could be walking in unprepared and counting on an attorney who is simply trying to take as much money as possible from you in cahoots with his buddies he has martini’s with at the end of the day.

🚨🇭🇰 HONG KONG ACTIVATES AI FACIAL RECOGNITION ACROSS EXPANDING SURVEILLANCE NETWORK!

POLICE LAUNCH BIOMETRIC IDENTIFICATION TECHNOLOGY AS CITY TARGETS 60,000 CAMERAS BY 2028

NOVEMBER 16, 2026 | NTLD — NAVIGATING THE LAST DAYS
Hong Kong has activated artificial intelligence-powered facial recognition within its expanding SmartView police surveillance system, marking a significant development in the use of biometric monitoring across public spaces.

The rollout began Monday, November 16, according to Agence France-Presse (AFP), with the announcement confirmed by Hong Kong Police Commissioner Joe Chow Yat-ming.

The technology is intended to help police identify criminal suspects, investigate offenses and locate vulnerable missing persons.

HOW DOES THE SYSTEM WORK?

The SmartView surveillance network combines police-operated CCTV cameras with footage from other government agencies, transport facilities and participating private properties.

AI software can analyze images and compare facial characteristics to help identify individuals of interest.

Police say facial recognition can be activated for specific investigations rather than continuously processing every camera simultaneously.

60,000 CAMERAS BY 2028

Hong Kong authorities plan to expand the surveillance network to approximately 60,000 cameras by 2028.

That is a future target—not the number currently operating.

The SmartView program began in 2024, and police credit the existing network with helping investigate nearly 2,200 criminal cases and contributing to more than 2,800 arrests.

Those effectiveness figures are police-reported statistics.

FACIAL DATA STORED FOR UP TO 180 DAYS

According to Hong Kong public broadcaster RTHK, ordinary surveillance footage is generally retained for approximately one month.

However, certain facial-recognition records—including facial characteristics, location information and timestamps—may be stored for up to 180 days.

This longer retention period has raised questions about personal privacy, access controls and government oversight.

PRIVATE SHOPPING MALLS JOINING THE NETWORK

Police have also confirmed that at least four shopping malls have agreed to integrate their CCTV systems into SmartView.

The expansion could allow investigators to search footage across a wider range of public and privately operated locations.

WHY ARE PEOPLE CONCERNED?

Hong Kong authorities say the technology will strengthen public safety and accelerate investigations.

Critics warn that facial recognition can also enable extensive tracking of people's movements, create risks of mistaken identification and potentially be used to monitor political activity.

These concerns are especially significant given Hong Kong's national security legislation and restrictions on political dissent since the 2019 protests.

Police Commissioner Joe Chow has pledged that the technology will not be abused.

IMPORTANT DISTINCTION

The activation is confirmed.

However, there is no evidence that all 60,000 planned cameras are already installed or that every camera is continuously identifying everyone who passes.

BIBLE PERSPECTIVE — 1 THESSALONIANS 5:21 (KJV)

“Prove all things; hold fast that which is good.”

From a Christian perspective, the expansion of biometric identification raises questions about privacy, individual liberty and the potential misuse of centralized authority.

Although some prophecy interpreters associate growing surveillance capabilities with the control systems described in Revelation 13, this development does not establish that the biblical mark of the beast has arrived.

• Insider Paper — November 16, 2026

• Radio Television Hong Kong (RTHK) — November 6, 2026

text:
On November 30, Chinese foreign ministry spokesman Lijian Zhao pinned an image to his Twitter profile. In it, a soldier stands on an Australian flag and grins maniacally as he holds a bloodied knife to a boy’s throat. The boy, whose face is covered by a semi-transparent veil, carries a lamb. Alongside the image, Zhao tweeted, “Shocked by murder of Afghan civilians & prisoners by Australian soldiers. We strongly condemn such acts, &call [sic] for holding them accountable.”

The tweet is referencing a recent announcement by the Australian Defence Force, which found “credible information” that 25 Australian soldiers were involved in the murders of 39 Afghan civilians and prisoners between 2009 and 2013. The image purports to show an Australian soldier about to slit the throat of an innocent Afghan child. Explosive stuff.

Except the image is fake. Upon closer examination, it’s not even very convincing. It could have been put together by a Photoshop novice. This image is a so-called cheapfake, a piece of media that has been crudely manipulated, edited, mislabeled, or improperly contextualized in order to spread disinformation.

The cheapfake is now at the heart of a major international incident. Australia’s prime minister, Scott Morrison, said China should be “utterly ashamed” and demanded an apology for the “repugnant” image. Beijing has refused, instead accusing Australia of “barbarism” and of trying to “deflect public attention” from alleged war crimes by its armed forces in Afghanistan.

There are two important political lessons to draw from this incident. The first is that Beijing sanctioned the use of a cheapfake by one of its top diplomats to actively spread disinformation on Western online platforms. China has traditionally exercised caution in such matters, aiming to present itself as a benign and responsible superpower. This new approach is a significant departure.

More broadly, however, this skirmish also shows the growing importance of visual disinformation as a political tool. Over the last decade, the proliferation of manipulated media has reshaped political realities. (Consider, for instance, the cheapfakes that catalyzed a genocide against the Rohingya Muslims in Burma, or helped spread covid disinformation.) Now that global superpowers are openly sharing cheapfakes on social media, what’s to stop them (or any other actor) from deploying more sophisticated visual disinformation as it emerges?

For years, journalists and technologists have warned about the dangers of “deepfakes.” Broadly, deepfakes are a type of “synthetic media’” that has been manipulated or created by artificial intelligence. They can also be understood as the “superior” successor to cheapfakes.

Technological advances are simultaneously improving the quality of visual disinformation and making it easier for anyone to generate. As it becomes possible to produce deepfakes through smartphone apps, almost anyone will be able to create sophisticated visual disinformation at next to no cost.

False alarm

Deepfake warnings reached a fever pitch ahead of the US presidential election this year. For months, politicians, journalists, and academics debated how to counter the perceived threat. In the run-up to the vote, state legislatures in Texas and California even preemptively outlawed the use of deepfakes to sway elections.

In retrospect, these fears were overstated. Apart from a few interesting developments, including a tongue-in-cheek creation by the Russian-state broadcaster Russia Today (RT) in which a defeated Donald Trump admits to being Russian president Vladimir Putin’s pawn, there was little election-related deepfakery to report. Certainly nothing materialized that could be objectively said to have swayed the outcome. Rather than being used to sabotage or exploit politicians, deepfakes are still most often used to create nonconsensual porn.

Although deepfakes haven’t yet become the weapons of mass disinformation that some predicted, there’s no room for complacency. The potential risk is largely mitigated, for now, by technical limitations. As deepfake-creation technologies improve, the floodgates will open.

And even before then, the mere awareness of deepfakes is already having a harmful effect. In the near future, bad actors will be able to produce deepfakes about everything, and simply dismiss any authentic media as fake. This “double bonus” for bad actors is known as the “liar’s dividend.” Although the term was coined in a seminal 2018 paper on deepfakes, it doesn’t pertain to deepfakes alone. The concept extends to all disinformation, including cheapfakes.

Cheapfakes everywhere

Since the infamous doctored video of House Speaker Nancy Pelosi appeared in 2019, cheapfakes have become a regular feature of US political life. This year, they helped sustain a high-profile disinformation operation advanced by the president and his closest associates. The false assertion that the election was marred by widespread voter fraud was consistently reinforced by cheapfakes.

One example is a viral video of President-elect Joe Biden saying, “We have put together, I think, the most extensive and inclusive voter fraud organization in the history of American politics.” When properly contextualized, Biden’s comments can be understood as describing a program to protect voters in the event of baseless litigation regarding the election result. Nonetheless, the clip was shared by both Trump and press secretary Kayleigh McEnany and portrayed as an admission of fraud.

Even as votes were still being counted, authentic videos of election workers transcribing votes and collecting ballots in a routine manner were shared, by people including Trump himself, as “evidence” of vote dumping and tampering. Meanwhile, a viral cheapfake showing a man “tearing up” ballots turned out to be the work of a TikTok prankster.

The allegations of widespread voter fraud are baseless, and courts across America are dismissing attempts by Trump’s legal team to dispute the election result. Earlier this month, Attorney General Bill Barr (who steps down on December 23) finally admitted that the US Justice Department has uncovered no evidence of fraud.

But cheapfakes appear to have had real-world consequences: in early December, Gabriel Sterling, Georgia’s voting-system implementation manager, cited instances of intimidation and death threats against election workers, pleading, “It’s all gone too far! It has to stop!” A Georgia election worker had to go into hiding after a 34-second cheapfake that falsely accused him of throwing away an absentee ballot went viral.

Belief in the narrative of the “rigged election” falls starkly along partisan lines. A Politico/Morning Consult poll conducted after the election found that 70% of Republican voters said they did not believe it had been “free and fair.” The number of GOP voters expressing similar distrust of the process before the election was 35%. Conversely, only half of Democratic voters (52%) said they believed the election would be “free and fair” before November 3. In polls conducted after Biden’s victory, the figure skyrocketed to 90%.

What to believe?

The growing prevalence of visual disinformation appears to be affecting politics in two distinct ways. First, it’s feeding the proliferation of all kinds of disinformation. Bad actors are acting with more impunity, confident that they can avoid scrutiny and accountability. At the time of writing, the cheapfake shared by Lijian Zhao was still pinned to his Twitter profile.

Second, the growing prevalence of visual disinformation makes us more susceptible to all disinformation. As the public becomes more aware of the many ways in which media can be manipulated, it will become more skeptical of all media, including authentic media.

This skepticism makes it easier for bad actors to dismiss real events as fake. It may also lead to increasingly subjective and partisan interpretations of events by the public itself. Consider, for example, the widely held belief among Republican voters that the 2020 US election was not free and fair. This is demonstrably false, but as public opinion data suggests, it’s not only Republicans voters who distrust the electoral process. Until they won, Democratic voters were also skeptical. If a Republican candidate wins in 2024, will public opinion flip again along partisan lines?

While the most dire predictions about politically motivated deepfakes were not realized in 2020, we must analyze their evolution in the context of cheapfakes and other forms of political disinformation. The cheapfakes of today offer valuable lessons about the deepfakes of the future. The question, then, should not be “When will political deepfakes emerge?” but “How we can mitigate the many ways in which visual disinformation is already reshaping our political reality?”

Nina Schick is the author of Deepfakes: The Coming Infocalypse.
